rapidly.c: Rapidly Rap"id*ly (răp"ĭd*ly̆), adv. In a rapid manner.

rapidness.c: Rapidness Rap"id*ness, n. Quality of being rapid; rapidity.

rapier.c: Rapier Ra"pi*er (rā"pĭ*ẽr), n. [F. rapière, perhaps for raspière, and ultimately of German origin, akin to E. rasp, v.] A straight sword, with a narrow and finely pointed blade, used only for thrusting.

rapiered.c: Rapiered Ra"pi*ered (-ẽrd), a. Wearing a rapier. “Scarletcoated, rapiered figures.” Lowell.

rapine.c: Rapine Rap"ine (răp"ĭn), n. [F. rapine; cf. Pr. & It. rapina; all fr. L. rapina, fr. rapere to seize and carry off by force. See Rapid, and cf. Raven rapine.] 1. The act of plundering; the seizing and carrying away of things by force; spoliation; pillage; plunder.
Rapine Rap"ine, v. t. To plunder. Sir G. Buck.

rappage.c: Rappage Rap"page (răp"paj; 48), n. (Founding) The enlargement of a mold caused by rapping the pattern.

rapparee.c: Rapparee Rap`pa*ree" (-pȧ*rē"), n. A wild Irish plunderer, esp. one of the 17th century; -- so called from his carrying a half-pike, called a rapary. [Written also raparee.]

rapped.c: Rapped Rapped (răpt), imp. & p. p. of Rap, to strike.
Rapped Rapped, imp. & p. p. of Rap, to snatch away.

rappee.c: Rappee Rap*pee" (răp*pē"), n. [F. râpé, fr. râper to grate, to rasp. See Rasp, v.] A pungent kind of snuff made from the darker and ranker kinds of tobacco leaves.

rappel.c: Rappel Rap"pel (răp"pĕl or răp*pĕl"), n. [F. Cf. Repeal.] (Mil.) The beat of the drum to call soldiers to arms.

rapper.c: Rapper Rap"per (răp"pẽr), n. [From Rap.] 1. One who, or that which, raps or knocks; specifically, the knocker of a door. Sterne.

rapport.c: Rapport Rap*port" (răp*pōrt"; F. rȧ`pôr"), n. [F., fr. rapporter to bring again or back, to refer; pref. re- re- + apporter to bring, L. apportare. Cf. Report.] Relation; proportion; conformity; correspondence; accord.

rapprochement.c: Rapprochement ‖Rap`proche`ment" (?), n. [F., fr. rapprocher to cause to approach again. See Re-; Approach.] Act or fact of coming or being drawn near or together; establishment or state of cordial relations.

rapscallion.c: Rapscallion Rap*scal"lion (răp*skăl"yŭn), n. [See Rascallion.] A rascal; a good-for-nothing fellow. [Colloq.] Howitt.

rapt.c: Rapt Rapt (răpt), imp. & p. p. of Rap, to snatch away.
Rapt Rapt, a. 1. Snatched away; hurried away or along.
Rapt Rapt, n. [From F. rapt abduction, rape, L. raptus, fr. rapere to seize and carry off, to transport; or fr. E. rapt, a. See Rapt, a., and Rapid.] 1. An ecstasy; a trance. [Obs.] Bp. Morton.
Rapt Rapt, v. t. 1. To transport or ravish. [Obs.] Drayton.

raptor.c: Raptor Rap"tor (răp"tẽr), n. [L. raptor, from rapere to ravish. See Rapid.] A ravisher; a plunderer. [Obs.]

raptores.c: Raptores ‖Rap*to"res (răp*tō"rēz), n. pl. [NL. See Raptor.] (Zool.) An order of birds, same as Accipitres. Called also Raptatores.

raptorial.c: Raptorial Rap*to"ri*al (răp*tō"rĭ*ail), a. (Zool.) (a) Rapacious; living upon prey; -- said especially of certain birds. (b) Adapted for seizing prey; -- said of the legs, claws, etc., of insects, birds, and other animals. (c) Of or pertaining to the Raptores. See Illust. (f) of Aves.

rapture.c: Rapture Rap"ture (răp"tur; 135), n. [L. rapere, raptum, to carry off by force. See Rapid.] 1. A seizing by violence; a hurrying along; rapidity with violence. [Obs.]
Rapture Rap"ture, v. t. [imp. & p. p. Raptured (-turd; 135); p. pr. & vb. n. Rapturing.] To transport with excitement; to enrapture. [Poetic] Thomson.

rapturist.c: Rapturist Rap"tur*ist, n. An enthusiast. [Obs.] J. Spencer.

rapturize.c: Rapturize Rap"tur*ize (-īz), v. t. & i. To put, or be put, in a state of rapture. [R.]

rapturous.c: Rapturous Rap"tur*ous (-ŭs), a. Ecstatic; transporting; ravishing; feeling, expressing, or manifesting rapture; as, rapturous joy, pleasure, or delight; rapturous applause.

rapturously.c: Rapturously Rap"tur*ous*ly, adv. In a rapturous manner.

rare.c: Rare Rare, a. [Compar. Rarer (râr"ẽr); superl. Rarest.] [Cf. AS. hrēr, or E. rare early. √18.] Nearly raw; partially cooked; not thoroughly cooked; underdone; as, rare beef or mutton.
Rare Rare, a. [Compar. Rarer (râr"ẽr); superl. Rarest.] [F., fr. L. rarus thin, rare.] 1. Not frequent; seldom met with or occurring; unusual; as, a rare event.

rarebit.c: Rarebit Rare"bit (râr"bĭt), n. A dainty morsel; a Welsh rabbit. See Welsh rabbit, under Rabbit.

rareeshow.c: Raree-show Rar"ee-show` (râr"e-shō`), n. [Contr. fr. rarity-show.] A show carried about in a box; a peep show. Pope.

rarefaction.c: Rarefaction Rar`e*fac"tion (răr`e*făk"shŭn), n. [Cf. F. raréfaction. See Rarefy.] The act or process of rarefying; the state of being rarefied; -- opposed to condensation; as, the rarefaction of air.

rarefiable.c: Rarefiable Rar"e*fi`a*ble (răr"e*fī`ȧ*b'l), a. [Cf. F. raréfiable.] Capable of being rarefied. Boyle.

rarefy.c: Rarefy Rar"e*fy (răr"e*fī; 277), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Rarefied (răr"e*fīd); p. pr. & vb. n. Rarefying (răr"e*fī`ĭng).] [F. raréfier; L. rarus rare + -ficare (in comp.) to make; cf. L. rarefacere. See -fy.] To make rare, thin, porous, or less dense; to expand or enlarge without adding any new portion of matter to; -- opposed to condense.
Rarefy Rar"e*fy, v. i. To become less dense; to become thin and porous. “Earth rarefies to dew.” Dryden.

rarely.c: Rarely Rare"ly (râr"ly̆), adv. 1. In a rare manner or degree; seldom; not often; as, things rarely seen.

rareness.c: Rareness Rare"ness, n. The state or quality of being rare.

rareripe.c: Rareripe Rare"ripe` (-rīp`), a. [Rare early + ripe. Cf. Rathripe.] Early ripe; ripe before others, or before the usual season.
Rareripe Rare"ripe`, n. An early ripening fruit, especially a kind of freestone peach.

rarification.c: Rarification Rar`i*fi*ca"tion (răr`ĭ*fĭ*kā"shŭn), n. See Rarefaction. [R.] Am. Chem. Journal.

rarity.c: Rarity Rar"i*ty (răr"ĭ*ty̆; 277), n.; pl. Rarities (răr"ĭ*tĭz). [L. raritas: cf. F. rareté. See Rare.] 1. The quality or state of being rare; rareness; thinness; as, the rarity (contrasted with the density) of gases.

rasante.c: Rasante ‖Ra`sante" (rȧ`zäNt"), a. [F., p. pr. of raser to graze.] (Fort.) Sweeping; grazing; -- applied to a style of fortification in which the command of the works over each other, and over the country, is kept very low, in order that the shot may more effectually sweep or graze the ground before them. H. L. Scott.

rascal.c: Rascal Ras"cal (răs"kail), n. [OE. rascaille rabble, probably from an OF. racaille, F. racaille the rabble, rubbish, probably akin to F. racler to scrape, (assumed) LL. rasiculare, rasicare, fr. L. radere, rasum. See Rase, v.]
Rascal Ras"cal, a. Of or pertaining to the common herd or common people; low; mean; base. “The rascal many.” Spencer. “The rascal people.” Shak.

rascaldom.c: Rascaldom Ras"cal*dom (-dŭm), n. State of being a rascal; rascality; domain of rascals; rascals, collectively. Emerson.

rascallion.c: Rascallion Ras*cal"lion (răs*kăl"yŭn), n. [From Rascal] A low, mean wretch; a rogue; same as rascal, n.. 2; now disused, replaced by rapscalion. [archaic] [Written also rascalion.]

rascally.c: Rascally Ras"cal*ly (răs"kail*ly̆), a. Like a rascal; trickish or dishonest; base; worthless; -- often in humorous disparagement, without implication of dishonesty.

rase.c: Rase Rase (rāz), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Rased (rāzd); p. pr. & vb. n. Rasing.] [F. raser, LL. rasare to scrape often, v. freq. fr. L. radere, rasum, to scrape, shave; cf. Skr. rad to scratch, gnaw, L. rodere to gnaw. Cf. Raze, Razee, Razor, Rodent.] 1. To rub along the surface of; to graze. [Obsoles.]
Rase Rase, v. i. To be leveled with the ground; to fall; to suffer overthrow. [Obs.]
Rase Rase, n. 1. A scratching out, or erasure. [Obs.]

rash.c: Rash Rash (răsh), v. t. [For arace.] 1. To pull off or pluck violently. [Obs.]

Rash Rash, n. [OF. rasche an eruption, scurf, F. rache; fr. (assumed) LL. rasicare to scratch, fr. L. radere, rasum, to scrape, scratch, shave. See Rase, and cf. Rascal.] (Med.) A fine eruption or efflorescence on the body, with little or no elevation.

Rash Rash, n. [Cf. F. ras short-nap cloth, It. & Sp. raso satin (cf. Rase); or cf. It. rascia serge, G. rasch, probably fr. Arras in France (cf. Arras).] An inferior kind of silk, or mixture of silk and worsted. [Obs.] Donne.

Rash Rash, a. [Compar. Rasher (-ẽr); superl. Rashest.] [Probably of Scand. origin; cf. Dan. & Sw. rask quick, brisk, rash, Icel. röskr vigorous, brave, akin to D. & G. rasch quick, of uncertain origin.] 1. Sudden in action; quick; hasty. [Obs.] “Strong as aconitum or rash gunpowder.” Shak.
Rash Rash (răsh), v. t. To prepare with haste. [Obs.] Foxe.

rasher.c: Rasher Rash"er (răsh"ẽr), n. [In sense 1, probably fr. rash, a., as being hastily cooked.] 1. A thin slice of bacon.

rashly.c: Rashly Rash"ly, adv. In a rash manner; with precipitation.

rashness.c: Rashness Rash"ness, n. The quality or state of being rash.

raskolnik.c: Raskolnik ‖Ras*kol"nik (răs*kŏl"nĭk), n.; pl. Raskolniki (răs*kŏl"nĭk*ē) or Raskolniks (#). [Russ. raskol'nik dissenter, fr. raskol dissent.] The name applied by the Russian government to any subject of the Greek faith who dissents from the established church. The Raskolniki embrace many sects, whose common characteristic is a clinging to antique traditions, habits, and customs. The schism originated in 1667 in an ecclesiastical dispute as to the correctness of the translation of the religious books. The dissenters, who have been continually persecuted, are believed to number about 20,000,000, although the Holy Synod officially puts the number at about 2,000,000. They are officially divided into three groups according to the degree of their variance from orthodox beliefs and observances, as follows: I. “Most obnoxious.” the Judaizers; the Molokane, who refuse to recognize civil authority or to take oaths; the Dukhobortsy, or Dukhobors, who are communistic, marry without ceremony, and believe that Christ was human, but that his soul reappears at intervals in living men; the Khlysty, who countenance anthropolatory, are ascetics, practice continual self-flagellation, and reject marriage; the Skoptsy, who practice castration; and a section of the Bezpopovtsy, or priestless sect, which disbelieve in prayers for the Czar and in marriage. II. “Obnoxious:” the Bezpopovtsy, who pray for the Czar and recognize marriage. III. “Least obnoxious:” the Popovtsy, who dissent from the orthodox church in minor points only. [Written also rascolnik.]

rasores.c: Rasores ‖Ra*so"res (rȧ*zō"rēz), n. pl. [NL., fr. L. radere, rasum, to scratch. See Rase, v. t.] (Zool.) An order of birds; the Gallinae.

rasorial.c: Rasorial Ra*so"ri*al (rȧ*zō"rĭ*ail; 277), a. (Zool.) Of or pertaining to the Rasores, or gallinaceous birds, as the peacock, domestic fowl, partridge, quail, and the like.

rasp.c: Rasp Rasp (rȧsp), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Rasped (rȧspt); p. pr. & vb. n. Rasping.] [OF. rasper, F. râper, to scrape, grate, rasp, fr. OHG. raspōn to scrape together, to collect, probably akin to E. rap. Cf. Rap to snatch.]
Rasp Rasp, n. [OE. raspe, OF. raspe, F. râpe. See Rasp, v.]

raspatory.c: Raspatory Rasp"a*to*ry (rȧsp"ȧ*to*ry̆), n. [LL. raspatorium: cf. F. raspatoir. See Rasp, v.] A surgeon's rasp. Wiseman.

raspberry.c: Raspberry Rasp"ber*ry (răz"bĕr*ry̆; 277), n. [From E. rasp, in allusion to the apparent roughness of the fruit.] (Bot.) (a) The thimble-shaped fruit of the Rubus Idaeus and other similar brambles; as, the black, the red, and the white raspberry. (b) The shrub bearing this fruit.

rasper.c: Rasper Rasp"er (rȧsp"ẽr), n. One who, or that which, rasps; a scraper.

raspy.c: Raspy Rasp"y (rȧsp"y̆), a. Like a rasp, or the sound made by a rasp; grating. R. D. Blackmore.

rasse.c: Rasse Rasse (răs), n. [Cf. Malay rāsa taste, sensation.] (Zool.) A carnivore (Viverricula Mallaccensis) allied to the civet but smaller, native of China and the East Indies. It furnishes a perfume resembling that of the civet, which is highly prized by the Javanese. Called also Malacca weasel, and lesser civet.

rasure.c: Rasure Ra"sure (rā"zhur; 135), n. [L. rasura, fr. radere, rasum, to scrape, to shave. See Rase, v.] 1. The act of rasing, scraping, or erasing; erasure; obliteration.

rat.c: Rat Rat (răt), n. [AS. ræt; akin to D. rat, OHG. rato, ratta, G. ratte, ratze, OLG. ratta, LG. & Dan. rotte, Sw. råtta, F. rat, Ir. & Gael radan, Armor. raz, of unknown origin. Cf. Raccoon.] 1. (Zool.) One of several species of small rodents of the genus Rattus (formerly included in Mus) and allied genera, of the family Muridae, distinguished from mice primarily by being larger. They infest houses, stores, and ships, especially the Norway rat, also called brown rat, (Rattus norvegicus formerly Mus decumanus), the black rat (Rattus rattus formerly Mus rattus), and the roof rat (formerly Mus Alexandrinus, now included in Rattus rattus). These were introduced into America from the Old World. The white rat used most commonly in laboratories is primarily a strain derived from Rattus rattus.

Rat Rat, v. i. [imp. & p. p. Ratted; p. pr. & vb. n. Ratting.] 1. In English politics, to desert one's party from interested motives; to forsake one's associates for one's own advantage; in the trades, to work for less wages, or on other conditions, than those established by a trades union.

rata.c: Rata Ra"ta (rä"tȧ), n. [Maori.] (Bot.) A New Zealand forest tree (Metrosideros robusta), also, its hard dark red wood, used by the Maoris for paddles and war clubs.

ratability.c: Ratability Rat`a*bil"i*ty (rāt`ȧ*bĭl"ĭ*ty̆), n. The quality or state of being ratable.

ratable.c: Ratable Rat"a*ble (rāt"ȧ*b'l), a. 1. Capable of being rated, or set at a certain value.

ratafia.c: Ratafia Rat`a*fi"a (răt`ȧ*fē"ȧ), n. [F., fr. Malay arak arrack + tāfīa a spirit distilled from molasses.] A spirituous liquor flavored with the kernels of cherries, apricots, peaches, or other fruit, spiced, and sweetened with sugar; -- a term applied to the liqueurs called noyau, curaçao, etc. [Written also ratifia and ratafee.]

rataplan.c: Rataplan ‖Ra`ta`plan" (rȧ`tȧ`pläN"), n. [F.] The iterative sound of beating a drum, or of a galloping horse.

ratch.c: Ratch Ratch (răch), n. [See Rack the instrument, Ratchet.] A ratchet wheel, or notched bar, with which a pawl or click works.

ratchet.c: Ratchet Ratch"et (-ĕt), n. [Properly a diminutive from the same word as rack: cf. F. rochet. See 2d Ratch, Rack the instrument.] 1. A pawl, click, or detent, for holding or propelling a ratchet wheel, or ratch, etc.

rate.c: Rate Rate (rāt), v. t. & i. [Perh. fr. E. rate, v. t., to value at a certain rate, to estimate, but more prob. fr. Sw. rata to find fault, to blame, to despise, to hold cheap; cf. Icel. hrat refuse, hrati rubbish.] To chide with vehemence; to scold; to censure violently; to berate. Spenser.
Rate Rate (?), n. [OF., fr. L. rata (sc. pars), fr. ratus reckoned, fixed by calculation, p. p. of reri to reckon, to calculate. Cf. Reason.] 1. Established portion or measure; fixed allowance.
Rate Rate, v. t. [imp. & p. p. Rated; p. pr. & vb. n. Rating.] 1. To set a certain estimate on; to value at a certain price or degree.
Rate Rate, v. i. 1. To be set or considered in a class; to have rank; as, the ship rates as a ship of the line.

ratel.c: Ratel Ra"tel (rā"tĕl), n. [F.] (Zool.) Any carnivore of the genus Mellivora, allied to the weasels and the skunks; -- called also honey badger.

ratepayer.c: Ratepayer Rate"pay`er (-pā`ẽr), n. One who pays rates or taxes.

rater.c: Rater Rat"er (rāt"ẽr), n. One who rates or estimates.
Rater Rat"er, n. One who rates or scolds.

rath.c: Rath Rath (răth), n. [Ir. rath.] 1. A hill or mound. [Ireland] Spenser.

rathe.c: Rathe Rath { Rath, Rathe } (răth), a. [AS. hræð, hræd, quick, akin to OHG. hrad, Icel. hraðr.] Coming before others, or before the usual time; early. [Obs. or Poetic]
Rathe Rath { Rath, Rathe, } adv. Early; soon; betimes. [Obs. or Poetic]

rather.c: Rather Rath"er (răth"ẽr), a. [Compar. of Rath, a.] Prior; earlier; former. [Obs.]
Rather Rath"er (răth"ẽr; 277), adv. [AS. hraðor, compar. of hraðe, hræðe, quickly, immediately. See Rath, a.]

rathripe.c: Rathripe Rath"ripe` (răth"rīp`), a. Rareripe, or early ripe. -- n. A rareripe. [Obs. or Prov. Eng.]

rathskeller.c: Rathskeller ‖Raths"kel`ler (räts"kĕl*lẽr), n. [G., also ratskeller, prop., town-hall cellar.] Orig., in Germany, the cellar or basement of the city hall, usually rented for use as a restaurant where beer is sold; hence, a beer saloon of the German type below the street level, where, usually, drinks are served only at tables and simple food may also be had; -- sometimes loosely used, in English, of what are essentially basement restaurants where liquors are served.

ratification.c: Ratification Rat`i*fi*ca"tion (răt`ĭ*fĭ*kā"shŭn), n. [Cf. F. ratification.] The act of ratifying; the state of being ratified; confirmation; sanction; as, the ratification of a treaty.

ratifier.c: Ratifier Rat"i*fi`er (răt"ĭ*fī`ẽr), n. One who, or that which, ratifies; a confirmer. Shak.

ratify.c: Ratify Rat"i*fy (răt"ĭ*fī), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Ratified (răt"ĭ*fīd); p. pr. & vb. n. Ratifying (răt"ĭ*fī`ĭng).] [F. ratifier, fr. L. ratus fixed by calculation, firm, valid + -ficare (in comp.) to make. See Rate, n., and -fy.] To approve and sanction; to make valid; to confirm; to establish; to settle; especially, to give sanction to, as something done by an agent or servant; as, to ratify an agreement, treaty, or contract; to ratify a nomination.

ratihabition.c: Ratihabition Rat`i*ha*bi"tion (-hȧ*bĭsh"ŭn), n. [L. ratihabitio; ratus fixed, valid + habere to hold.] Confirmation or approbation, as of an act or contract. [Obs.] Jer. Taylor.

ratio.c: Ratio Ra"ti*o (rā"shĭ*o or rā"sho), n. [L., fr. reri, ratus, to reckon, believe, think, judge. See Reason.] 1. (Math.) The relation which one quantity or magnitude has to another of the same kind. It is expressed by the quotient of the division of the first by the second; thus, the ratio of 3 to 6 is expressed by or ½; of a to b by a/b; or (less commonly) the second term is made the dividend; as, a:b = b/a.

ratiocinate.c: Ratiocinate Ra`ti*oc"i*nate (răsh`ĭ*ŏs"ĭ*nāt), v. i. [L. ratiocinatus, p. p. of ratiocinari, fr. ratio reason. See Ratio.] To reason, esp. deductively; to offer reason or argument.

ratiocination.c: Ratiocination Ra`ti*oc`i*na"tion (răsh`ĭ*ŏs"ĭ*nā"shŭn), n. [L. ratiocinatio: cf. F. ratiocination.] The process of reasoning, or deducing conclusions from premises; deductive reasoning.

ratiocinative.c: Ratiocinative Ra`ti*oc"i*na*tive (răsh`ĭ*ŏs"ĭ*na*tĭv), a. [L. ratiocinativus.] Characterized by, or addicted to, ratiocination; consisting in the comparison of propositions or facts, and the deduction of inferences from the comparison; argumentative; as, a ratiocinative process.

ration.c: Ration Ra"tion (rā"shŭn or răsh"ŭn), n. [F., fr. L. ratio a reckoning, calculation, relation, reference, LL. ratio ration. See Ratio.] 1. A fixed daily allowance of provisions assigned to a soldier in the army, or a sailor in the navy, for his subsistence.
Ration Ra"tion, v. t. To supply with rations, as a regiment.

rational.c: Rational Ra"tion*al (răsh"ŭn*ail), a. [L. rationalis: cf. F. rationnel. See Ratio, Reason, and cf. Rationale.] 1. Relating to the reason; not physical; mental.
Rational Ra"tion*al, n. A rational being. Young.

rationale.c: Rationale Ra`tion*a"le (răsh`ŭ*năl" or răsh`ŭn*ā"le), n. [L. rationalis, neut. rationale. See Rational, a.] An explanation or exposition of the principles of some opinion, action, hypothesis, phenomenon, or the like; also, the principles themselves.

rationalism.c: Rationalism Ra"tion*al*ism (răsh"ŭn*ail*ĭz'm), n. [Cf. F. rationalisme.] 1. (Theol.) The doctrine or system of those who deduce their religious opinions from reason or the understanding, as distinct from, or opposed to, revelation.

rationalist.c: Rationalist Ra"tion*al*ist, n. [Cf. F. rationaliste.] One who accepts rationalism as a theory or system; also, disparagingly, a false reasoner. See Citation under Reasonist.

rationalistical.c: Rationalistical Rationalistic { Ra`tion*al*is"tic (răsh"ŭn*ail*ĭs"tĭk), Ra`tion*al*is"tic*al (-tĭ*kail), } a. Belonging to, or in accordance with, the principles of rationalism. -- Ra`tion*al*is"tic*al*ly, adv.

rationality.c: Rationality Ra`tion*al"i*ty (răsh"ŭn*ăl"ĭ*ty̆; 277), n.; pl. -ties (-tĭz). [F. rationalité, or L. rationalitas.] The quality or state of being rational; agreement with reason; possession of reason; due exercise of reason; reasonableness.

rationalization.c: Rationalization Ra`tion*al*i*za"tion (răsh`ŭn*ail*ĭ*zā"shŭn), n. The act or process of rationalizing.

rationalize.c: Rationalize Ra"tion*al*ize (răsh"ŭn*ail*īz), v. t. 1. To make rational; also, to convert to rationalism.
Rationalize Ra"tion*al*ize, v. i. To use, and rely on, reason in forming a theory, belief, etc., especially in matters of religion: to accord with the principles of rationalism.

rationally.c: Rationally Ra"tion*al*ly, adv. In a rational manner.

rationalness.c: Rationalness Ra"tion*al*ness, n. The quality or state of being rational; rationality.

ratitae.c: Ratitae ‖Ra*ti"tae (rȧ*tī"te), n. pl. [NL., fr. L. ratis a raft; cf. L. ratitus marked with the figure of a raft.] (Zool.) An order of birds in which the wings are small, rudimentary, or absent, and the breastbone is destitute of a keel. The ostrich, emu, moa, and apteryx are examples.

ratitate.c: Ratitate Rat"i*tate (răt"ĭ*tat), a. (Zool.) Of or pertaining to the Ratitae.

ratite.c: Ratite Rat"ite (răt"īt), a. (Zool.) Of or pertaining to the Ratitae. -- n. One of the Ratitae.

ratlins.c: Ratlins Ratlines { Rat"lines, Rat"lins } (răt"lĭnz), n. pl. [Of uncertain origin.] (Naut.) The small transverse ropes attached to the shrouds and forming the steps of a rope ladder. [Written also ratlings, and rattlings.] Totten.

raton.c: Raton Rat"on (răt"ŏn), n. [Cf. Raccoon.] A small rat. [Obs.] Piers Plowman.

ratoon.c: Ratoon Ra*toon" (rȧ*tōon"), n. 1. Same as Rattoon, n.
Ratoon Ra*toon", v. i. Same as Rattoon, v. i.

ratsbane.c: Ratsbane Rats"bane` (răts"bān`), n. [Rat + bane.] Rat poison; white arsenic.

rattail.c: Rat-tail Rat"-tail` (răt"tāl`), a. Like a rat's tail in form; as, a rat-tail file, which is round, slender, and tapering. See Illust. of File.
Rat-tail Rat"-tail`, n. 1. (Far.) pl. An excrescence growing from the pastern to the middle of the shank of a horse.

rattailed.c: Rat-tailed Rat"-tailed` (răt"tāld`), a. (Zool.) Having a long, tapering tail like that of a rat.

rattan.c: Rattan Rat*tan" (răt*tăn"), n. [Malay rōtan.] [Written also ratan.] (Bot.) One of the long slender flexible stems of several species of palms of the genus Calamus, mostly East Indian, though some are African and Australian. They are exceedingly tough, and are used for walking sticks, wickerwork, chairs and seats of chairs, cords and cordage, and many other purposes.

ratteen.c: Ratteen Rat*teen" (răt*tēn"), n. [F. ratine.] A thick woolen stuff quilled or twilled.

ratten.c: Ratten Rat"ten (răt"t'n), v. t. [Prov. E. ratten a rat, hence the verb literally means, to do mischief like a rat.] To deprive feloniously of the tools used in one's employment (as by breaking or stealing them), for the purpose of annoying; as, to ratten a mechanic who works during a strike. [Trades-union Cant] J. McCarthy.

ratter.c: Ratter Rat"ter (răt"tẽr), n. 1. One who, or that which, rats, as one who deserts his party.

rattinet.c: Rattinet Rat`ti*net" (-tĭ*nĕt"), n. A woolen stuff thinner than ratteen.

ratting.c: Ratting Rat"ting (răt"tĭng), n. 1. The conduct or practices of one who rats. See Rat, v. i., 1. Sydney Smith.

rattle.c: Rattle Rat"tle (răt"t'l), v. i. [imp. & p. p. Rattled (-t'ld); p. pr. & vb. n. Rattling (-tlĭng).] [Akin to D. ratelen, G. rasseln, AS. hrætele a rattle, in hrætelwyrt rattlewort; cf. Gr. kradai`nein to swing, wave. Cf. Rail a bird.] 1. To make a quick succession of sharp, inharmonious noises, as by the collision of hard and not very sonorous bodies shaken together; to clatter.
Rattle Rat"tle (răt"t'l), v. t. 1. To cause to make a rattling or clattering sound; as, to rattle a chain.
Rattle Rat"tle, n. 1. A rapid succession of sharp, clattering sounds; as, the rattle of a drum. Prior.

rattlebox.c: Rattlebox Rat"tle*box` (răt"t'l*bŏks`), n. 1. A toy that makes a rattling sound; a rattle.

rattlehead.c: Rattlehead Rat"tle*head` (răt"t'l*hĕd`), n. An empty, noisy talker.

rattlepate.c: Rattlepate Rat"tle*pate` (răt"t'l*pāt`), n. A rattlehead. C. Kingsley.

rattlepated.c: Rattle-pated Rat"tle-pat`ed, a. Rattle-headed. “A noisy, rattle-pated fellow.” W. Irving.

rattler.c: Rattler Rat"tler (răt"tlẽr), n. One who, or that which, rattles.

rattlesnake.c: Rattlesnake Rat"tle*snake` (răt"t'l*snāk`), n. (Zool.) Any one of several species of venomous American snakes belonging to the genera Crotalus and Caudisona, or Sistrurus; sometimes also called rattler. They have a series of horny interlocking joints at the end of the tail which make a sharp rattling sound when shaken. The common rattlesnake of the Northern United States (Crotalus horridus), and the diamondback rattlesnake (also called diamondback rattler, and diamondback) of the South and East (Crotalus adamanteus) and West (Crotalus atrox), are the best known. See Illust. of Fang.

rattletrap.c: Rattletrap Rat"tle*trap` (-trăp`), n. Any machine or vehicle that does not run smoothly. [Colloq.] A. Trollope.

rattleweed.c: Rattleweed Rat"tle*weed` (-wēd`), n. (Bot.) Any plant of the genus Astragalus. See Milk vetch.

rattlewort.c: Rattlewort Rat"tle*wort` (-wûrt`), n. [AS. hrætelwyrt.] (Bot.) Same as Rattlebox.

rattoon.c: Rattoon Rat*toon" (răt*tōon"), n. [Sp. retoño.] One of the stems or shoots of sugar cane of the second year's growth from the root, or later. See Plant-cane.

Rattoon Rat*toon", v. i. [imp. & p. p. Rattooned (-tōond"); p. pr. & vb. n. Rattooning.] [Cf. Sp. retoñar.] To sprout or spring up from the root, as sugar cane from the root of the previous year's planting.

raucid.c: Raucid Rau"cid (rä"sĭd), a. [L. raucus hoarse; cf. LL. raucidus.] Hoarse; raucous. [R.] Lamb.

raucity.c: Raucity Rau"ci*ty (rä"sĭ*ty̆), n. [L. raucitas, from raucus hoarse: cf. F. raucité.] Harshness of sound; rough utterance; hoarseness; as, the raucity of a trumpet, or of the human voice.

raucous.c: Raucous Rau"cous (rä"kŭs), a. [L. raucus.] Hoarse; harsh; rough; as, a raucous, thick tone. “His voice slightly raucous.” Aytoun. -- Rau"cous*ly, adv.

raught.c: Raught Raught (rät), obs. imp. & p. p. of Reach. Shak.
Raught Raught, obs. imp. & p. p. of Reck. Chaucer.

raunch.c: Raunch Raunch (ränch), v. t. See Ranch. Spenser.

ravage.c: Ravage Rav"age (răv"aj; 48), n. [F., fr. (assumed) L. rapagium, rapaticum, fr. rapere to carry off by force, to ravish. See Rapacious, Ravish.] Desolation by violence; violent ruin or destruction; devastation; havoc; waste; as, the ravage of a lion; the ravages of fire or tempest; the ravages of an army, or of time.

Ravage Rav"age, v. t. [imp. & p. p. Ravaged (răv"ajd); p. pr. & vb. n. Ravaging (răv"a*jĭng).] [F. ravager. See Ravage, n.] To lay waste by force; to desolate by violence; to commit havoc or devastation upon; to spoil; to plunder; to consume.

ravager.c: Ravager Rav"a*ger (-a*jẽr), n. One who, or that which, ravages or lays waste; spoiler.

rave.c: Rave Rave, n. [Prov. E. raves, or rathes, a frame laid on a wagon, for carrying hay, etc.] One of the upper side pieces of the frame of a wagon body or a sleigh.

Rave Rave (rāv), v. i. [imp. & p. p. Raved (rāvd); p. pr. & vb. n. Raving.] [F. rêver to rave, to be delirious, to dream; perhaps fr. L. rabere to rave, rage, be mad or furious. Cf. Rage, Reverie.] 1. To wander in mind or intellect; to be delirious; to talk or act irrationally; to be wild, furious, or raging, as a madman.
Rave Rave, v. t. To utter in madness or frenzy; to say wildly; as, to rave nonsense. Young.

ravehook.c: Ravehook Rave"hook (rāv"hŏok), n. (Shipbuilding) A tool, hooked at the end, for enlarging or clearing seams for the reception of oakum.

ravel.c: Ravel Rav"el (răv"'l), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Raveled (-'ld) or Ravelled; p. pr. & vb. n. Raveling or Ravelling.] [OD. ravelen, D. rafelen, akin to LG. rebeln, rebbeln, reffeln.] 1. To separate or undo the texture of; to unravel; to take apart; to untwist; to unweave or unknit; -- often followed by out; as, to ravel a twist; to ravel out a stocking.
Ravel Rav"el, v. i. 1. To become untwisted or unwoven; to be disentangled; to be relieved of intricacy.

raveler.c: Raveler Rav"el*er (-ẽr), n. [Also raveller.] One who ravels.

ravelin.c: Ravelin Rave"lin (răv"lĭn; 277), n. [F.; cf. Sp. rebellin, It. revellino, rivellino; perhaps fr. L. re- again + vallum wall.] (Fort.) A detached work with two embankments which make a salient angle. It is raised before the curtain on the counterscarp of the place. Formerly called demilune and half-moon.

raveling.c: Raveling Rav"el*ing (răv"'l*ĭng), n. [Also ravelling.] 1. The act of untwisting or of disentangling.

raven.c: Raven Ra"ven (rā"v'n), n. [AS. hræfn; akin to D. raaf, G. rabe, OHG. hraban, Icel. hrafn, Dan. ravn, and perhaps to L. corvus, Gr. ko`rax. √19.] (Zool.) A large black passerine bird (Corvus corax), similar to the crow, but larger, and has a harsh, loud call. It is native of the northern parts of Europe, Asia and America, and is noted for its sagacity.
Raven Ra"ven, a. Of the color of the raven; jet black; as, raven curls; raven darkness.
Raven Rav"en (răv"'n), n. [OF. ravine impetuosity, violence, F. ravine ravine. See Ravine, Rapine.] [Written also ravin, and ravine.] 1. Rapine; rapacity. Ray.
Raven Rav"en, v. t. [imp. & p. p. Ravened (răv"'nd); p. pr. & vb. n. Ravening.] [Written also ravin, and ravine.]
Raven Rav"en, v. i. To prey with rapacity; to be greedy; to show rapacity. [Written also ravin, and ravine.]

ravenala.c: Ravenala ‖Rav`e*na"la (răv`e*nä"lȧ), n. [Malagasy.] (Bot.) A genus of plants related to the banana.

ravener.c: Ravener Rav"en*er (răv"'n*ẽr), n. 1. One who, or that which, ravens or plunders. Gower.

ravening.c: Ravening Rav"en*ing, n. Eagerness for plunder; rapacity; extortion. Luke xi. 39.
Ravening Rav"en*ing, a. Greedily devouring; rapacious; as, ravening wolves. -- Rav"en*ing*ly, adv.

ravenous.c: Ravenous Rav"en*ous (răv"'n*ŭs), a. [From 2d Raven.] 1. Devouring with rapacious eagerness; furiously voracious; hungry even to rage; as, a ravenous wolf or vulture.

ravensduck.c: Raven's-duck Ra"ven's-duck` (rā"v'nz-dŭk`), n. [Cf. G. ravenstuch.] A fine quality of sailcloth. Ham. Nav. Encyc.

ravine.c: Ravine Ravin { Rav"in, Rav"ine } (răv"'n), n. [See 2d Raven.] Food obtained by violence; plunder; prey; raven. “Fowls of ravyne.” Chaucer.
Ravine Ravin { Rav"in, Rav"ine, } v. t. & i. See Raven, v. t. & i.

Ravine Ra*vine" (rȧ*vēn"), n. [F., a place excavated by a torrent, a ravine, fr. ravir to snatch or tear away, L. rapere; cf. L. rapina rapine. See Ravish, and cf. Rapine, Raven prey.] 1. A torrent of water. [Obs.] Cotgrave.

raving.c: Raving Rav"ing (rāv"ĭng), a. Talking irrationally and wildly; as, a raving lunatic. -- Rav"ing*ly, adv.

ravish.c: Ravish Rav"ish (răv"ĭsh), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Ravished (-ĭsht); p. pr. & vb. n. Ravishing.] [OE. ravissen, F. ravir, fr. L. rapere to snatch or tear away, to ravish. See Rapacious, Rapid, and -ish.] 1. To seize and carry away by violence; to snatch by force.

ravisher.c: Ravisher Rav"ish*er (-ẽr), n. One who ravishes (in any sense).

ravishingly.c: Ravishingly Rav"ish*ing*ly, adv. In a ravishing manner.

ravissant.c: Ravissant Rav"is*sant (răv"ĭs*sănt), a. [F.] (Her.) In a half-raised position, as if about to spring on prey.

raw.c: Raw Raw (rä), a. [Compar. Rawer (rä"ẽr); superl. Rawest.] [AS. hreáw; akin to D. raauw, LG. rau, G. roh, OHG. rō, Icel. hrār, Dan. raa, Sw. rå, L. crudus, Gr. kre`as flesh, Skr. kravis raw flesh. √18. Cf. Crude, Cruel.] 1. Not altered from its natural state; not prepared by the action of heat; as, raw sienna; specifically, not cooked; not changed by heat to a state suitable for eating; not done; as, raw meat.
Raw Raw, n. A raw, sore, or galled place; a sensitive spot; as, to touch one on the raw.

rawboned.c: Rawboned Raw"boned` (-bōnd`), a. Having little flesh on the bones; gaunt. Shak.

rawhead.c: Rawhead Raw"head` (rä"hĕd`), n. A specter mentioned to frighten children; as, rawhead and bloodybones.

rawhide.c: Rawhide Raw"hide` (rä"hīd`), n. A cowhide, or coarse riding whip, made of untanned (or raw) hide twisted.

rawly.c: Rawly Raw"ly, adv. 1. In a raw manner; unskillfully; without experience.

rawness.c: Rawness Raw"ness, n. The quality or state of being raw.

ray.c: Ray Ray (rā), v. t. [An aphetic form of array; cf. Beray.] 1. To array. [Obs.] Sir T. More.
Ray Ray, n. Array; order; arrangement; dress. [Obs.]

Ray Ray, n. [OF. rai, F. rais, fr. L. radius a beam or ray, staff, rod, spoke of a wheel. Cf. Radius.] 1. One of a number of lines or parts diverging from a common point or center, like the radii of a circle; as, a star of six rays.

Ray Ray, v. t. [imp. & p. p. Rayed (rād); p. pr. & vb. n. Raying.] [Cf. OF. raier, raiier, rayer, L. radiare to irradiate. See Ray, n., and cf. Radiate.] 1. To mark with long lines; to streak. [Obs.] Chaucer.
Ray Ray, v. i. To shine, as with rays. Mrs. Browning.

Ray Ray, n. [F. raie, L. raia. Cf. Roach.] (Zool.) (a) Any one of numerous elasmobranch fishes of the order Raiae, including the skates, torpedoes, sawfishes, etc. (b) In a restricted sense, any of the broad, flat, narrow-tailed species, as the skates and sting rays. See Skate.
Ray grass Ray" grass` (rā" grȧs`). [Etymol. of ray is uncertain.] (Bot.) A perennial European grass (Lolium perenne); -- called also rye grass, and red darnel. See Darnel, and Grass.

rayah.c: Rayah ‖Ra"yah (rā"yȧ or rä"yȧ), n. [Ar. ra'iyah a herd, a subject, fr. ra'a to pasture, guard.] A person not a Mohammedan, who pays the capitation tax. [Turkey.]

rayless.c: Rayless Ray"less (rā"lĕs), a. Destitute of rays; hence, dark; not illuminated; blind; as, a rayless sky; rayless eyes.

rayonnant.c: Rayonnant Ray"on*nant (rā"ŏn*nănt), a. [F.] (Her.) Darting forth rays, as the sun when it shines out.

raze.c: Raze Raze (rāz), n. [See Race.] A Shakespearean word (used once) supposed to mean the same as race, a root. [Obs.]
Raze Raze, v. t. [imp. & p. p. Razed (rāzd); p. pr. & vb. n. Razing.] [F. raser. See Rase, v. t.] [Written also rase.] 1. To erase; to efface; to obliterate.

razed.c: Razed Razed (rāzd), a. Slashed or striped in patterns. [Obs.] “Two Provincial roses on my razed shoes.” Shak.

razee.c: Razee Ra*zee" (rȧ*zē"), n. [F. vaisseau rasé, fr. raser to raze, to cut down ships. See Raze, v. t., Rase, v. t.] (Naut.) An armed ship having her upper deck cut away, and thus reduced to the next inferior rate, as a seventy-four cut down to a frigate. Totten.

Razee Ra*zee", v. t. [imp. & p. p. Razeed (rȧ*zēd"); p. pr. & vb. n. Razeeing.] To cut down to a less number of decks, and thus to an inferior rate or class, as a ship; hence, to prune or abridge by cutting off or retrenching parts; as, to razee a book, or an article.

razor.c: Razor Ra"zor (rā"zẽr), n. [OE. rasour, OF. rasur, LL. rasor: cf. F. rasoir, LL. rasorium. See Raze, v. t., Rase, v. t.] 1. A keen-edged knife of peculiar shape, used in shaving the hair from the face or the head; also called a straight razor. “Take thee a barber's razor.” Ezek. v. 1.

razorable.c: Razorable Ra"zor*a*ble (rā"zẽr*ȧ*b'l), a. Ready for the razor; fit to be shaved. [R.] Shak.

razorbacked.c: Razor-backed Ra"zor-backed" (-băkt`), a. (Zool.) Having a sharp, lean, or thin back; as, a razor-backed hog, perch, etc.

razorbill.c: Razorbill Ra"zor*bill` (-bĭl`), n. (Zool.) (a) A species of auk (Alca torda) common in the Arctic seas. See Auk, and Illust. in Appendix. (b) See Cutwater, 3.

razure.c: Razure Ra"zure (rā"zhur; 135), n. [See Rasure.] 1. The act of erasing or effacing, or the state of being effaced; obliteration. See Rasure.

razzia.c: Razzia ‖Raz"zi*a (rä"ze*ä), n. [F., fr. Ar. ghāzīa (pron. razia in Algeria).] A plundering and destructive incursion; a foray; a raid.

re.c: Re- Re- (rē-). [L. re-, older form (retained before vowels) red-: cf. F. re-, ré-.] A prefix signifying back, against, again, anew; as, recline, to lean back; recall, to call back; recede; remove; reclaim, to call out against; repugn, to fight against; recognition, a knowing again; rejoin, to join again; reiterate; reassure. Combinations containing the prefix re- are readily formed, and are for the most part of obvious signification.
Re Re (rā). [It.] (Mus.) A syllable applied in solmization to the second tone of the diatonic scale of C; in the American system, to the second tone of any diatonic scale.
Re proval Re prov"al (-al), n. Reproof. Sir P. Sidney.
Re sign Re sign", n. Resignation. [Obs.] Beau. & Fl.

reabsorb.c: Reabsorb Re`ab*sorb" (rē`ăb*sôrb"), v. t. To absorb again; to draw in, or imbibe, again what has been effused, extravasated, or thrown off; to swallow up again; as, to reabsorb chyle, lymph, etc.; -- used esp. of fluids.

reabsorption.c: Reabsorption Re`ab*sorp"tion (rē`ăb*sôrp"shŭn), n. The act or process of reabsorbing.

reaccess.c: Reaccess Re`ac*cess" (rē`ăk*sĕs" or re*ăk"sĕs), n. A second access or approach; a return. Hakewill.

reaccuse.c: Reaccuse Re`ac*cuse" (rē`ăk*kūz"), v. t. To accuse again. Cheyne.

reach.c: Reach Reach (rēch), v. i. To retch. Cheyne.
Reach Reach, n. An effort to vomit. [R.]

Reach Reach, v. t. [imp. & p. p. Reached (rēcht) (Raught, the old preterit, is obsolete); p. pr. & vb. n. Reaching.] [OE. rechen, AS. rǣcan, rǣcean, to extend, stretch out; akin to D. reiken, G. reichen, and possibly to AS. rīce powerful, rich, E. rich. √115.] 1. To extend; to stretch; to thrust out; to put forth, as a limb, a member, something held, or the like.
Reach Reach, v. i. 1. To stretch out the hand.

Reach Reach, n. 1. The act of stretching or extending; extension; power of reaching or touching with the person, or a limb, or something held or thrown; as, the fruit is beyond my reach; to be within reach of cannon shot.

reachless.c: Reachless Reach"less, a. Being beyond reach; lofty.

react.c: React Re*act" (rē*ăkt"), v. t. To act or perform a second time; to do over again; to reenact; as, to react a play; the same scenes were reacted at Rome.

React Re*act" (re*ăkt"), v. i. 1. To return an impulse or impression; to resist the action of another body by an opposite force; as, every body reacts on the body that impels it from its natural state.

reactance.c: Reactance Re*act"ance (re*ăk"tains), n. [React + -ance.] (Elec.) The influence of a coil of wire upon an alternating current passing through it, tending to choke or diminish the current, or the similar influence of a condenser; inductive resistance. Reactance is measured in ohms. The reactance of a circuit is equal to the component of the impressed electro-motive force at right angles to the current divided by the current, that is, the component of the impedance due to the self-inductance or capacity of the circuit.
Reactance coil Reactance coil (Elec.) A choking coil.

reaction.c: Reaction Re*ac"tion (re*ăk"shŭn), n. [Cf. F. réaction.] 1. Any action in resisting other action or force; counter tendency; movement in a contrary direction; reverse action.

reactionary.c: Reactionary Re*ac"tion*a*ry (-a*ry̆), a. Being, causing, or favoring reaction; as, reactionary movements.
Reactionary Re*ac"tion*a*ry, n.; pl. Reactionaries (-rĭz). One who favors reaction, or seeks to undo political progress or revolution.

reactionist.c: Reactionist Re*ac"tion*ist, n. A reactionary. C. Kingsley.

reactive.c: Reactive Re*act"ive (re*ăkt"ĭv), a. [Cf. F. réactif.] Having power to react; tending to reaction; of the nature of reaction. -- Re*act"ive*ly, adv. -- Re*act"ive*ness, n.

read.c: Read Read (rēd), n. Rennet. See 3d Reed. [Prov. Eng.]

Read Read (rēd), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Read (rĕd); p. pr. & vb. n. Reading.] [OE. reden, ræden, AS. rǣdan to read, advise, counsel, fr. rǣd advice, counsel, rǣdan (imperf. reord) to advise, counsel, guess; akin to D. raden to advise, G. raten, rathen, Icel. rāða, Goth. rēdan (in comp.), and perh. also to Skr. rādh to succeed. √116. Cf. Riddle.] 1. To advise; to counsel. [Obs.] See Rede.
Read Read, v. i. 1. To give advice or counsel. [Obs.]
Read Read, n. [AS. rǣd counsel, fr. rǣdan to counsel. See Read, v. t.] 1. Saying; sentence; maxim; hence, word; advice; counsel. See Rede. [Obs.]
Read Read (rĕd), imp. & p. p. of Read, v. t. & i.
Read Read (rĕd), a. Instructed or knowing by reading; versed in books; learned.

readability.c: Readability Read`a*bil"i*ty (rēd`ȧ*bĭl"ĭ*ty̆), n. The state of being readable; readableness.

readable.c: Readable Read"a*ble (rēd"ȧ*b'l), a. Such as can be read; legible; fit or suitable to be read; worth reading; interesting. -- Read"a*ble*ness, n. -- Read"a*bly, adv.

readdress.c: Readdress Re`ad*dress" (rē`ăd*drĕs"), v. t. To address a second time; -- often used reflexively.

readept.c: Readept Re`a*dept" (-ȧ*dĕpt"), v. t. [Pref. re- + L. adeptus, p. p. of adipisci to obtain.] To regain; to recover. [Obs.]

readeption.c: Readeption Re`a*dep"tion (-dĕp"shŭn), n. A regaining; recovery of something lost. [Obs.] Bacon.

reader.c: Reader Read"er (rēd"ẽr), n. [AS. rǣdere.] 1. One who reads. Specifically: (a) One whose distinctive office is to read prayers in a church. (b) (University of Oxford, Eng.) One who reads lectures on scientific subjects. Lyell. (c) A proof reader. (d) One who reads manuscripts offered for publication and advises regarding their merit.

readership.c: Readership Read"er*ship, n. The office of reader. Lyell.

readily.c: Readily Read"i*ly (rĕd"ĭ*ly̆), adv. 1. In a ready manner; quickly; promptly. Chaucer.

readiness.c: Readiness Read"i*ness, n. The state or quality of being ready; preparation; promptness; aptitude; willingness.

reading.c: Reading Read"ing (rēd"ĭng), n. 1. The act of one who reads; perusal; also, printed or written matter to be read.
Reading Read"ing, a. 1. Of or pertaining to the act of reading; used in reading.

readjourn.c: Readjourn Re`ad*journ" (rē`ăd*jûrn"), v. t. To adjourn a second time; to adjourn again.

readjournment.c: Readjournment Re`ad*journ"ment (rē`ăd*jûrn"meint), n. The act of readjourning; a second or repeated adjournment.

readjust.c: Readjust Re`ad*just" (rē`ăd*jŭst"), v. t. To adjust or settle again; to put in a different order or relation; to rearrange.

readjuster.c: Readjuster Re`ad*just"er (rē`ăd*jŭst"ẽr), n. One who, or that which, readjusts; in some of the States of the United States, one who advocates a refunding, and sometimes a partial repudiation, of the State debt without the consent of the State's creditors.

readjustment.c: Readjustment Re`ad*just"ment (rē`ăd*jŭst"meint), n. A second adjustment; a new or different adjustment.

readmission.c: Readmission Re`ad*mis"sion (rē`ăd*mĭsh"ŭn), n. The act of admitting again, or the state of being readmitted; as, the readmission of fresh air into an exhausted receiver; the readmission of a student into a seminary.

readmit.c: Readmit Re`ad*mit" (-mĭt"), v. t. To admit again; to give entrance or access to again.

readmittance.c: Readmittance Re`ad*mit"tance (-tains), n. Allowance to enter again; a second admission.

readopt.c: Readopt Re`a*dopt" (rē`ȧ*dŏpt"), v. t. To adopt again. Young.

readorn.c: Readorn Re`a*dorn" (-dôrn"), v. t. To adorn again or anew.

readvance.c: Readvance Re`ad*vance" (rē`ăd*vȧns"), v. i. To advance again.

readvertency.c: Readvertency Re`ad*vert"en*cy (rē`ăd*vẽrt"ein*sy̆), n. The act of adverting to again, or of reviewing. [R.] Norris.

ready.c: Ready Read"y (rĕd"y̆), a. [Compar. Readier (rĕd"ĭ*ẽr); superl. Readiest.] [AS. rǣde; akin to D. gereed, bereid, G. bereit, Goth. garáids fixed, arranged, and possibly to E. ride, as meaning originally, prepared for riding. Cf. Array, 1st Curry.] 1. Prepared for what one is about to do or experience; equipped or supplied with what is needed for some act or event; prepared for immediate movement or action; as, the troops are ready to march; ready for the journey. “When she redy was.” Chaucer.
Ready Read"y (rĕd"y̆), adv. In a state of preparation for immediate action; so as to need no delay.
Ready Read"y, n. Ready money; cash; -- commonly with the; as, he was well supplied with the ready. [Slang]
Ready Read"y, v. t. To dispose in order. [Obs.] Heywood.

readymade.c: Ready-made Read"y-made` (rĕd"y̆-mād`), a. Made already, or beforehand, in anticipation of need; not made to order; as, ready-made clothing; ready-made jokes.

reaffirm.c: Reaffirm Re`af*firm" (rē`ăf*fẽrm"), v. t. To affirm again.

reaffirmation.c: Reaffirmation Reaffirmance { Re`af*firm"ance (rē`ăf*fẽrm"ains), Re*af`fir*ma"tion (rē*ăf`fẽr*mā"shŭn), } n. A second affirmation.

reafforest.c: reafforest re-afforest re`af*for"est (rē`ăf*fŏr"ĕst), v. t. To convert again into a forest, as a region of country; to re-establish a forest after clear-cutting or fire, etc.; -- used more often without the hyphen.

reafforestation.c: Reafforestation Re`af*for`es*ta"tion (-ĕs*tā"shŭn), n. The act or process of converting again into a forest.

reagent.c: Reagent Re*a"gent (re*ā"jeint), n. (Chem.) A substance capable of producing with another a reaction, especially when employed to detect the presence of other bodies; a test.

reaggravation.c: Reaggravation Re*ag`gra*va"tion (re*ăg`grȧ*vā"shŭn), n. (R. C. Ch.) The last monitory, published after three admonitions and before the last excommunication.

reagree.c: Reagree Re`a*gree" (rē`ȧ*grē"), v. i. To agree again.

reak.c: Reak Reak (rēk), n. [√115. Cf. Wrack seaweed.] A rush. [Obs.] “Feeds on reaks and reeds.” Drant.
Reak Reak, n. [Cf. Icel. hrekkr, or E. wreak vengeance.] A prank. [Obs.] “They play such reaks.” Beau. & Fl.

real.c: Real Re"al (rē"ail), n. [Sp., fr. real royal, L. regalis. See Regal, and cf. Ree a coin.] A former small Spanish silver coin; also, a denomination of money of account, formerly the unit of the Spanish monetary system.
Real Re*al" (ra*äl"), a. Royal; regal; kingly. [Obs.] “The blood real of Thebes.” Chaucer.
Real Re"al (rē"ail), a. [LL. realis, fr. L. res, rei, a thing: cf. F. réel. Cf. Rebus.] 1. Actually being or existing; not fictitious or imaginary; as, a description of real life.

realgar.c: Realgar Re*al"gar (re*ăl"gẽr), n. [F. réalgar, Sp. rejalgar, Ar. rahj al ghār powder of the mine.] (Min.) Arsenic sulphide, a mineral of a brilliant red color; red orpiment. It is also an artificial product.

realism.c: Realism Re"al*ism (rē"ail*ĭz'm), n. [Cf. F. réalisme.] 1. (Philos.) (a) As opposed to nominalism, the doctrine that genera and species are real things or entities, existing independently of our conceptions. According to realism the Universal exists ante rem (Plato), or in re (Aristotle). (b) As opposed to idealism, the doctrine that in sense perception there is an immediate cognition of the external object, and our knowledge of it is not mediate and representative.

realist.c: Realist Re"al*ist, n. [Cf. F. réaliste.] 1. (Philos.) One who believes in realism; esp., one who maintains that generals, or the terms used to denote the genera and species of things, represent real existences, and are not mere names, as maintained by the nominalists.

realistic.c: Realistic Re`al*is"tic (-ĭs"tĭk), a. Of or pertaining to the realists; in the manner of the realists; characterized by realism rather than by imagination.

realistically.c: Realistically Re`al*is"tic*al*ly, adv. In a realistic manner.

reality.c: Reality Re*al"i*ty (re*ăl"ĭ*ty̆), n.; pl. Realities (-tĭz). [Cf. F. réalité, LL. realitas. See 3d Real, and cf. 2d Realty.] 1. The state or quality of being real; actual being or existence of anything, in distinction from mere appearance; fact.

realizable.c: Realizable Re"al*i`za*ble (rē"ail*ī`zȧ*b'l), a. Capable of being realized.

realization.c: Realization Re`al*i*za"tion (rē`ail*ĭ*zā"shŭn), n. [Cf. F. réalisation.] The act of realizing, or the state of being realized.

realize.c: Realize Re"al*ize (rē"ail*īz), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Realized (-īzd); p. pr. & vb. n. Realizing (-ī`zĭng).] [Cf. F. réaliser.] 1. To make real; to convert from the imaginary or fictitious into the actual; to bring into concrete existence; to effectuate; to accomplish; as, to realize a scheme or project.
Realize Re"al*ize, v. i. To convert any kind of property into money, especially property representing investments, as shares in stock companies, bonds, etc.

realizer.c: Realizer Re"al*i`zer (-ī`zẽr), n. One who realizes. Coleridge.

realizing.c: Realizing Re"al*i`zing (-zĭng), a. Serving to make real, or to impress on the mind as a reality; as, a realizing view of the danger incurred. -- Re"al*i`zing*ly, adv.

reallege.c: Reallege Re`al*lege" (-ăl*lĕj"), v. t. To allege again. Cotgrave.

really.c: Re-ally Re"-al*ly" (-lī"), v. t. [Pref. re- + ally, v. t.] To bring together again; to compose or form anew. Spenser.
Really Re"al*ly (rē"ail*ly̆), adv. In a real manner; with or in reality; actually; in truth.

realm.c: Realm Realm (rĕlm), n. [OE. realme, ream, reaume, OF. reialme, roialme, F. royaume, fr. (assumed) LL. regalimen, from L. regalis royal. See Regal.] 1. A royal jurisdiction or domain; a region which is under the dominion of a king; a kingdom.

realmless.c: Realmless Realm"less, a. Destitute of a realm. Keats.

realness.c: Realness Re"al*ness (rē"ail*nĕs), n. The quality or condition of being real; reality.

realty.c: Realty Re"al*ty (-ty̆), n. [OF. réalté, LL. regalitas, fr. L. regalis. See Regal.] 1. Royalty. [Obs.] Chaucer.
Realty Re"al*ty, n. [Contr. from 1st Reality.] 1. Reality. [Obs.] Dr. H. More.

ream.c: Ream Ream (rēm), n. [AS. reám, akin to G. rahm.] Cream; also, the cream or froth on ale. [Scot.]
Ream Ream, v. i. To cream; to mantle. [Scot.]
Ream Ream, v. t. [Cf. Reim.] To stretch out; to draw out into thongs, threads, or filaments.
Ream Ream, n. [OE. reme, OF. rayme, F. rame (cf. Sp. resma), fr. Ar. rizma a bundle, especially of paper.] A bundle, package, or quantity of paper, usually consisting of twenty quires or 480 sheets.

Ream Ream, v. t. [imp. & p. p. Reamed (rēmd); p. pr. & vb. n. Reaming.] [Cf. G. räumen to remove, to clear away, fr. raum room. See Room.] To bevel out, as the mouth of a hole in wood or metal; in modern usage, to enlarge or dress out, as a hole, with a reamer.

reamer.c: Reamer Ream"er (-ẽr), n. One who, or that which, reams; specifically, an instrument with cutting or scraping edges, used, with a twisting motion, for enlarging a round hole, as the bore of a cannon, etc.

reamputation.c: Reamputation Re*am`pu*ta"tion (rē*ăm`pu*tā"shŭn), n. (Surg.) The second of two amputations performed upon the same member.

reanimate.c: Reanimate Re*an"i*mate (re*ăn"ĭ*māt), v. t. To animate anew; to restore to animation or life; to infuse new life, vigor, spirit, or courage into; to revive; to reinvigorate; as, to reanimate a drowned person; to reanimate disheartened troops; to reanimate languid spirits. Glanvill.

reanimation.c: Reanimation Re*an`i*ma"tion (re*ăn"ĭ*mā"shŭn), n. The act or operation of reanimating, or the state of being reanimated; reinvigoration; revival.

reannex.c: Reannex Re`an*nex" (rē`ăn*nĕks"), v. t. To annex again or anew; to reunite. “To reannex that duchy.” Bacon.

reanswer.c: Reanswer Re*an"swer (re*ăn"sẽr), v. t. & i. To answer in return; to repay; to compensate; to make amends for.

reap.c: Reap Reap (rēp), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Reaped (rēpt); p. pr. & vb. n. Reaping.] [OE. repen, AS. rīpan to seize, reap; cf. D. rapen to glean, reap, G. raufen to pluck, Goth. raupjan, or E. ripe.] 1. To cut with a sickle, scythe, or reaping machine, as grain; to gather, as a harvest, by cutting.
Reap Reap, v. i. To perform the act or operation of reaping; to gather a harvest.
Reap Reap, n. [Cf. AS. rīp harvest. See Reap, v.] A bundle of grain; a handful of grain laid down by the reaper as it is cut. [Obs. or Prov. Eng.] Wright.

reapparel.c: Reapparel Re`ap*par"el (rē`ăp*păr"ĕl), v. t. To clothe again.

reappear.c: Reappear Re`ap*pear" (rē`ăp*pēr"), v. i. To appear again.

reappearance.c: Reappearance Re`ap*pear"ance (-ains), n. A second or new appearance; the act or state of appearing again.

reapplication.c: Reapplication Re*ap`pli*ca"tion (rē*ăp`plĭ*kā"shŭn), n. The act of reapplying, or the state of being reapplied.

reapply.c: Reapply Re`ap*ply" (rē`ăp*plī"), v. t. & i. To apply again.

reappoint.c: Reappoint Re`ap*point" (-point"), v. t. To appoint again.

reappointment.c: Reappointment Re`ap*point"ment (-meint), n. The act of reappointing, or the state of being reappointed.

reapportion.c: Reapportion Re`ap*por"tion (-pōr"shŭn), v. t. To apportion again.

reapportionment.c: Reapportionment Re`ap*por"tion*ment (-meint), n. A second or a new apportionment.

reapproach.c: Reapproach Re`ap*proach" (rē`ăp*prōch"), v. i. & t. To approach again or anew.

rear.c: Rear Rear, n. [OF. riere behind, backward, fr. L. retro. Cf. Arrear.] 1. The back or hindmost part; that which is behind, or last in order; -- opposed to front.
Rear Rear, a. Being behind, or in the hindmost part; hindmost; as, the rear rank of a company.
Rear Rear (rēr), v. t. To place in the rear; to secure the rear of. [R.]

Rear Rear, v. t. [imp. & p. p. Reared (rērd); p. pr. & vb. n. Rearing.] [AS. rǣran to raise, rear, elevate, for rǣsan, causative of rīsan to rise. See Rise, and cf. Raise.] 1. To raise; to lift up; to cause to rise, become erect, etc.; to elevate; as, to rear a monolith.
Rear Rear, v. i. To rise up on the hind legs, as a horse; to become erect.

reardoss.c: Reardoss Reardorse { Rear"dorse (-dôrs), Rear"doss (-dŏs) }, n. A reredos.

rearer.c: Rearer Rear"er (rēr"ẽr), n. One who, or that which, rears.

reargue.c: Reargue re-argue Re*ar"gue, Re-ar"gue (rē*är"gū), v. t. To argue anew or again; as, This politician will be forced into re-arguing an old national campaign. Usually used without the hyphen.

reargument.c: Reargument Re*ar"gu*ment (-gu*meint), n. An arguing over again, as of a motion made in court.

rearhorse.c: Rear-horse Rear"-horse` (rēr"hôrs`), n. [So called because it rears up when disturbed.] (Zool.) A mantis.

rearmost.c: Rearmost Rear"most` (-mōst`), a. Farthest in the rear; last.

rearmouse.c: Rearmouse Reremouse { Rear"mouse`, Rere"mouse` (-mous`) }, n. [AS. hrēremūs; probably fr. hrēran to agitate, stir (akin to G. rühren, Icel. hræra) + mūs mouse.] (Zool.) The leather-winged bat (Vespertilio murinus). [Written also reermouse.]

rearrange.c: Rearrange re-arrange re`-ar*range", Re`ar*range" (rē`ăr*rānj"), v. t. To arrange again; to put into a different order; to arrange in a different way; as, Please re-arrange these files in alphabetical order. Usually used without the hyphen.

rearrangement.c: Rearrangement Re`ar*range"ment (-meint), n. The act of rearranging, or the state of being rearranged.

rearward.c: Rearward Rear"ward` (rēr"wärd`-wẽrd), n. [Rear + ward.] The last troop; the rear of an army; a rear guard. Also used figuratively. Shak.
Rearward Rear"ward (-wẽrd), a. & adv. At or toward the rear.

reascend.c: Reascend Re`as*cend" (rē`ăs*sĕnd"), v. i. To rise, mount, or climb again.
Reascend Re`as*cend", v. t. To ascend or mount again; to reach by ascending again.

reascension.c: Reascension Re`as*cen"sion (-sĕn"shŭn), n. The act of reascending; a remounting.

reascent.c: Reascent Re`as*cent" (-sĕnt"), n. A returning ascent or ascension; acclivity. Cowper.

reason.c: Reason Rea"son (rē"z'n), n. [OE. resoun, F. raison, fr. L. ratio (akin to Goth. raþjō number, account, garaþjan to count, G. rede speech, reden to speak), fr. reri, ratus, to reckon, believe, think. Cf. Arraign, Rate, Ratio, Ration.] 1. A thought or a consideration offered in support of a determination or an opinion; a just ground for a conclusion or an action; that which is offered or accepted as an explanation; the efficient cause of an occurrence or a phenomenon; a motive for an action or a determination; proof, more or less decisive, for an opinion or a conclusion; principle; efficient cause; final cause; ground of argument.

Reason Rea"son (rē"z'n), v. i. [imp. & p. p. Reasoned (rē"z'nd); p. pr. & vb. n. Reasoning.] [Cf. F. raisonner. See Reason, n.] 1. To exercise the rational faculty; to deduce inferences from premises; to perform the process of deduction or of induction; to ratiocinate; to reach conclusions by a systematic comparison of facts.
Reason Rea"son, v. t. 1. To arrange and present the reasons for or against; to examine or discuss by arguments; to debate or discuss; as, I reasoned the matter with my friend.

reasonable.c: Reasonable Rea"son*a*ble (rē"z'n*ȧ*b'l), a. [OE. resonable, F. raisonnable, fr. L. rationabilis. See Reason, n.] 1. Having the faculty of reason; endued with reason; rational; as, a reasonable being.

reasonableness.c: Reasonableness Rea"son*a*ble*ness, n. Quality of being reasonable.

reasonably.c: Reasonably Rea"son*a*bly, adv. 1. In a reasonable manner.

reasoner.c: Reasoner Rea"son*er (rē"z'n*ẽr), n. One who reasons or argues; as, a fair reasoner; a close reasoner; a logical reasoner.

reasoning.c: Reasoning Rea"son*ing, n. 1. The act or process of adducing a reason or reasons; manner of presenting one's reasons.

reasonless.c: Reasonless Rea"son*less, a. 1. Destitute of reason; as, a reasonless man or mind. Shak.

reassemblage.c: Reassemblage Re`as*sem"blage (rē`ăs*sĕm"blaj), n. Assemblage a second time or again.

reassemble.c: Reassemble re-assemble Re`as*sem"ble, Re`-as*sem"ble (rē`ăs*sĕm"b'l), v. t. & i. To assemble again; -- usually after having taking something apart. Usually used without the hyphen.

reassert.c: Reassert Re`as*sert" (rē`ăs*sẽrt"), v. t. To assert again or anew; to maintain after an omission to do so.

reassertion.c: Reassertion Re`as*ser"tion (rē`ăs*sẽr"shŭn), n. A second or renewed assertion of the same thing.

reassessment.c: Reassessment Re`as*sess"ment (rē`ăs*sĕs"meint, n. A renewed or second assessment.

reassign.c: Reassign Re`as*sign" (rē`ăs*sīn"), v. t. To assign back or again; to transfer back what has been assigned.

reassignment.c: Reassignment Re`as*sign"ment (rē`ăs*sīn"meint), n. The act of reassigning.

reassimilate.c: Reassimilate Re`as*sim"i*late (rē`ăs*sĭm"ĭ*lāt), v. t. & i. To assimilate again. -- Re`as*sim`i*la"tion (rē`ăs*sĭm"ĭ*lā"shŭn), n.

reassociate.c: Reassociate Re`as*so"ci*ate (rē`ăs*sō"shĭ*āt), v. t. & i. To associate again; to bring again into close relations.

reassume.c: Reassume Re`as*sume" (rē`ăs*sūm"), v. t. To assume again or anew; to resume. -- Re`as*sump"tion (rē`ăs*sŭmp"shŭn), n.

reassurance.c: Reassurance Re`as*sur"ance (rē`ȧ*shür"ains), n. 1. Assurance or confirmation renewed or repeated. Prynne.

reassure.c: Reassure Re`as*sure" (rē`ȧ*shür"), v. t. 1. To assure anew; to restore confidence to; to free from fear or terror.

reasty.c: Reasty Reas"ty (rēs"ty̆), a. [Etymol. uncertain.] Rusty and rancid; -- applied to salt meat. [Obs. or Prov. Eng.] Tusser. -- Reas"ti*ness (rēs"tĭ*nĕs), n. [Obs. or Prov. Eng.]

reattach.c: Reattach Re`at*tach" (rē`ăt*tăch"), v. t. To attach again.

reattachment.c: Reattachment Re`at*tach"ment (rē`ăt*tăch"meint), n. The act of reattaching; a second attachment.

reattain.c: Reattain Re`at*tain" (rē`ăt*tān"), v. t. To attain again.

reattainment.c: Reattainment Re`at*tain"ment (rē`ăt*tān"meint), n. The act of reattaining.

reattempt.c: Reattempt Re`at*tempt" (rē`ăt*tĕmt"; 215), v. t. To attempt again.

reaumur.c: Reaumur Ré`au`mur" (ra`ō`mụr"), a. Of or pertaining to René Antoine Ferchault de Réaumur; conformed to the scale adopted by Réaumur in graduating the thermometer he invented. -- n. A Réaumur thermometer or scale.

reave.c: Reave Reave (rēv), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Reaved (rēvd), Reft (rĕft), or Raft (rȧft) (obs.); p. pr. & vb. n. Reaving.] [AS. reáfian, from reáf spoil, plunder, clothing, reófan to break (cf. bireófan to deprive of); akin to G. rauben to rob, Icel. raufa to rob, rjūfa to break, violate, Goth. biráubōn to despoil, L. rumpere to break; cf. Skr. lup to break. √114. Cf. Bereave, Rob, v. t., Robe, Rove, v. i., Rupture.] To take away by violence or by stealth; to snatch away; to rob; to despoil; to bereave. [Archaic]. “To reave his life.” Spenser.

reawake.c: Reawake Re`a*wake" (rē`ȧ*wāk"), v. i. To awake again.

rebanish.c: Rebanish Re*ban"ish (rē*băn"ĭsh), v. t. To banish again.

rebaptization.c: Rebaptization Re*bap`ti*za"tion (rē*băp`tĭ*zā"shŭn), n. [Cf. F. rebaptisation.] A second baptism. [Obs.] Hooker.

rebaptize.c: Rebaptize Re`bap*tize" (rē`băp*tīz"), v. t. [Pref. re- + baptize: cf. F. rebaptiser, L. rebaptizare.] To baptize again or a second time.

rebarbarize.c: Rebarbarize Re*bar"ba*rize (rē*bär"bȧ*rīz), v. t. To reduce again to barbarism. -- Re*bar`ba*ri*za"tion (rē*bär"bȧ*rĭ*zā"shŭn), n.

rebate.c: Rebate Re*bate" (re*bāt"), v. t. [F. rebattre to beat again; pref. re- re- + battre to beat, L. batuere to beat, strike. See Abate.] 1. To beat to obtuseness; to deprive of keenness; to blunt; to turn back the point of, as a lance used for exercise.
Rebate Re*bate", v. i. To abate; to withdraw. [Obs.] Foxe.
Rebate Re*bate", n. [See Rabbet.] 1. (Arch.) A rectangular longitudinal recess or groove, cut in the corner or edge of any body; a rabbet. See Rabbet.
Rebate Re*bate", v. t. To cut a rebate in. See Rabbet, v.

rebatement.c: Rebatement Re*bate"ment (re*bāt"meint), n. [Cf. OF. rabatement, fr. rabatre to diminish, F. rabattre.] Same as 3d Rebate, v.

rebato.c: Rebato Re*ba"to (re*bā"to), n. Same as Rabato. Burton.

rebec.c: Rebec Re"bec (rē"bĕk), n. [F., fr. It. ribeca, ribeba, fr. Ar. rabāb a musical instrument of a round form.] 1. (Mus.) An instrument formerly used which somewhat resembled the violin, having three strings, and being played with a bow. [Written also rebeck.] Milton.

rebel.c: Rebel Reb"el (rĕb"ĕl), a. [F. rebelle, fr. L. rebellis. See Rebel, v. i.] Pertaining to rebels or rebellion; acting in revolt; rebellious; as, rebel troops.
Rebel Reb"el, n. [F. rebelle.] One who rebels.

Rebel Re*bel" (re*bĕl"), v. i. [imp. & p. p. Rebelled (re*bĕld); p. pr. & vb. n. Rebelling.] [F. rebeller, fr. L. rebellare to make war again; pref. re- again + bellare to make war, fr. bellum war. See Bellicose, and cf. Revel to carouse.] 1. To renounce, and resist by force, the authority of the ruler or government to which one owes obedience. See Rebellion.

rebeldom.c: Rebeldom Reb"el*dom (rĕb"ĕl*dŭm), n. A region infested by rebels; rebels, considered collectively; also, conduct or quality characteristic of rebels. Thackeray.

rebeller.c: Rebeller Re*bel"ler (re*bĕl"lẽr), n. One who rebels; a rebel.

rebellion.c: Rebellion Re*bel"lion (re*bĕl"yŭn), n. [F. rébellion, L. rebellio. See Rebel, v. i. Among the Romans rebellion was originally a revolt or open resistance to their government by nations that had been subdued in war. It was a renewed war.] 1. The act of rebelling; open and avowed renunciation of the authority of the government to which one owes obedience, and resistance to its officers and laws, either by levying war, or by aiding others to do so; an organized uprising of subjects for the purpose of coercing or overthrowing their lawful ruler or government by force; revolt; insurrection.

rebellious.c: Rebellious Re*bel"lious (re*bĕl"yŭs), a. Engaged in rebellion; disposed to rebel; of the nature of rebels or of rebellion; resisting government or lawful authority by force. “Thy rebellious crew.” “Proud rebellious arms.” Milton. -- Re*bel"lious*ly, adv. -- Re*bel"lious*ness, n.

rebellow.c: Rebellow Re*bel"low (rē*bĕl"lo), v. i. To bellow again; to repeat or echo a bellow.

rebiting.c: Rebiting Re*bit"ing (rē*bīt"ĭng), n. (Etching) The act or process of deepening worn lines in an etched plate by submitting it again to the action of acid. Fairholt.

rebloom.c: Rebloom Re*bloom" (rē*blōom"), v. i. To bloom again. Crabbe.

reblossom.c: Reblossom Re*blos"som (rē*blŏs"sŭm), v. i. To blossom again.

reboant.c: Reboant Re*bo"ant (re*bō"aint), a. [L. reboans, p. pr. of reboare; pref. re- re- + boare to cry aloud.] Rebellowing; resounding loudly. [R.] Mrs. Browning.

reboation.c: Reboation Re`bo*a"tion (rē`bo*ā"shŭn), n. Repetition of a bellow. [R.] Bp. Patrick.

reboil.c: Reboil Re*boil" (rē*boil"), v. t. & i. [Pref. re- + boil: cf. F. rebouillir.] 1. To boil, or to cause to boil, again.

rebound.c: Rebound Re*bound" (re*bound"), v. i. [Pref. re- + bound: cf. F. rebondir.] 1. To spring back; to start back; to be sent back or reverberated by elastic force on collision with another body; as, a rebounding echo.
Rebound Re*bound", v. t. To send back; to reverberate.
Rebound Re*bound", n. 1. The act of rebounding; resilience.

rebozo.c: Rebozo ‖Re*bo"zo (?), n. [Sp. rebozo.] A kind of mantilla worn by women over the head and shoulders, and sometimes over part of the face. [Mexico & Sp. Amer.]

rebrace.c: Rebrace Re*brace" (rē*brās"), v. t. To brace again. Gray.

rebreathe.c: Rebreathe Re*breathe" (rē*brēth"), v. t. To breathe again.

rebuff.c: Rebuff Re*buff" (re*bŭf"), n. [It. ribuffo, akin to ribuffare to repulse; pref. ri- (L. re-) + buffo puff. Cf. Buff to strike, Buffet a blow.] 1. Repercussion, or beating back; a quick and sudden resistance.
Rebuff Re*buff", v. t. [imp. & p. p. Rebuffed (re*bŭft"); p. pr. & vb. n. Rebuffing.] To beat back; to offer sudden resistance to; to check; to repel or repulse violently, harshly, or uncourteously.

rebuild.c: Rebuild re-build Re*build", Re-build" (rē*bĭld"), v. t. To build again, as something which has been demolished; to construct anew; as, to rebuild a house, a wall, a wharf, or a city. Usually used without the hyphen.

rebuilder.c: Rebuilder Re*build"er (rē*bĭld"ẽr), n. One who rebuilds. Bp. Bull.

rebukable.c: Rebukable Re*buk"a*ble (re*būk"ȧ*b'l), a. Worthy of rebuke or reprehension; reprehensible. Shak.

rebuke.c: Rebuke Re*buke" (re*būk"), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Rebuked (re*būkt"); p. pr. & vb. n. Rebuking.] [OF. rebouquier to dull, blunt, F. reboucher; perhaps fr. pref. re- re- + bouche mouth, OF. also bouque, L. bucca cheek; if so, the original sense was, to stop the mouth of; hence, to stop, obstruct.] To check, silence, or put down, with reproof; to restrain by expression of disapprobation; to reprehend sharply and summarily; to chide; to reprove; to admonish.
Rebuke Re*buke" (re*būk"), n. 1. A direct and pointed reproof; a reprimand; also, chastisement; punishment.

rebukeful.c: Rebukeful Re*buke"ful (re*būk"fụl), a. Containing rebuke; of the nature of rebuke. [Obs.] -- Re*buke"ful*ly, adv. [Obs.]

rebukingly.c: Rebukingly Re*buk"ing*ly, adv. By way of rebuke.

rebullition.c: Rebullition Re`bul*li"tion (rē`bŭl*lĭsh"ŭn), n. The act of boiling up or effervescing. [R.] Sir H. Wotton.

rebury.c: Rebury Re*bur"y (rē*bĕr"ry̆), v. t. To bury again. Ashmole.

rebus.c: Rebus Re"bus (rē"bŭs), n.; pl. Rebuses (rē"bŭs*ĕz). [L. rebus by things, abl. pl. of res a thing: cf. F. rébus. Cf. 3d Real.] 1. A mode of expressing words and phrases by pictures of objects whose names resemble those words, or the syllables of which they are composed; enigmatical representation of words by figures; hence, a peculiar form of riddle made up of such representations.
Rebus Re"bus, v. t. To mark or indicate by a rebus.

rebut.c: Rebut Re*but" (re*bŭt"), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Rebutted; p. pr. & vb. n. Rebutting.] [OF. rebouter to repulse, drive back; pref. re- + bouter to push, thrust. See 1st Butt, Boutade.]
Rebut Re*but", v. i. 1. To retire; to recoil. [Obs.] Spenser.

rebuttable.c: Rebuttable Re*but"ta*ble (re*bŭt"tȧ*b'l), a. Capable of being rebutted.

rebuttal.c: Rebuttal Re*but"tal (re*bŭt"tail), n. (Law) The giving of evidence on the part of a plaintiff to destroy the effect of evidence introduced by the defendant in the same suit.

rebutter.c: Rebutter Re*but"ter (re*bŭt"tẽr), n. (Law) The answer of a defendant in matter of fact to a plaintiff's surrejoinder.

recadency.c: Recadency Re*ca"den*cy (rē*kā"dein*sy̆), n. A falling back or descending a second time; a relapse. W. Montagu.

recalcitrant.c: Recalcitrant Re*cal"ci*trant (re*kăl"sĭ*traint), a. [L. recalcitrans, p. pr. of recalcitrare to kick back; pref. re- re- + calcitrare to kick, fr. calx heel. Cf. Inculcate.] Kicking back; recalcitrating; hence, showing repugnance or opposition; refractory.

recalcitrate.c: Recalcitrate Re*cal"ci*trate (re*kăl"sĭ*trāt), v. t. To kick against; to show repugnance to; to rebuff.
Recalcitrate Re*cal"ci*trate, v. i. To kick back; to kick against anything; hence, to express repugnance or opposition.

recalcitration.c: Recalcitration Re*cal`ci*tra"tion (re*kăl"sĭ*trā"shŭn), n. A kicking back again; opposition; repugnance; refractoriness.

recall.c: Recall Re*call" (re*käl"), v. t. 1. To call back; to summon to return; as, to recall troops; to recall an ambassador.
Recall Re*call", n. 1. A calling back; a revocation.

recallable.c: Recallable Re*call"a*ble (re*käl"ȧ*b'l), a. Capable of being recalled.

recant.c: Recant Re*cant" (re*kănt"), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Recanted; p. pr. & vb. n. Recanting.] [L. recantare, recantatum, to recall, recant; pref. re- re- + cantare to sing, to sound. See 3d Cant, Chant.] To withdraw or repudiate formally and publicly (opinions formerly expressed); to contradict, as a former declaration; to take back openly; to retract; to recall.
Recant Re*cant", v. i. To revoke a declaration or proposition; to unsay what has been said; to retract; as, convince me that I am wrong, and I will recant. Dryden.

recantation.c: Recantation Re`can*ta"tion (rē`kăn*tā"shŭn), n. The act of recanting; a declaration that contradicts a former one; that which is thus asserted in contradiction; retraction.

recapacitate.c: Recapacitate Re`ca*pac"i*tate (rē`kȧ*păs"ĭ*tāt), v. t. To qualify again; to confer capacity on again. Atterbury.

recapitulate.c: Recapitulate Re*ca*pit"u*late (rē`kȧ*pĭt"u*lāt), v. t. [L. recapitulare, recapitulatum; pref. re- re- + capitulum a small head, chapter, section. See Capitulate.] To repeat, as the principal points in a discourse, argument, or essay; to give a summary of the principal facts, points, or arguments of; to relate in brief; to summarize.
Recapitulate Re`ca*pit"u*late (rē`kȧ*pĭt"u*lāt), v. i. To sum up, or enumerate by heads or topics, what has been previously said; to repeat briefly the substance.

recapitulation.c: Recapitulation Re`ca*pit`u*la"tion (rē`kȧ*pĭt"u*lā"shŭn), n. [LL. recapitulatio: cf. F. recapitulation.] 1. The act of recapitulating; a summary, or concise statement or enumeration, of the principal points, facts, or statements, in a preceding discourse, argument, or essay.

recapitulatory.c: Recapitulatory Re`ca*pit"u*la*to*ry (rē`kȧ*pĭt"u*lȧ*to*ry̆), a. Of the nature of a recapitulation; containing recapitulation.

recapper.c: Recapper Re*cap"per (re*kăp"pẽr), n. (Firearms) A tool used for applying a fresh percussion cap or primer to a cartridge shell in reloading it.

recaption.c: Recaption Re*cap"tion (re*kăp"shŭn), n. (Law) The act of retaking, as of one who has escaped after arrest; reprisal; the retaking of one's own goods, chattels, wife, or children, without force or violence, from one who has taken them and who wrongfully detains them. Blackstone.

recaptor.c: Recaptor Re*cap"tor (re*kăp"tẽr), n. One who recaptures; one who takes a prize which had been previously taken.

recapture.c: Recapture Re*cap"ture (re*kăp"tur; 135), n. 1. The act of retaking or recovering by capture; especially, the retaking of a prize or goods from a captor.
Recapture Re*cap"ture, v. t. To capture again; to retake.

recarbonize.c: Recarbonize Re*car"bon*ize (re*kär"bŏn*īz), v. t. (Metal.) To restore carbon to; as, to recarbonize iron in converting it into steel.

recarnify.c: Recarnify Re*car"ni*fy (re*kär"nĭ*fī), v. t. To convert again into flesh. [Obs.] Howell.

recarriage.c: Recarriage Re*car"riage (re*kăr"rĭj), n. Act of carrying back.

recarry.c: Recarry Re*car"ry (re*kăr"ry̆), v. t. To carry back. Walton.

recast.c: Recast Re*cast" (rē*kȧst"), v. t. 1. To throw again. Florio.

recche.c: Recche Rec"che (rĕk"kei), v. i. To reck. [Obs.] Chaucer.

recede.c: Recede Re*cede" (re*sēd"), v. i. [imp. & p. p. Receded; p. pr. & vb. n. Receding.] [L. recedere, recessum; pref. re- re- + cedere to go, to go along: cf. F. recéder. See Cede.] 1. To move back; to retreat; to withdraw.
Recede Re*cede" (rē*sēd"), v. t. [Pref. re- + cede. Cf. Recede, v. i.] To cede back; to grant or yield again to a former possessor; as, to recede conquered territory.

receipt.c: Receipt Re*ceipt" (re*sēt"), n. [OE. receite, OF. recete, recepte, F. recette, fr. L. recipere, receptum, to receive. See Receive.] 1. The act of receiving; reception. “At the receipt of your letter.” Shak.
Receipt Re*ceipt", v. t. [imp. & p. p. Receipted; p. pr. & vb. n. Receipting.] 1. To give a receipt for; as, to receipt goods delivered by a sheriff.
Receipt Re*ceipt", v. i. To give a receipt, as for money paid.

receiptment.c: Receiptment Re*ceipt"ment (re*sēt"meint), n. (O. Eng. Law) The receiving or harboring a felon knowingly, after the commission of a felony. Burrill.

receiptor.c: Receiptor Re*ceipt"or (re*sēt"ẽr), n. One who receipts; specifically (Law), one who receipts for property which has been taken by the sheriff.

receivability.c: Receivability Re*ceiv`a*bil"i*ty (re*sēv`ȧ*bĭl"ĭ*ty̆), n. The quality of being receivable; receivableness.

receivable.c: Receivable Re*ceiv"a*ble (re*sēv"ȧ*b'l), a. [Cf. F. recevable.] Capable of being received. -- Re*ceiv"a*ble*ness, n.

receive.c: Receive Re*ceive" (re*sēv"), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Received (re*sēvd"); p. pr. & vb. n. Receiving.] [OF. receveir, recevoir, F. recevoir, fr. L. recipere; pref. re- re- + capere to take, seize. See Capable, Heave, and cf. Receipt, Reception, Recipe.] 1. To take, as something that is offered, given, committed, sent, paid, or the like; to accept; as, to receive money offered in payment of a debt; to receive a gift, a message, or a letter.
Receive Re*ceive" (re*sēv"), v. i. 1. To receive visitors; to be at home to receive calls; as, she receives on Tuesdays.

receivedness.c: Receivedness Re*ceiv"ed*ness, n. The state or quality of being received, accepted, or current; as, the receivedness of an opinion. Boyle.

receiver.c: Receiver Re*ceiv"er (re*sēv"ẽr), n. [Cf. F. receveur.] 1. One who takes or receives in any manner.

receivers.c: Receiver's certificate Re*ceiv"er's cer*tif"i*cate (?). An acknowledgement of indebtedness made by a receiver under order of court to obtain funds for the preservation of the assets held by him, as for operating a railroad. Receivers' certificates are ordinarily a first lien on the assets, prior to that of bonds or other securities.

receivership.c: Receivership Re*ceiv"er*ship, n. The state or office of a receiver.

recelebrate.c: Recelebrate Re*cel"e*brate (rē*sĕl"e*brāt), v. t. To celebrate again, or anew. -- Re*cel`e*bra"tion (rē*sĕl"e*brā"shŭn), n.

recency.c: Recency Re"cen*cy (rē"sein*sy̆), n. [LL. recentia, fr. L. recens. See Recent.] The state or quality of being recent; newness; new state; late origin; lateness in time; freshness; as, the recency of a transaction, of a wound, etc.

recense.c: Recense Re*cense" (re*sĕns"), v. t. [L. recensere; pref. re- again + censere to value, estimate: cf. F. recenser.] To review; to revise. [R.] Bentley.

recension.c: Recension Re*cen"sion (re*sĕn"shŭn), n. [L. recensio: cf. F. recension.] 1. The act of reviewing or revising; review; examination; enumeration. Barrow.

recensionist.c: Recensionist Re*cen"sion*ist, n. One who makes recensions; specifically, a critical editor.

recent.c: Recent Re"cent (rē"seint), a. [L. recens, -entis: cf. F. récent.] 1. Of late origin, existence, or occurrence; lately come; not of remote date, antiquated style, or the like; not already known, familiar, worn out, trite, etc.; fresh; novel; new; modern; as, recent news.

recenter.c: Recenter Re*cen"ter (rē*sĕn"tẽr), v. t. [Pref. re- + center.] To center again; to restore to the center. Coleridge.

recently.c: Recently Re"cent*ly (rē"seint*ly̆), adv. Newly; lately; freshly; not long since; as, advices recently received.

recentness.c: Recentness Re"cent*ness, n. Quality or state of being recent.

receptacle.c: Receptacle Re*cep"ta*cle (re*sĕp"tȧ*k'l), n. [F. réceptacle, L. receptaculum, fr. receptare, v. intens. fr. recipere to receive. See Receive.] 1. That which serves, or is used, for receiving and containing something, as for examople, a basket, a vase, a bag, a reservoir; a repository.

receptacular.c: Receptacular Rec`ep*tac"u*lar (rĕs`ĕp*tăk"u*lẽr), a. [Cf. F. réceptaculaire.] (Bot.) Pertaining to the receptacle, or growing on it; as, the receptacular chaff or scales in the sunflower.

receptaculum.c: Receptaculum ‖Rec`ep*tac"u*lum (rĕs`ĕp*tăk"u*lŭm), n.; pl. Receptacula (rĕs`ĕp*tăk"u*lȧ). [L.] (Anat.) A receptacle; as, the receptaculum of the chyle.

receptary.c: Receptary Rec"ep*ta*ry (rĕs"ĕp*ta*ry̆), a. Generally or popularly admitted or received. [Obs.] Sir T. Browne.
Receptary Rec"ep*ta*ry, n. That which is received. [Obs.] “Receptaries of philosophy.” Sir T. Browne.

receptibility.c: Receptibility Re*cep`ti*bil"i*ty (re*sĕp`tĭ*bĭl"ĭ*ty̆), n. 1. The quality or state of being receptible; receivableness.

receptible.c: Receptible Re*cep"ti*ble (re*sĕp"tĭ*b'l), a. [L. receptibilis.] Such as may be received; receivable.

reception.c: Reception Re*cep"tion (re*sĕp"shŭn), n. [F. réception, L. receptio, fr. recipere, receptum. See Receive.] 1. The act of receiving; receipt; admission; as, the reception of food into the stomach; the reception of a letter; the reception of sensation or ideas; reception of evidence.

receptive.c: Receptive Re*cep"tive (re*sĕp"tĭv), a. [Cf. F. réceptif. See Receive.] Having the quality of receiving; able or inclined to take in, absorb, hold, or contain; receiving or containing; as, a receptive mind.

receptiveness.c: Receptiveness Re*cep"tive*ness, n. The quality of being receptive.

receptivity.c: Receptivity Rec`ep*tiv"i*ty (rĕs`ĕp*tĭv"ĭ*ty̆ or rē`sĕp*tĭv"ĭ*ty̆), n. [Cf. F. réceptivité.] 1. The state or quality of being receptive.

receptory.c: Receptory Re*cep"to*ry (re*sĕp"to*ry̆; 277), n. [Cf. L. receptorium a place of shelter.] Receptacle. [Obs.] Holland.

recess.c: Recess Re*cess" (re*sĕs"), n. [L. recessus, fr. recedere, recessum. See Recede.] 1. A withdrawing or retiring; a moving back; retreat; as, the recess of the tides.
Recess Re*cess", v. t. [imp. & p. p. Recessed; p. pr. & vb. n. Recessing.] To make a recess in; as, to recess a wall.
Recess Re*cess", n. [G.] A decree of the imperial diet of the old German empire. Brande & C.

recessed.c: Recessed Re*cessed" (re*sĕst"), a. 1. Having a recess or recesses; as, a recessed arch or wall.

recession.c: Recession Re*ces"sion (re*sĕsh"ŭn), n. [L. recessio, fr. recedere, recessum. See Recede.] 1. The act of receding or withdrawing, as from a place, a claim, or a demand. South.
Recession Re*ces"sion, n. [Pref. re- + cession.] The act of ceding back; restoration; repeated cession; as, the recession of conquered territory to its former sovereign.

recessional.c: Recessional Re*ces"sion*al (?), a. Of or pertaining to recession or withdrawal.

rechabite.c: Rechabite Re"chab*ite (rē"kăb*īt), n. (Jewish Hist.) One of the descendants of Jonadab, the son of Rechab, all of whom by his injunction abstained from the use of intoxicating drinks and even from planting the vine. Jer. xxxv. 2-19. Also, in modern times, a member of a certain society of abstainers from alcoholic liquors.

rechange.c: Rechange Re*change" (rē*chānj"), v. t. & i. To change again, or change back.

recharge.c: Recharge Re*charge" (rē*chärj"), v. t. & i. [Pref. re- + charge: cf. F. recharger.] 1. To charge or accuse in return.
