reembarkation.c: Reembarkation Re*em`bar*ka"tion (r?*?m`b?r*k?"sh?n), n. A putting, or going, on board a vessel again.

reembody.c: Reembody Re`em*bod"y (r?`?m*b?d"?), v. t. To embody again.

reembrace.c: Reembrace Re`em*brace" (-br?s"), v. i. To embrace again.

reemerge.c: Reemerge re-emerge Re`e*merge", Re`-e*merge" (r?`?*m?rj"), v. i. To emerge again.

reenact.c: Reenact Re-enact Re`en*act", Re`-en*act" (r?`?n*?kt"), v. t. 1. To enact again.

reenaction.c: Reenaction Re`en*ac"tion (-?k"sh?n), n. The act of reenacting; the state of being reenacted.

reenactment.c: Reenactment Re`en*act"ment (-?kt"ment), n. The enacting or passing of a law a second time; the renewal of a law.

reencourage.c: Reencourage Re`en*cour"age (-k?r"?j;), v. t. To encourage again.

reendow.c: Reendow Re`en*dow" (-dou"), v. t. To endow again.

reenforce.c: Reenforce re-enforce Re`en*force", Re`-en*force" (rē`ĕn*fōrs"), v. t. [Pref. re- + enforce: cf. F. renforcer.] 1. To strengthen with new force, assistance, material, or support; as, to reenforce an argument; to reenforce a garment; especially, to strengthen with additional troops, as an army or a fort, or with additional ships, as a fleet. [Written also reinforce.]

Reenforce Re`en*force", n. [See Reenforce, v., and cf. Ranforce, Reinforce.] Something which reenforces or strengthens. Specifically: (a) That part of a cannon near the breech which is thicker than the rest of the piece, so as better to resist the force of the exploding powder. See Illust. of Cannon. (b) An additional thickness of canvas, cloth, or the like, around an eyelet, buttonhole, etc. [Written also reinforce.]

reenforced.c: Reenforced concrete Reenforced concrete. Concrete having within its mass a system of iron or steel supports, such as bars, rods, or a heavy mesh, to provide increased tensile strength and shear resistance. Same as Ferro-concrete.

reenforcement.c: Reenforcement Re`en*force"ment (r?`?n*f?rs"ment), n. 1. The act of reenforcing, or the state of being reenforced.

reengage.c: Reengage Re`en*gage" (-g?j), v. t. & i. To engage a second time or again.

reengagement.c: Reengagement Re`en*gage"ment (-ment), n. A renewed or repeated engagement.

reengrave.c: Reengrave Re`en*grave" (-gr?v"), v. t. To engrave anew.

reenjoy.c: Reenjoy Re`en*joy" (-joi"), v. i. To enjoy anew. Pope.

reenkindle.c: Reenkindle Re`en*kin"dle (-k?n"d'l), v. t. To enkindle again.

reenlist.c: Reenlist Re`en*list" (-l?st"), v. t. & i. To enlist again.

reenslave.c: Reenslave Re`en*slave" (-sl?v"), v. t. To enslave again.

reenter.c: Reenter re-enter Re*en"ter, Re-en"ter (r?*?n"t?r), v. t. 1. To enter again; as, You cannot re-enter the country with this visa.
Reenter Re*en"ter, v. i. To enter anew or again.

reentering.c: Reentering Re*en"ter*ing, n. (Calico Printing.) The process of applying additional colors, by applications of printing blocks, to patterns already partly colored.

reenthrone.c: Reenthrone Re`en*throne" (-thr?n"), v. t. To enthrone again; to replace on a throne.

reentrance.c: Reentrance Re*en"trance (rē`ĕn"trains), n. The act entering again; reentry. Hooker.

reentrant.c: Reentrant Re*en"trant (rē`ĕn"traint), a. Reentering; pointing or directed inwards; as, a reentrant angle.

reentry.c: Reentry Re*en"try (rē`ĕn"try̆), n. 1. A second or new entry; as, a reentry into public life.

reerect.c: Reerect Re`e*rect" (r?`?*r?kt"), v. t. To erect again.

reestablish.c: Reestablish Re`es*tab"lish (r?`?s*t?b"l?sh), v. t. To establish anew; to fix or confirm again; to restore; as, to reestablish a covenant; to reestablish health.

reestablisher.c: Reestablisher Re`es*tab"lish*er (-?r), n. One who establishes again.

reestablishment.c: Reestablishment Re`es*tab"lish*ment (-mnt), n. The act reestablishing; the state of being reestablished. Addison.

reestate.c: Reestate Re`es*tate" (-t?t), v. t. To reestablish. [Obs.] Walis.

reeve.c: Reeve Reeve (rēv), n. (Zool.) The female of the ruff.

reexamination.c: Reexamination Re`ex*am`i*na"tion (-?*n?"sh?n), n. A repeated examination. See under Examination.

reexamine.c: Reexamine Re`ex*am"ine (--?n), v. t. To examine anew. Hooker.

reexchange.c: Reexchange Re`ex*change" (r?`?ks*ch?nj"), v. t. To exchange anew; to reverse (a previous exchange).
Reexchange Re`ex*change" n. 1. A renewed exchange; a reversal of an exchange.

reexhibit.c: Reexhibit Re`ex*hib"it (r?`?gz*?b"?t or -?ks*h?b"?t), v. t. To exhibit again.

reexpel.c: Reexpel Re`ex*pel" (r?`?ks*p?l"), v. t. To expel again.

reexperience.c: Reexperience Re`ex*pe"ri*ence (-p?`r?-ens), n. A renewed or repeated experience.

reexport.c: Reexport Re`ex*port" (-p?rt"), v. t. To export again, as what has been imported.
Reexport Re*ex"port (r?*?ks"p?rt), n. Any commodity reexported; -- chiefly in the plural.

reexportation.c: Reexportation Re*ex`por*ta"tion (-p?r*t?"sh?n), n. The act of reexporting, or of exporting an import. A. Smith.

reexpulsion.c: Reexpulsion Re`ex*pul"sion (r?`?ks*p?l"sh?n), n. Renewed or repeated expulsion. Fuller.

reezed.c: Reezed Reezed (rēzd), a. Grown rank; rancid; rusty. [Obs.] “Reezed bacon.” Marston.

refaction.c: Refaction Re*fac"tion (r?*f?k"sh?n), n. [See Refection.] Recompense; atonement; retribution. [Obs.] Howell.

refait.c: Refait ‖Re*fait" (?), n. [F.] (Card Playing) A drawn game; specif. (Trente et quarante), A state of the game in which the aggregate pip value of cards dealt to red equals that of those dealt to black. All bets are then off; unless the value is 31, in which case the banker wins half the stakes.

refar.c: Refar Re*far" (r?*f?r"), v. t. [Cf. F. refaire to do over again.] To go over again; to repeat. [Obs.]

refashion.c: Refashion Re*fash"ion (r?*f?sh"?n), v. t. To fashion anew; to form or mold into shape a second time. MacKnight.

refashionment.c: Refashionment Re*fash"ion*ment (-ment), n. The act of refashioning, or the state of being refashioned. [R.] Leigh Hunt.

refasten.c: Refasten Re*fas"ten (r?*f?s"'n), v. t. To fasten again.

refect.c: Refect Re*fect" (r?*f?kt), v. t. [L. refectus, p. p. of reficere; pref. re- re- + facere to make.] To restore after hunger or fatigue; to refresh. [Archaic] Sir T. Browne.

refection.c: Refection Re*fec"tion (r?*f?k"sh?n), n. [L. refectio: cf. F. réfection. See Refect, Fact.] Refreshment after hunger or fatigue; a repast; a lunch.

refectory.c: Refectory Re*fec"to*ry (-o*ry̆), n.; pl.; Refectories (-r?z). [LL. refectorium: cf. F. réfectoire. See Refection.] A room for refreshment; originally, a dining hall in monasteries or convents.

refel.c: Refel Re*fel" (r?*f?l"), v. t. [L. refellere; pref. re- re- + fallere to deceive.] To refute; to disprove; as, to refel the tricks of a sophister. [Obs.]

refer.c: Refer Re*fer" (re*fẽr"), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Referred (re*fẽrd"); p. pr. & vb. n. Referring.] [F. référer, L. referre; pref. re- re- + ferre to bear. See Bear to carry.] 1. To carry or send back. [Obs.] Chaucer.
Refer Re*fer", v. i. 1. To have recourse; to apply; to appeal; to betake one's self; as, to refer to a dictionary.

referable.c: Referable Ref"er*a*ble (r?f"?r*?*b'l), a. Capable of being referred, or considered in relation to something else; assignable; ascribable. [Written also referrible.]

referee.c: Referee Ref`er*ee" (-?), n. One to whom a thing is referred; a person to whom a matter in dispute has been referred, in order that he may settle it.

reference.c: Reference Ref"er*ence (r?f"?r-ens), n. [See Refer.] 1. The act of referring, or the state of being referred; as, reference to a chart for guidance.

referendary.c: Referendary Ref`er*en"da*ry (r?f`?r*?n"d?*r?), n. [LL. referendarius, fr. L. referendus to be referred, gerundive of referre: cf. F. référendaire. See Refer.] 1. One to whose decision a cause is referred; a referee. [Obs.] Bacon.

referendum.c: Referendum ‖Ref`er*en"dum (r?f`?r*?n"d?m), n.; pl. -da (#) [Gerundive fr. L. referre. See Refer.] 1. A diplomatic agent's note asking for instructions from his government concerning a particular matter or point.

referential.c: Referential Ref`er*en"tial (-shal), a. Containing a reference; pointing to something out of itself; as, notes for referential use. -- Ref`er*en"tial*ly, adv.

referment.c: Referment Re*fer"ment (r?*f?r"ment), n. The act of referring; reference. Laud.
Re-ferment Re`-fer*ment" (r?`f?r*m?nt"), v. t. & i. To ferment, or cause to ferment, again. Blackmore.

refigure.c: Refigure Re*fig"ure (r?*f?g"?r), v. t. To figure again. Shak.

refill.c: Refill Re*fill" (r?*f?l"), v. t. & i. To fill, or become full, again.

refind.c: Refind Re*find" (r?*f?nd), v. t. To find again; to get or experience again. Sandys.

refine.c: Refine Re*fine" (r?*f?n"), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Refined (-find"); p. pr. & vb. n. Refining.] [Pref. re- + fine to make fine: cf. F. raffiner.] 1. To reduce to a fine, unmixed, or pure state; to free from impurities; to free from dross or alloy; to separate from extraneous matter; to purify; to defecate; as, to refine gold or silver; to refine iron; to refine wine or sugar.
Refine Re*fine", v. i. 1. To become pure; to be cleared of feculent matter.

refined.c: Refined Re*fined" (-f?nd"), a. Freed from impurities or alloy; purifed; polished; cultured; delicate; as; refined gold; refined language; refined sentiments.

refinement.c: Refinement Re*fine"ment (r?*f?n"ment), n. [Cf. F. raffinement.] 1. The act of refining, or the state of being refined; as, the refinement or metals; refinement of ideas.

refiner.c: Refiner Re*fin"er (-f?n"?r), n. One who, or that which, refines.

refinery.c: Refinery Re*fin"er*y (-?), n.; pl. Refineries (-?z). [Cf. F. raffinerie.] 1. The building and apparatus for refining or purifying, esp. metals and sugar.

refit.c: Refit Re*fit" (r?*f?t"), v. t. 1. To fit or prepare for use again; to repair; to restore after damage or decay; as, to refit a garment; to refit ships of war. Macaulay.
Refit Re*fit", v. i. To obtain repairs or supplies; as, the fleet returned to refit.

refitment.c: Refitment Re*fit"ment (-ment), n. The act of refitting, or the state of being refitted.

refix.c: Refix Re*fix" (r?*f?ks"), v. t. To fix again or anew; to establish anew. Fuller.

reflame.c: Reflame Re*flame" (r?*fl?m"), v. i. To kindle again into flame.

reflect.c: Reflect Re*flect" (r?*fl?kt"), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Reflected; p. pr. & vb. n. Reflecting.] [L. reflectere, reflexum; pref. re- re- + flectere to bend or turn. See Flexible, and cf. Reflex, v.] 1. To bend back; to give a backwa?d turn to; to throw back; especially, to cause to return after striking upon any surface; as, a mirror reflects rays of light; polished metals reflect heat.
Reflect Re*flect" v. i. 1. To throw back light, heat, or the like; to return rays or beams.

reflected.c: Reflected Re*flect"ed, a. 1. Thrown back after striking a surface; as, reflected light, heat, sound, etc.

reflectent.c: Reflectent Re*flect"ent (r?*fl?kt"ent), a. [L. reflectens, p. pr. of reflectere. See Reflect.] 1. Bending or flying back; reflected. “The ray descendent, and the ray reflectent flying with so great a speed.” Sir K. Digby.

reflectible.c: Reflectible Re*flect"i*ble (-?*b'l), a. Capable of being reflected, or thrown back; reflexible.

reflecting.c: Reflecting Re*flect"ing, a. 1. Throwing back light, heat, etc., as a mirror or other surface.

reflectingly.c: Reflectingly Re*flect"ing*ly, adv. With reflection; also, with censure; reproachfully. Swift.

reflection.c: Reflection Re*flec"tion (r?*fl?k"sh?n), n. [L. reflexio: cf. F. réflexion. See Riflect.] [Written also reflexion.] 1. The act of reflecting, or turning or sending back, or the state of being reflected. Specifically: (a) The return of rays, beams, sound, or the like, from a surface. See Angle of reflection, below.

reflective.c: Reflective Re*flect"ive (r?*fl?kt"?v), a. [Cf. F. réflectif. Cf. Reflexive.] 1. Throwing back images; as, a reflective mirror.

reflector.c: Reflector Re*flect"or (-ẽr), n. [Cf. F. réflecteur.] 1. One who, or that which, reflects. Boyle.

reflet.c: Reflet ‖Re*flet" (rei*flĕ"), n. [F., reflection. See Reflect.] Luster; special brilliancy of surface; -- used esp. in ceramics to denote the peculiar metallic brilliancy seen in lustered pottery such as majolica; as, silver reflet; gold reflet.

reflex.c: Reflex Re"flex (r?"fl?ks), a. [L. reflexus, p. p. of reflectere: cf. F. réflexe. See Reflect.] 1. Directed back; attended by reflection; retroactive; introspective.
Reflex Re"flex (r?"fl?ks; formerly r?*fl?ks"), n. [L. reflexus a bending back. See Reflect.] 1. Reflection; the light reflected from an illuminated surface to one in shade.
Reflex Re*flex" (r?*fl?ks"), v. t. [L. reflexus, p. p. of reflectere. See Reflect.] 1. To reflect. [Obs.] Shak.

reflexed.c: Reflexed Re*flexed" (r?*fl?kst"), a. Bent backward or outward.

reflexibility.c: Reflexibility Re*flex`i*bil"i*ty (r?*fl?ks`?*b?l"?*t?), n. [Cf. F. réflexibilité.] The quality or capability of being reflexible; as, the reflexibility of the rays of light. Sir I. Newton.

reflexible.c: Reflexible Re*flex"i*ble (r?*fl?ks"?*b'l), a. [CF. F. réflexible.] Capable of being reflected, or thrown back.

reflexity.c: Reflexity Re*flex"i*ty (r?*fl?ks"?*t?), n. The state or condition of being reflected. [R.]

reflexive.c: Reflexive Re*flex"ive (-?v), a. 1. [Cf. F. réflexif.] Bending or turned backward; reflective; having respect to something past.

reflexly.c: Reflexly Re*flex"ly, adv. In a reflex manner; reflectively.

reflorescence.c: Reflorescence Re`flo*res"cence (r?`fl?*r?s"sens), n. (Bot.) A blossoming anew of a plant after it has apparently ceased blossoming for the season.

reflourish.c: Reflourish Re*flour"ish (r?*fl?r"?sh), v. t. & i. To flourish again.

reflow.c: Reflow Re*flow" (r?*fl?"), v. i. To flow back; to ebb.

reflower.c: Reflower Re*flow"er (rē*flou"ẽr), v. i. & t. To flower, or cause to flower, again. Sylvester.

refluctuation.c: Refluctuation Re*fluc`tu*a"tion (r?*fl?k`t?*?"sh?n; 135), n. A flowing back; refluence.

refluency.c: Refluency Refluence { Ref"lu*ence (r?f"l?-ens), Ref"lu*en*cy (-en*s?), } n. The quality of being refluent; a flowing back.

refluent.c: Refluent Ref"lu*ent (-ent), a. [L. refluens, p. pr. of refluere to flow back; pref. re- re- + fluere to flow. See Flurent.] Flowing back; returning; ebbing. Cowper.

reflux.c: Reflux Re"flux` (r?"fl?ks`), a. Returning, or flowing back; reflex; as, reflux action.
Reflux Re"flux`, n. [F. reflux. See Refluent, Flux.] A flowing back, as the return of a fluid; ebb; reaction; as, the flux and reflux of the tides.

refocillate.c: Refocillate Re*foc"il*late (r?*f?s"?l*l?t), v. t. [L. refocillatus, p. p. of refocillare; pref. re- re- + focillare to revive by warmth.] To refresh; to revive. [Obs.] Aubrey.

refocillation.c: Refocillation Re*foc`il*la"tion (-l?"sh?n), n. Restoration of strength by refreshment. [Obs.] Middleton.

refold.c: Refold Re*fold" (r?*f?ld"), v. t. To fold again.

refoment.c: Refoment Re`fo*ment" (r?`f?*m?nt"), v. t. To foment anew.

reforest.c: Reforest Re*for"est (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Reforested (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Reforesting.] To replant with trees; to reafforest; to reforestize.

reforestization.c: Reforestization Re*for`est*i*za`tion (r?*f?r`?st*?*z?"sh?n), n. The act or process of reforestizing.

reforestize.c: Reforestize Re*for"est*ize (r?*f?r"?st*?z), v. t. To convert again into a forest; to plant again with trees.

reforge.c: Reforge Re*forge" (r?*f?rj"), v. t. [Pref. re- + forge: cf. F. reforger.] To forge again or anew; hence, to fashion or fabricate anew; to make over. Udall.

reform.c: Reform Re*form" (r?*f?rm"), v. t. [F. réformer, L. reformare; pref. re- re- + formare to form, from forma form. See Form.] To put into a new and improved form or condition; to restore to a former good state, or bring from bad to good; to change from worse to better; to amend; to correct; as, to reform a profligate man; to reform corrupt manners or morals.
Reform Re*form", v. i. To return to a good state; to amend or correct one's own character or habits; as, a man of settled habits of vice will seldom reform.
Reform Re*form", n. [F. réforme.] Amendment of what is defective, vicious, corrupt, or depraved; reformation; as, reform of elections; reform of government.

Re-form Re-form" (r?*f?rm"), v. t. & i. [imp. & p. p. Re-formed (-f?rmd"); p. pr. & vb. n. Re-forming.] To give a new form to; to form anew; to take form again, or to take a new form; as, to re-form the line after a charge.

reformable.c: Reformable Re*form"a*ble (r?*f?rm"?*b'l), a. Capable of being reformed. Foxe.

reformado.c: Reformado Ref`or*ma"do (-m?"d?), n. [Sp., fr. reformar, L. reformare. SEe Reform, v. t.] 1. A monk of a reformed order. [Obs.] Weever.

reformalize.c: Reformalize Re*form"al*ize (r?*f?rm"al*?z), v. i. To affect reformation; to pretend to correctness. [R.]

reformation.c: Reformation Ref`or*ma"tion (r?f`?r*m?"sh?n), n. [F. réformation, L. reformatio.] 1. The act of reforming, or the state of being reformed; change from worse to better; correction or amendment of life, manners, or of anything vicious or corrupt; as, the reformation of manners; reformation of the age; reformation of abuses.
Re-formation Re`-for*ma"tion (r?`f?r*m?"sh?n), n. The act of forming anew; a second forming in order; as, the reformation of a column of troops into a hollow square.

reformative.c: Reformative Re*form"a*tive (r?*f?rm"?*t?v), a. Forming again; having the quality of renewing form; reformatory. Good.

reformatory.c: Reformatory Re*form"a*to*ry (-t?*r?), a. Tending to produce reformation; reformative.
Reformatory Re*form"a*to*ry, n.; pl. -ries (-r?z). An institution for promoting the reformation of offenders.

reformed.c: Reformed Re*formed" (r?*f?rmd"), a. 1. Corrected; amended; restored to purity or excellence; said, specifically, of the whole body of Protestant churches originating in the Reformation. Also, in a more restricted sense, of those who separated from Luther on the doctrine of consubstantiation, etc., and carried the Reformation, as they claimed, to a higher point. The Protestant churches founded by them in Switzerland, France, Holland, and part of Germany, were called the Reformed churches.

reformer.c: Reformer Re*form"er (r?*f?rm"?r), n. 1. One who effects a reformation or amendment; one who labors for, or urges, reform; as, a reformer of manners, or of abuses.

reformist.c: Reformist Re*form"ist, n. [Cf. F. réformiste.] A reformer.

reformly.c: Reformly Re*form"ly, adv. In the manner of a reform; for the purpose of reform. [Obs.] Milton.

refortification.c: Refortification Re*for`ti*fi*ca"tion (r?*f?r`t?*f?*k?"sh?n), n. A fortifying anew, or a second time. Mitford.

refortify.c: Refortify Re*for"ti*fy (r?*f?r"t?*f?), v. t. To fortify anew.

refossion.c: Refossion Re*fos"sion (r?*f?sh"?n), n. [L. refodere, refossum, to dig up again. See Fosse.] The act of digging up again. [Obs.] Bp. Hall.

refound.c: Refound Re*found" (r?*found"), v. t. [Pref. re- + found to cast; cf. F. refondare. Cf. Refund.] 1. To found or cast anew. “Ancient bells refounded.” T. Warton.
Refound Re*found", imp. & p. p. of Refind, v. t.

refract.c: Refract Re*fract" (r?*fr$kt"), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Refracted; p. pr. & vb. n. Refracting.] [L. refractus, p. p. of refringere; pref. re- re- + frangere to break: cf. F. réfracter. SEe FRacture, and cf. Refrain, n.] 1. To bend sharply and abruptly back; to break off.

refractable.c: Refractable Re*fract"a*ble (-?*b'l), a. Capable of being refracted.

refracted.c: Refracted Re*fract"ed, a. 1. (Bot. & Zool.) Bent backward angularly, as if half-broken; as, a refracted stem or leaf.

refracting.c: Refracting Re*fract"ing, a. Serving or tending to refract; as, a refracting medium.

refraction.c: Refraction Re*frac"tion (r?*fr?k"sh?n), n. [F. réfraction.] 1. The act of refracting, or the state of being refracted.

refractive.c: Refractive Re*fract"ive (r?*fr?kt"?v), a. [Cf. F. réfractif. See Refract.] Serving or having power to refract, or turn from a direct course; pertaining to refraction; as, refractive surfaces; refractive powers.

refractiveness.c: Refractiveness Re*fract"ive*ness, n. The quality or condition of being refractive.

refractometer.c: Refractometer Re`frac*tom"e*ter (r?`fr?k*t?m"?*t?r), n. [Refraction + -meter.] (Opt.) A contrivance for exhibiting and measuring the refraction of light.

refractor.c: Refractor Re*fract"or (r?-fr?kt"?r), n. Anything that refracts; specifically: (Opt.) A refracting telescope, in which the image to be viewed is formed by the refraction of light in passing through a convex lens.

refractorily.c: Refractorily Re*frac"to*ri*ly (r?*fr?k"t?*r?*l?), adv. In a refractory manner; perversely; obstinately.

refractoriness.c: Refractoriness Re*frac"to*ri*ness, n. The quality or condition of being refractory.

refractory.c: Refractory Re*frac"to*ry (-r?), a. [L. refractorius, fr. refringere: cf. F. refractaire. See Refract.] 1. Obstinate in disobedience; contumacious; stubborn; unmanageable; as, a refractory child; a refractory beast.
Refractory Re*frac"to*ry, n. 1. A refractory person. Bp. Hall.

refracture.c: Refracture Re*frac"ture (r?*fr?k"t?r;135), n. (Surg.) A second breaking (as of a badly set bone) by the surgeon.
Refracture Re*frac"ture, v. t. (Surg.) To break again, as a bone.

refragable.c: Refragable Ref"ra*ga*ble (r?f"r?*g?*b'l), a. [LL. refragabilis, fr. L. refragari to oppose.] Capable of being refuted; refutable. [R.] -- Ref"ra*ga*ble*ness, n. [R.] -- Ref`ra*ga*bil"i*ty (-b?l`?*t?), n. [R.]

refragate.c: Refragate Ref"ra*gate (-g?t), v. i. [L. refragatus, p. p. of refragor.] To oppose. [R.] Glanvill.

refrain.c: Refrain Re*frain" (re*frān"), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Refrained (-frānd"); p. pr. & vb. n. Refraining.] [OE. refreinen, OF. refrener, F. refréner, fr. L. refrenare; influenced by OF. refraindre to restrain, moderate, fr. LL. refrangere, for L. refringere to break up, break (see Refract). L. refrenare is fr. pref. re- back + frenum bridle; cf. Skr. dhṛ to hold.] 1. To hold back; to restrain; to keep within prescribed bounds; to curb; to govern.
Refrain Re*frain", v. i. To keep one's self from action or interference; to hold aloof; to forbear; to abstain.

Refrain Re*frain", n. [F. refrain, fr. OF. refraindre; cf. Pr. refranhs a refrain, refranher to repeat. See Refract,Refrain, v.] The burden of a song; a phrase or verse which recurs at the end of each of the separate stanzas or divisions of a poetic composition.

reframe.c: Reframe Re*frame" (re*frām), v. t. To frame again or anew.

refrangibility.c: Refrangibility Re*fran`gi*bil"i*ty (r?*fr?n`j?*b?l"?*t?), n. [Cf. F. réfrangibilité.] The quality of being refrangible.

refrangible.c: Refrangible Re*fran"gi*ble (-fr?n"j?*b'l), a. [Cf. F. réfrangible. See Refract.] Capable of being refracted, or turned out of a direct course, in passing from one medium to another, as rays of light. -- Re*fran"gi*ble*ness, n.

refrenation.c: Refrenation Ref`re*na"tion (r?f`r?*n?"sh?n), n. [L. refrenatio. See Refrain, v. t.] The act of refraining. [Obs.]

refresh.c: Refresh Re*fresh" (r?*fr?sh"), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Refreshed (-fr?sht"); p. pr. & vb. n. Refreshing.] [OE. refreshen, refreschen, OF. refreschir (cf. OF. rafraischir, rafreschir, F. rafra?chir); pref. re- re- + fres fresh. F. frais. See Fresh, a.] 1. To make fresh again; to restore strength, spirit, animation, or the like, to; to relieve from fatigue or depression; to reinvigorate; to enliven anew; to reanimate; as, sleep refreshes the body and the mind. Chaucer.
Refresh Re*fresh", n. The act of refreshing. [Obs.] Daniel.

refresher.c: Refresher Re*fresh"er (-?r), n. 1. One who, or that which, refreshes.

refreshful.c: Refreshful Re*fresh"ful (-f?l), a. Full of power to refresh; refreshing. -- Re*fresh"ful*ly, adv.

refreshing.c: Refreshing Re*fresh"ing, a. Reviving; reanimating. -- Re*fresh"ing*ly, adv. -- Re*fresh"ing*ness, n.

refreshment.c: Refreshment Re*fresh"ment (-ment), n. [CF. OF. refreschissement, F. rafraîchissement.] 1. The act of refreshing, or the state of being refreshed; restoration of strength, spirit, vigor, or liveliness; relief after suffering; new life or animation after depression.

refret.c: Refret Re*fret" (r?*fr?t"), n. [OF. refret, L. refractus, p. p. See Refrain, n., Refract.] Refrain. [Obs.] Bailey.

refreyd.c: Refreyd Re*freyd" (r?*fr?d"), v. t. [OF. refreidier.] To chill; to cool. [Obs.]

refrication.c: Refrication Ref`ri*ca"tion (r?f`r?*k?"sh?n), n. [L. refricare to rub again.] A rubbing up afresh; a brightening. [Obs.]

refrigerant.c: Refrigerant Re*frig"er*ant (r?*fr?j"?r-ant), a. [L. refrigerans, p. pr. of refrigerare: cf. F. réfrigérant. See Refrigerate.] Cooling; allaying heat or fever. Bacon.

Refrigerant Re*frig"er*ant, n. That which makes to be cool or cold; specifically, a medicine or an application for allaying fever, or the symptoms of fever; -- used also figuratively. Holland. “A refrigerant to passion.” Blair.

refrigerate.c: Refrigerate Re*frig"er*ate (-āt), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Refrigerated (-ā`tĕd); p. pr. & vb. n. Refrigerating.] [L. refrigeratus, p. p. of refrigerare; pref. re- re- + frigerare to make cool, fr. frigus, frigoris, coolness. See Frigid.] To cause to become cool; to make or keep cold or cool.

refrigeration.c: Refrigeration Re*frig`er*a"tion (-?"sh?n), n. [Cf. F. réfrigération, L. refrigeratio.] The act or process of refrigerating or cooling, or the state of being cooled.

refrigerative.c: Refrigerative Re*frig"er*a*tive (r?*fr?j"?r*?*t?v), a. [Cf. F. réfrigératif.] Cooling; allaying heat. -- n. A refrigerant.

refrigerator.c: Refrigerator Re*frig"er*a`tor (-?`t?r), n. That which refrigerates or makes cold; that which keeps cool. Specifically: (a) A box or room for keeping food or other articles cool, usually by means of ice. (b) An apparatus for rapidly cooling heated liquids or vapors, connected with a still, etc.

refrigeratory.c: Refrigeratory Re*frig"er*a*to*ry (-?*t?*r?), a. [L. refrigeratorius.] Mitigating heat; cooling.

Refrigeratory Re*frig"er*a*to*ry, n.; pl. -ries (-fr?z). [CF. F. réfrigératoire.] That which refrigerates or cools. Specifically: (a) In distillation, a vessel filled with cold water, surrounding the worm, the vapor in which is thereby condensed. (b) The chamber, or tank, in which ice is formed, in an ice machine.

refringency.c: Refringency Re*frin"gen*cy (r?*fr?n"jen*s?), n. The power possessed by a substance to refract a ray; as, different substances have different refringencies. Nichol.

refringent.c: Refringent Re*frin"gent (-jent), a. [L. refringens, p. pr. of refringere. See Refract.] Pertaining to, or possessing, refringency; refractive; refracting; as, a refringent prism of spar. Nichol.

reft.c: Reft Reft (r?ft), imp. & p. p. of Reave. Bereft.
Reft Reft, n. A chink; a rift. See Rift. Rom. of R.

refuge.c: Refuge Ref"uge (r?f"?j), n. [F. réfuge, L. refugium, fr. refugere to flee back; pref. re- + figere. SEe Fugitive.]
Refuge Ref"uge (r?f"?j), v. t. To shelter; to protect. [Obs.]

refugee.c: Refugee Ref`u*gee" (r?f`?*j?"), n. [F. réfugié, fr. se réfugier to take refuge. See Refuge, n.] 1. One who flees to a shelter, or place of safety.

refulgency.c: Refulgency Refulgence { Re*ful"gence (r?*f?l"jens), Re*ful"gen*cy (-jen*s?), } n. [L. refulgentia. See Refulgent.] The quality of being refulgent; brilliancy; splender; radiance.

refulgent.c: Refulgent Re*ful"gent (r?*f?l"jeint), a. [L. refulgens, p. pr. of refulgere to flash back, to shine bright; pref. re- re- + fulgere to shine. See Fulgent.] Casting a bright light; radiant; brilliant; resplendent; shining; splendid; as, refulgent beams. -- Re*ful"gent*ly, adv.

refund.c: Refund Re*fund" (r?*f?nd"), v. t. [Pref. re- + fund.] To fund again or anew; to replace (a fund or loan) by a new fund; as, to refund a railroad loan.
Refund Re*fund" (r?*f?nd"), v. t. [L. refundere; pref. re- re- + fundere to pour: cf. F. refondre, refonder. See Fuse to melt, and cf. Refound to cast again, 1st Refuse.] 1. To pour back. [R. & Obs.]

refundment.c: Refundment Re*fund"ment (-ment), n. The act of refunding; also, that which is refunded. [R.] Lamb.

refurbish.c: Refurbish Re*fur"bish (r?*f?r"b?sh), v. t. To furbish anew.

refurnish.c: Refurnish Re*fur"nish (-n?sh), v. t. To furnish again.

refurnishment.c: Refurnishment Re*fur"nish*ment (-ment), n. The act of refurnishing, or state of being refurnished.

refusable.c: Refusable Re*fus"a*ble (r?*f?z"?*b'l), a. [Cf. F. refusable. See Refuse.] Capable of being refused; admitting of refusal.

refusal.c: Refusal Re*fus"al (-al), n. 1. The act of refusing; denial of anything demanded, solicited, or offered for acceptance.

refuse.c: Refuse Re*fuse" (r?*f?z"), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Refused (-f?zd"); p. pr. & vb. n. Refusing.] [F. refuser, either from (assumed) LL. refusare to refuse, v. freq. of L. refundere to pour back, give back, restore (see Refund to repay), or. fr. L. recusare to decline, refuse cf. Accuse, Ruse), influenced by L. refutare to drive back, repel, refute. Cf. Refute.] 1. To deny, as a request, demand, invitation, or command; to decline to do or grant.
Refuse Re*fuse", v. i. To deny compliance; not to comply.
Refuse Ref`use (r?f"?s;277), n. [F. refus refusal, also, that which is refused. See Refuse to deny.] That which is refused or rejected as useless; waste or worthless matter.
Refuse Ref"use, a. Refused; rejected; hence; left as unworthy of acceptance; of no value; worthless.

refuser.c: Refuser Re*fus"er (r?*f?z"?r), n. One who refuses or rejects.

refut.c: Refut Ref"ut (rĕf"ụt), n. [OF. refuite.] Refuge. “Thou haven of refut.” [Obs.] Chaucer.

refutability.c: Refutability Re*fut`a*bil"i*ty (r?*f?t`?*b?l"?*t?), n. The quality of being refutable.

refutable.c: Refutable Re*fut"a*ble (r?*f?t"?*b'l;277), a. [Cf. F. réfutable.] Admitting of being refuted or disproved; capable of being proved false or erroneous.

refutal.c: Refutal Re*fut"al (r?*f?t"al), n. Act of refuting; refutation.

refutation.c: Refutation Ref`u*ta"tion (r?f`?*t?"sh?n), n. [L. refutatio: cf. F. réfutation.] The act or process of refuting or disproving, or the state of being refuted; proof of falsehood or error; the overthrowing of an argument, opinion, testimony, doctrine, or theory, by argument or countervailing proof.

refutatory.c: Refutatory Re*fut"a*to*ry (re*fūt"ȧ*to*ry̆), a. [L. refutatorius: cf. F. réfutatoire.] Tending to refute; refuting.

refute.c: refute re*fute" (re*fūt"), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Refuted; p. pr. & vb. n. Refuting.] [F. réfuter, L. refuteare to repel, refute. Cf. Confute, Refuse to deny.] To disprove and overthrow by argument, evidence, or countervailing proof; to prove to be false or erroneous; to confute; as, to refute arguments; to refute testimony; to refute opinions or theories; to refute a disputant.

refuter.c: Refuter Re*fut"er (re*fūt"ẽr), n. One who, or that which, refutes.

regain.c: Regain Re*gain" (r?*g?n"), v. t. [Pref. re- + gain: cf. F. regagner.] To gain anew; to get again; to recover, as what has escaped or been lost; to reach again.

regal.c: Regal Re"gal (rē"gail), a. [L. regalis, fr. rex, regis, a king. See Royal, and cf. Rajah, Realm, Regalia.] Of or pertaining to a king; kingly; royal; as, regal authority, pomp, or sway. “The regal title.” Shak.
Regal Re"gal, n. [F. régale, It. regale. CF. Rigoll.] (Mus.) A small portable organ, played with one hand, the bellows being worked with the other, -- used in the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries.

regale.c: Regale ‖Re*ga"le (re*gā"le), n. [LL. regale, pl. regalia, fr. L. regalis: cf. F. régale. See Regal.] A prerogative of royalty. [R.] Johnson.

Regale Re*gale" (re*gāl"), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Regaled (re*gāld"); p. pr. & vb. n. Regaling.] [F. régaler, Sp. regalar to regale, to caress, to melt, perhaps fr. L. regalare to thaw (cff. Gelatin), or cf. Sp. gala graceful, pleasing address, choicest part of a thing (cf. Gala), or most likely from OF. galer to rejoice, gale pleasure.] To entertain in a regal or sumptuous manner; to entertain with something that delights; to gratify; to refresh; as, to regale the taste, the eye, or the ear.
Regale Re*gale", v. i. To feast; to fare sumtuously.
Regale Re*gale", n. [F. régal. See Regale, v. t.] A sumptuous repast; a banquet. Johnson. Cowper.

regalement.c: Regalement Re*gale"ment (re*gāl"meint), n. The act of regaling; anything which regales; refreshment; entertainment.

regalia.c: Regalia Re*ga"li*a (re*gā"lĭ*ȧ), n. pl. [LL., from L. regalisregal. See Regal.] 1. That which belongs to royalty. Specifically: (a) The rights and prerogatives of a king. (b) Royal estates and revenues. (c) Ensigns, symbols, or paraphernalia of royalty.
Regalia Re*ga"li*a, n. A kind of cigar of large size and superior quality; also, the size in which such cigars are classed.

regalian.c: Regalian Re*ga"li*an (-an), a. Pertaining to regalia; pertaining to the royal insignia or prerogatives. Hallam.

regalism.c: Regalism Re"gal*ism (r?"gal*?z'm), n. The doctrine of royal prerogative or supremacy. [R.] Cardinal Manning.

regality.c: Regality Re*gal"i*ty (r?*g?l"?*t?), n. [LL. regalitas, from L. regalis regal, royal. See Regal, and cf. Royality.]

regally.c: Regally Re"gal*ly (r?"gal*l?), adv. In a regal or royal manner.

regard.c: Regard Re*gard" (r?*g?rd"), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Regarded; p. pr. & vb. n. Regarding.] [F. regarder; pref. re- re + garder to guard, heed, keep. See Guard, and cf. Reward.] 1. To keep in view; to behold; to look at; to view; to gaze upon.
Regard Re*gard" (r?*g?rd"), v. i. To look attentively; to consider; to notice. [Obs.] Shak.
Regard Re*gard", n. [F. regard See Regard, v. t.] 1. A look; aspect directed to another; view; gaze.

regardable.c: Regardable Re*gard"a*ble (-?*b'l), a. Worthy of regard or notice; to be regarded; observable. [R.] Sir T. Browne.

regardant.c: Regardant Re*gard"ant (-ant), a. [F. regardant, fr. regarder. See Regard, v. t.] [Written also regardant.] 1. Looking behind; looking backward watchfully.

regardful.c: Regardful Re*gard"ful (-f?l), a. Heedful; attentive; observant. -- Re*gard"ful*ly, adv.

regardless.c: Regardless Re*gard"less, a. 1. Having no regard; heedless; careless; as, regardless of life, consequences, dignity.

regather.c: Regather Re*gath"er (r?*g?th"?r), v. t. To gather again.

regatta.c: Regatta Re*gat"ta (r?*g?t"t?), n.; pl. Regattas (-t?z). [It. regatta, regata.] Originally, a gondola race in Venice; now, a rowing or sailing race, or a series of such races.

regelate.c: Regelate Re"ge*late (r?"j?*l?t or r?j"?-), v. i. (Physics) To freeze together again; to undergo regelation, as ice.

regelation.c: Regelation Re`ge*la"tion (-l?"sh?n), n. [Pref. re- + L. gelatio a freezing.] (Physics) The act or process of freezing anew, or together,as two pieces of ice.

regency.c: Regency Re"gen*cy (r?*jen*s?), n.; pl. Regencies (-s?z). [CF. F. régence, LL. regentia. See Regent, a.] 1. The office of ruler; rule; authority; government.

regeneracy.c: Regeneracy Re*gen"er*a*cy (r?*j?n"?r*?*s?), n. [See Regenerate.] The state of being regenerated. Hammond.

regenerate.c: Regenerate Re*gen"er*ate (-?t), a. [L. regeneratus, p. p. of regenerare to regenerate; pref. re- re- + generare to beget. See Generate.] 1. Reproduced.
Regenerate Re*gen"er*ate (r?*j?n"?r*?t), v. t. 1. To generate or produce anew; to reproduce; to give new life, strength, or vigor to.

regenerateness.c: Regenerateness Re*gen"er*ate*ness (-?t*n?s), n. The quality or state of being rgenerate.

regeneration.c: Regeneration Re*gen`er*a"tion (-?"sh?n), n. [L. regeneratio: cf. F. régéneration.] 1. The act of regenerating, or the state of being regenerated.

regenerative.c: Regenerative Re*gen"er*a*tive (r?*j?n"?r*?*t?v), a. Of or pertaining to regeneration; tending to regenerate; as, regenerative influences. H. Bushnell.

regeneratively.c: Regeneratively Re*gen"er*a*tive*ly, adv. So as to regenerate.

regenerator.c: Regenerator Re*gen"er*a`tor (-?`t?r), n. 1. One who, or that which, regenerates.

regeneratory.c: Regeneratory Re*gen"er*a*to*ry (-?*t?*r?), a. Having power to renew; tending to reproduce; regenerating. G. S. Faber.

regent.c: Regent Re"gent (r?"jent), a. [L. regens, -entis, p. pr. of regere to rule: cf. F. régent. See Regiment.] 1. Ruling; governing; regnant. “Some other active regent principle... which we call the soul.” Sir M. Hale.
Regent Re"gent, n. [F. régent. See Regent, a.] 1. One who rules or reigns; a governor; a ruler. Milton.

Regent diamond Re"gent di"a*mond. A famous diamond of fine quality, which weighs about 137 carats and is among the state jewels of France. It is so called from the Duke of Orleans, Regent of France, to whom it was sold in 1717 by Pitt the English Governor of Madras (whence also called the Pitt diamond), who bought it of an Indian merchant in 1701.

regentess.c: Regentess Re"gent*ess, n. A female regent. [R.] Cotgrave.

regentship.c: Regentship Re"gent*ship, n. The office of a regent; regency.

regerminate.c: Regerminate Re*ger"mi*nate (r?*j?r"m?*n?t), v. i. [Pref. re- + germinate: cf. L. regerminare.] To germinate again.

regermination.c: Regermination Re*ger`mi*na"tion (-n?"sh?n), n. [L. regerminatio.] A germinating again or anew.

regest.c: Regest Re*gest" (r?*j?st"), n. [L. regesta, pl.: cf. OF. regestes, pl. See Register.] A register. [Obs.] Milton.

reget.c: Reget Re*get" (r?*g?t"), v. t. To get again.

regian.c: Regian Re"gi*an (r?"j?-an), n. [L. regius regal.] An upholder of kingly authority; a royalist. [Obs.] Fuller.

regible.c: Regible Reg"i*ble (rĕj"ĭ*b'l), a. [L. regibilis, from regere to rule.] Governable; tractable. [Obs.]

regicidal.c: Regicidal Reg"i*ci`dal (rĕj"ĭ*sī`dail), a. Pertaining to regicide, or to one committing it; having the nature of, or resembling, regicide. Bp. Warburton.

regicide.c: Regicide Reg"i*cide (rĕj"ĭ*sīd), n. [F. régicide; L. rex, regis, a king + caedere to kill. Cf. Homicide.] 1. One who kills or who murders a king; specifically (Eng. Hist.), one of the judges who condemned Charles I. to death.

regidor.c: Regidor ‖Re`gi*dor" (?), n.; pl. -dores (#). [Sp., fr. regir to rule, L. regere.] One of a body of officers charged with the government of Spanish municipalities, corresponding to the English alderman.

regie.c: Regie ‖Ré`gie" (?), n. [F.] 1. Direct management of public finance or public works by agents of the government for government account; -- opposed to the contract system.

regild.c: Regild Re*gild" (rē*gĭld"), v. t. To gild anew.

regime.c: Regime ‖Ré`gime" (r?`zh?m"), n. [F. See Regimen.] 1. Mode or system of rule or management; character of government, or of the prevailing social system.

regimen.c: Regimen Reg"i*men (r?j"?*m?n), n. [L. regimen, -inis, fr. regere to guide, to rule. See Right, and cf. Regal, Régime, Regiment.] 1. Orderly government; system of order; adminisration. Hallam.

regiment.c: Regiment Reg"i*ment (-ment), n. [F. régiment a regiment of men, OF. also government, L. regimentum government, fr. regere to guide, rule. See Regimen.] 1. Government; mode of ruling; rule; authority; regimen. [Obs.] Spenser. “Regiment of health.” Bacon.
Regiment Reg"i*ment (-meint), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Regimented; p. pr. & vb. n. Regimenting.] 1. To form into a regiment or into regiments. Washington.

regimental.c: Regimental Reg`i*men"tal (-mĕn"tail), a. Belonging to, or concerning, a regiment; as, regimental officers, clothing.

regimentally.c: Regimentally Reg`i*men"tal*ly, adv. In or by a regiment or regiments; as, troops classified regimentally.

regimentals.c: Regimentals Reg`i*men"tals (-talz), n. pl. (Mil.) The uniform worn by the officers and soldiers of a regiment; military dress; -- formerly used in the singular in the same sense. Colman.

regiminal.c: Regiminal Re*gim"i*nal (r?*j?m"?*nal), a. Of or relating to regimen; as, regiminal rules.

region.c: Region Re"gion (r?"j?n), n. [F. région, from L. regio a direction, a boundary line, region, fr. regere to guide, direct. See Regimen.] 1. One of the grand districts or quarters into which any space or surface, as of the earth or the heavens, is conceived of as divided; hence, in general, a portion of space or territory of indefinite extent; country; province; district; tract.

regional.c: Regional Re"gion*al (-al), a. Of or pertaining to a particular region; sectional.

regious.c: Regious Re"gi*ous (-j?*?s), a. [L. regius royal, fr. rex, regis, king.] Regal; royal. [Obs.] Harrington.

register.c: Register Reg"is*ter (r?j"?s*t?r), n. [OE. registre, F. registre, LL. registrum,regestum, L. regesta, pl., fr. regerere, regestum, to carry back, to register; pref. re- re- + gerere to carry. See Jest, and cf. Regest.] 1. A written account or entry; an official or formal enumeration, description, or record; a memorial record; a list or roll; a schedule.

Register Reg"is*ter (rĕj"ĭs*tẽr), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Registere (-t?rd); p. pr. & vb. n. Registering.] [Cf. F. regisrer, exregistrer, LL. registrare. See Register, n.] 1. To enter in a register; to record formally and distinctly, as for future use or service.
Register Reg"is*ter, v. i. 1. To enroll one's name in a register.

registering.c: Registering Reg"is*ter*ing, a. Recording; -- applied to instruments; having an apparatus which registers; as, a registering thermometer. See Recording.

registership.c: Registership Reg"is*ter*ship, n. The office of a register.

registrant.c: Registrant Reg"is*trant (-trant), n. [L. registrans, p. pr.] One who registers; esp., one who, by virtue of securing an official registration, obtains a certain right or title of possession, as to a trade-mark.

registrar.c: Registrar Reg"is*trar (-tr?r), n. [LL. registrarius, or F. régistraire. See Register.] One who registers; a recorder; a keeper of records; as, a registrar of births, deaths, and marriages. See Register, n., 3.

registrarship.c: Registrarship Reg"is*trar*ship, n. The office of a registrar.

registration.c: Registration Reg`is*tra"tion (-tr?"sh?n), n. [LL. registratio, or F. régistration. See Register, v.] 1. The act of registering; registry; enrollment.

registry.c: Registry Reg"is*try (r?j"?s*tr?), n. 1. The act of recording or writing in a register; enrollment; registration.

regius.c: Regius ‖Re"gi*us (r?l"?*?s), a. [L. regius, from rex, regis, a king.] Of or pertaining to a king; royal.

regive.c: Regive Re*give" (r?*g?v"), v. t. To give again; to give back.

regle.c: Regle Re"gle (r?g"'l), v. t. [See Reglement.] To rule; to govern. [Obs.] “To regle their lives.” Fuller.

reglement.c: Reglement Re"gle*ment (r?g"'l*ment), n. [F. réglement, fr. régler, L. regulare. See Regulate.] Regulation. [Obs.]

reglementary.c: Reglementary Reg`le*men"ta*ry (-l?*m?n"t?*r?), a. [F. réglementaire, fr. réglement.] Regulative. [R.]

reglet.c: Reglet Reg"let (r?g"l?t), n. [F. réglet, dim. of règle a rule, L. regula. See Rule.] 1. (Arch.) A flat, narrow molding, used chiefly to separate the parts or members of compartments or panels from one another, or doubled, turned, and interlaced so as to form knots, frets, or other ornaments. See Illust. (12) of Column.

regma.c: Regma ‖Reg"ma (r?g"m?), n. [NL., fr. Gr.????, -???, fracture, fr.?????? to break.] (Bot.) A kind of dry fruit, consisting of three or more cells, each which at length breaks open at the inner angle.

regmacarp.c: Regmacarp Reg"ma*carp (-k?rp), n. [Regma + Gr.??? fruit.] (Bot.) Any dry dehiscent fruit.

regnal.c: Regnal Reg"nal (r?g"nal), a. [L. regnum reign.] Of or pertaining to the reign of a monarch; as, regnal years.

regnancy.c: Regnancy Reg"nan*cy (-nan*s?), n. The condition or quality of being regnant; sovereignty; rule. Coleridge.

regnant.c: Regnant Reg"nant (-nant), a. [L. regnans, -antis, p. pr. of regnare to reign: cf. F régnant. See Reign.] 1. Exercising regal authority; reigning; as, a queen regnant.

regne.c: Regne Regne (r?n), n. & v. See Reign. [Obs.] Chaucer.

regorge.c: Regorge Re*gorge" (r?*g?rj"), v. t. [F. regorder; re- + gorger to gorge. Cf. Regurgitate.] 1. To vomit up; to eject from the stomach; to throw back. Hayward.

regrade.c: Regrade Re*grade" (r?*gr?d"), v. i. [L. re- re- + gradi to go. Cf. Regrede. ] To retire; to go back. [Obs.] W. Hales.

regraft.c: Regraft Re*graft" (r?*gr?ft"), v. t. To graft again.

regrant.c: Regrant Re*grant" (r?*gr?nt"), v. t. To grant back; to grant again or anew. Ayliffe.
Regrant Re*grant", n. 1. The act of granting back to a former proprietor.

regrate.c: Regrate Re*grate" (r?*gr?t"), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Regrated; p. pr. & vb. n. Regrating.] [F. regratter, literally, to scrape again. See Re-, and Grate, v. t.] 1. (Masonry) To remove the outer surface of, as of an old hewn stone, so as to give it a fresh appearance.

Regrate Re*grate", v. t. [F. regratter to regrate provisions; of uncertain origin.] (Eng.Law) To buy in large quantities, as corn, provisions, etc., at a market or fair, with the intention of selling the same again, in or near the same place, at a higher price, -- a practice which was formerly treated as a public offense.

regrater.c: Regrater Re*grat"er (-?r), n. [F. regrattier.] One who regrates.

regratery.c: Regratery Re*grat"er*y, n. The act or practice of regrating.

regratiatory.c: Regratiatory Re*gra"ti*a*to*ry (r?*gr?"sh?*?*t?*r?), n. A returning or giving of thanks. [Obs.] Skelton.

regrator.c: Regrator Re*grat"or (r?*gr?t"?r), n. One guilty of regrating.

regrede.c: Regrede Re*grede" (r?*gr?d"), v. i. [L. regredi to go back. Cf. Regrade, Regress.] To go back; to retrograde, as the apsis of a planet's orbit. [R.] Todhunter.

regredience.c: Regredience Re*gre"di*ence (r?*gr?"d?-ens), n. A going back; a retrogression; a return. [R.] Herrick.

regreet.c: Regreet Re*greet" (r?*gr?t"), v. t. To greet again; to resalute; to return a salutation to; to greet. Shak.
Regreet Re*greet", n. A return or exchange of salutation.

regress.c: Regress Re"gress (r?"gr?s), n. [L. regressus, fr. regredi, regressus. See Regrede.] 1. The act of passing back; passage back; return; retrogression. “The progress or regress of man”. F. Harrison.
Regress Re*gress" (r?*gr?s"), v. i. [imp. & p. p. Regressed (-gr?st"); p. pr. & vb. n. Regressing.] To go back; to return to a former place or state. Sir T. Browne.

regression.c: Regression Re*gres"sion (r?*gr?sh"?n), n. [L. regressio: cf. F. régression.] The act of passing back or returning; retrogression; retrogradation. Sir T. Browne.

regressively.c: Regressively Re*gress"ive*ly, adv. In a regressive manner.

regret.c: Regret Re*gret" (r?*gr?t"), n. [F., fr. regretter. See Regret, v.] 1. Pain of mind on account of something done or experienced in the past, with a wish that it had been different; a looking back with dissatisfaction or with longing; grief; sorrow; especially, a mourning on account of the loss of some joy, advantage, or satisfaction. “A passionate regret at sin.” Dr. H. More.

Regret Re*gret", v. t. [imp. & p. p. Regretted (-tĕd); p. pr. & vb. n. Regretting.] [F. regretter, OF. regreter; L. pref. re- re- + a word of Teutonic origin; cf. Goth. grētan to weep, Icel. grāta. See Greet to lament.] To experience regret on account of; to lose or miss with a sense of regret; to feel sorrow or dissatisfaction on account of (the happening or the loss of something); as, to regret an error; to regret lost opportunities or friends.

regretful.c: Regretful Re*gret"ful (-f?l), a. Full of regret; indulging in regrets; repining. -- Re*gret"ful*ly, adv.

regrow.c: Regrow Re*grow" (r?*gr?"), v. i. & t. To grow again.

regrowth.c: Regrowth Re*growth" (r?*gr?th"), n. The act of regrowing; a second or new growth. Darwin.

reguerdon.c: Reguerdon Re*guer"don (r?*g?r"d?n), v. t. [Pref. re- re- + guerdon: cf. OF. reguerdonner.] To reward. [Obs.] Shak.

regulable.c: Regulable Reg"u*la*ble (r?g"?*l?*b'l), a. Capable of being regulated. [R.]

regular.c: Regular Reg"u*lar (-l?r), a. [L. regularis, fr. regula a rule, fr. regere to guide, to rule: cf. F. régulier. See Rule.]

Regular Reg"u*lar (rĕg"u*lẽr), n. [LL. regularis: cf. F. régulier. See Regular, a.] 1. (R. C. Ch.) A member of any religious order or community who has taken the vows of poverty, chastity, and obedience, and who has been solemnly recognized by the church. Bp. Fitzpatrick.

regularia.c: Regularia ‖Reg`u*la"ri*a (rĕg`u*lā"rĭ*ȧ), n. pl. [NL.] (Zool.) A division of Echini which includes the circular, or regular, sea urchins.

regularity.c: Regularity Reg`u*lar"i*ty (-l?r"?*t?), n. [Cf. F. régularité.] The condition or quality of being regular; as, regularity of outline; the regularity of motion.

regularize.c: Regularize Reg"u*lar*ize (rĕg"u*lẽr*īz), v. t. To cause to become regular; to regulate. [R.]

regularly.c: Regularly Reg"u*lar*ly, adv. In a regular manner; in uniform order; methodically; in due order or time.

regulate.c: Regulate Reg"u*late (-lāt), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Regulated (-lā`tĕd); p. pr. & vb. n. Regulating.] [L. regulatus, p. p. of regulare, fr. regula. See Regular.] 1. To adjust by rule, method, or established mode; to direct by rule or restriction; to subject to governing principles or laws.

regulation.c: Regulation Reg`u*la"tion (-l?"sh?n), n. 1. The act of regulating, or the state of being regulated.

regulative.c: Regulative Reg"u*la*tive (r?g"?*l?*t?v), a. 1. Tending to regulate; regulating. Whewell.

regulator.c: Regulator Reg"u*la`tor (-l?`t?r), n. 1. One who, or that which, regulates.

reguline.c: Reguline Reg"u*line (r?g"?*l?n), a. [Cf. F. régulin. See Regulus.] (Chem. & Metal.) Of or pertaining to regulus.

regulize.c: Regulize Reg"u*lize (-l?z), v. t. (Old Chem.) To reduce to regulus; to separate, as a metal from extraneous matter; as, to regulize antimony. [Archaic]

regulus.c: Regulus Reg"u*lus (-l?s), n.; pl. E. Reguluses (-?z), L. Reguli (-l?). [L., a petty king, prince, dim. of rex, regis, a king: cf. F. régule. See Regal.] 1. A petty king; a ruler of little power or consequence.

regurgitate.c: Regurgitate Re*gur"gi*tate (r?*g?r"j?*t?t), v. t. [LL. regurgitare, regurgitatum; L. pref. re- re- + gurges, -itis, a gulf. Cf. Regorge.] To throw or pour back, as from a deep or hollow place; to pour or throw back in great quantity.
Regurgitate Re*gur"gi*tate, v. i. To be thrown or poured back; to rush or surge back.

regurgitation.c: Regurgitation Re*gur`gi*ta"tion (-t?"sh?n), n. [Cf. F. régurgitation.] 1. The act of flowing or pouring back by the orifice of entrance; specifically (Med.), the reversal of the natural direction in which the current or contents flow through a tube or cavity of the body. Quain.

rehabilitate.c: Rehabilitate Re`ha*bil"i*tate (r?`h?*b?l"?*t?t), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Rehabilitated (-t?`t?d); p. pr. & vb. n. Rehabilitating.] [Pref. re- re- + habilitate: cf. LL. rehabilitare, F. réhabiliter.] To invest or clothe again with some right, authority, or dignity; to restore to a former capacity; to reinstate; to qualify again; to restore, as a delinquent, to a former right, rank, or privilege lost or forfeited; -- a term of civil and canon law.

rehabilitation.c: Rehabilitation Re`ha*bil`i*ta"tion (-t?"sh?n), n. [Cf. LL. rehabilitatio, F. Réhabilitation.] The act of rehabilitating, or the state of being rehabilitated. Bouvier. Walsh.

rehash.c: Rehash Re*hash" (r?*h?sh"), v. t. To hash over again; to prepare or use again; as, to rehash old arguments.
Rehash Re*hash", n. Something hashed over, or made up from old materials.

rehear.c: Rehear Re*hear" (r?*h?r"), v. t. To hear again; to try a second time; as, to rehear a cause in Chancery.

rehearsal.c: Rehearsal Re*hears"al (r?*h?rs"a), n. The act of rehearsing; recital; narration; repetition; specifically, a private recital, performance, or season of practice, in preparation for a public exhibition or exercise. Chaucer.

rehearse.c: Rehearse Re*hearse" (r?*h?rs"), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Rehearsed (-h?rst"); p. pr. & vb. n. Rehearsing.] [OE. rehercen, rehersen, OF. reherser, rehercier, to harrow over again; pref. re- re- + hercier to harrow, fr. herce a harrow, F. herse. See Hearse.] 1. To repeat, as what has been already said; to tell over again; to recite. Chaucer.
Rehearse Re*hearse", v. i. To recite or repeat something for practice. “There will we rehearse.” Shak.

reheat.c: Reheat Re*heat" (r?*h?t"), v. t. 1. To heat again.

rehibition.c: Rehibition Re`hi*bi"tion (r?`h?*b?sh"?n), n. [Pref. re- + L. habere to have.] (Law) The returning of a thing purchased to the seller, on the ground of defect or frand.

rehibitory.c: Rehibitory Re*hib"i*to*ry (r?*h?b"?*t?*r?), a. (Law) Of or relating to rehibition; as, a rehibitory action.

rehire.c: Rehire Re*hire" (r?*h?r"), v. t. To hire again.

rehypothecate.c: Rehypothecate Re`hy*poth"e*cate (r?`h?*p?th"?*k?t), v. t. (Law) To hypothecate again. -- Re`hy*poth`e*ca"tion, n.

rei.c: Rei Rei (r?), n.;pl. Reis (r?"?s or r?z). [Pg. real, pl. reis. See Real a coin.] A portuguese money of account, in value about one tenth of a cent. [Spelt also ree.]

reichsrath.c: Reichsrath ‖Reichs"rath` (r?ks"r?t), n. [G] The parliament of Austria (exclusive of Hungary, which has its own diet, or parliament). It consists of an Upper and a Lower House, or a House of Lords and a House of Representatives.

reichsstand.c: Reichsstand ‖Reichs"stand` (r?ks"st?t`), n. [G.] A free city of the former German empire.

reichstag.c: Reichstag ‖Reichs"tag` (r?ks"t?g`), n. [G.] 1. [Note: from the 1913 definition] The Diet, or House of Representatives, of the German empire (and of the Weimar Republic), which was composed of members elected for a term of three years by the direct vote of the people. This term is no longer (in 1997) applied to the German parliament. See also Bundesrath.

reigle.c: Reigle Rei"gle (r?"g'l), n. [F. règle a rule, fr. L. regula. See Rule.] A hollow cut or channel for quiding anything; as, the reigle of a side post for a flood gate. Carew.
Reigle Rei"gle, v. t. To regulate; to govern. [Obs.]

reiglement.c: Reiglement Rei"gle*ment (-ment), n. [See Reglement.] Rule; regulation. [Obs.] Bacon. Jer. Taylor.

reign.c: Reign Reign (rān), n. [OE. regne, OF. reigne, regne, F. règne, fr. L. regnum, fr. rex, regis, a king, fr. regere to guide, rule. See Regal, Regimen.] 1. Royal authority; supreme power; sovereignty; rule; dominion.

Reign Reign (r?n), v. i. [imp. & p. p. Reigned (r?nd); p. pr. & vb. n. Reigning.] [OE. regnen, reinen, OF. regner, F. régner, fr. L. regnare, fr. regnum. See Reign, n.] 1. To possess or exercise sovereign power or authority; to exercise government, as a king or emperor;; to hold supreme power; to rule. Chaucer.

reillume.c: Reillume Re`il*lume" (r?`?l*l?m"), v. t. To light again; to cause to shine anew; to relume; to reillumine. “Thou must reillume its spark.” J. R. Drake.

reilluminate.c: Reilluminate Re`il*lu"mi*nate (-l?"m?*n?t), v. t. To enlighten again; to reillumine.

reillumination.c: Reillumination Re`il*lu`mi*na"tion (-n?"sh?n), n. The act or process of enlightening again.

reillumine.c: Reillumine Re`il*lu"mine (-l?"m?n), v. t. To illumine again or anew; to reillume.

reim.c: Reim Reim (r?m), n. [D. riem, akin to G riemen; CF. Gr.???? a towing line.] A strip of oxhide, deprived of hair, and rendered pliable, -- used for twisting into ropes, etc. [South Africa] Simmonds.

reimbark.c: Reimbark Re`im*bark" (r?`?m*b?rk"), v. t. & i. See Reembark.

reimbody.c: Reimbody Re`im*bod"y (-b?d"?), v. t. & i. [See Reembody.] To imbody again. Boyle.

reimbursable.c: Reimbursable Re`im*burs"a*ble (r?`?m*b?rs"?*b'l), a. [CF. F. remboursable.] Capable of being repaid; repayable.

reimburse.c: Reimburse Re`im*burse" (-b?rs"), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Reimbursed (-b?rst"); p. pr. & vb. n. Reimbursing.] [Pref. re- + imburse: cf. F. rembourser.] 1. To replace in a treasury or purse, as an equivalent for what has been taken, lost, or expended; to refund; to pay back; to restore; as, to reimburse the expenses of a war.

reimbursement.c: Reimbursement Re`im*burse"ment (-b?rs"ment), n. [Cf. F. rembursement.] The act reimbursing. A. Hamilton.

reimplant.c: Reimplant Re`im*plant" (-pl?nt"), v. t. To implant again.

reimport.c: Reimport Re`im*port" (-p?rt"), v. t. [Pref. re- + import: cf. F. remporter.] To import again; to import what has been exported; to bring back. Young.

reimportation.c: Reimportation Re*im`por*ta"tion (r?*?m`p?r*t?"sh?n), n. The act of reimporting; also, that which is reimported.

reimportune.c: Reimportune Re*im`por*tune" (-p?r*t?n"), v. t. To importune again.

reimpose.c: Reimpose Re`im*pose" (r?`?m*p?z), v. t. To impose anew.

reimpregnate.c: Reimpregnate Re`im*preg"nate (-pr?g"n?t), v. t. To impregnate again or anew. Sir T. Browne.

reimpress.c: Reimpress Re`im*press" (-pr?s"), v. t. To impress anew.

reimpression.c: Reimpression Re`im*pres"sion (-pr?sh"?n), n. A second or repeated impression; a reprint.

reimprint.c: Reimprint Re`im*print" (-pr?nt"), v. t. To imprint again.

reimprison.c: Reimprison Re`im*pris"on (-pr?z'n), v. t. To imprison again.

reimprisonment.c: Reimprisonment Re`im*pris"on*ment (-ment), n. The act of reimprisoning, or the state of being reimprisoned.

rein.c: Rein Rein (r?n), n. [F. rêne, fr. (assumed) LL. retina, fr. L. retinere to hold back. See Retain.] 1. The strap of a bridle, fastened to the curb or snaffle on each side, by which the rider or driver governs the horse.
Rein Rein, v. t. [imp. & p. p. Reined (r?nd); p. pr. & vb. n. Reining.] 1. To govern or direct with the reins; as, to rein a horse one way or another.
Rein Rein, v. i. To be guided by reins. [R.] Shak.

reinaugurate.c: Reinaugurate Re`in*au"gu*rate, v. t. To inaugurate anew.

reincit.c: Reincit Re"in*cit" (-s?t"), v. t. To incite again.

reincorporate.c: Reincorporate Re`in*cor"po*rate, v. t. To incorporate again.

reincrease.c: Reincrease Re`in*crease" (-kr?s"), v. t. To increase again.

reincur.c: Reincur Re`in*cur" (-k?r"), v. t. To incur again.

reindeer.c: Reindeer Rein"deer` (rān"dēr), n. [Icel. hreinn reindeer + E. deer. Icel. hreinn is of Lapp or Finnish origin; cf. Lappish reino pasturage.] [Formerly written also raindeer, and ranedeer.] (Zool.) Any ruminant of the genus Rangifer, of the Deer family, found in the colder parts of both the Eastern and Western hemispheres, and having long irregularly branched antlers, with the brow tines palmate.

reinduce.c: Reinduce Re`in*duce" (r?`?n*d?s"), v. t. To induce again.

reinette.c: Reinette Rei*nette" (r?*n?t"), n. [F. See 1st Rennet.] (Bot.) A name given to many different kinds of apples, mostly of French origin.

reinfect.c: Reinfect Re`in*fect" (r?`?n*f?kt), v. t. [Pref. re- + infect: cf. F. réinfecter.] To infect again.

reinforce.c: Reinforce Re`in*force" (-f?rs"), v. t. See Reenforce, v. t.

reinforced.c: Reinforced concrete Re`in*forced con"crete. Concrete having within its mass a system of iron or steel supports, such as bars, rods, or a heavy mesh, to provide increased tensile strength and shear resistance. Same as Ferro-concrete. [Also spelled reenforced concrete.]

reinfund.c: Reinfund Re`in*fund" (-f?nd"), v. i. [Pref. re- + L. infundere to pour in.] To flow in anew. [Obs.] Swift.

reingratiate.c: Reingratiate Re`in*gra"ti*ate (-gr?"sh?*?t), v. t. To ingratiate again or anew. Sir. T. Herbert.

reinhabit.c: Reinhabit Re`in*hab"it (-h?b"?t), v. t. To inhabit again. Mede.

reinless.c: Reinless Rein"less (r?n"l?s), a. Not having, or not governed by, reins; hence, not checked or restrained.

reins.c: Reins Reins (rānz), n. pl. [F. rein, pl. reins, fr. L. ren, pl. renes.] 1. The kidneys; also, the region of the kidneys; the loins.

reinsert.c: Reinsert Re`in*sert" (r?`?n*s?rt"), v. t. To insert again.

reinsertion.c: Reinsertion Re`in*ser"tion (-s?r"sh?n), n. The act of reinserting.

reinspect.c: Reinspect Re`in*spect" (-sp?kt"), v. t. To inspect again.

reinspection.c: Reinspection Re`in*spec"tion (-sp?k"sh?n), n. The act of reinspecting.

reinspire.c: Reinspire Re`in*spire" (-sp?r"), v. t. To inspire anew. Milton.

reinspirit.c: Reinspirit Re`in*spir"it (-sp`r"?t), v. t. To give fresh spirit to.

reinstall.c: reinstall re-install Re`in*stall", Re`-in*stall" (-st?l"), v. t. [Pref. re- + install: cf. F. réinstaller.] To install again; as, She reinstalled the the washer after it had been repaired. Milton.

reinstate.c: Reinstate Re`in*state" (-st?t"), v. t. To place again in possession, or in a former state; to restore to a state from which one had been removed; to instate again; as, to reinstate a king in the possession of the kingdom.

reinstatement.c: Reinstatement Re`in*state"ment (-ment), n. The act of reinstating; the state of being reinstated; re?stablishment.

reinstruct.c: Reinstruct Re`in*struct" (-str?kt"), v. t. To instruct anew.

reinsurance.c: Reinsurance Re`in*sur"ance (-sh?r"ans), n. 1. Insurance a second time or again; renewed insurance.

reinsure.c: Reinsure Re`in*sure" (-sh?r"), v. t. 1. To insure again after a former insurance has ceased; to renew insurance on.

reinsurer.c: Reinsurer Re`in*sur"er (-sh?r"?r), n. One who gives reinsurance.

reintegrate.c: Reintegrate Re*in"te*grate (r?*?n"t?*gr?t), v. t. [Pref. re- + integrate. Cf. Redintegrate.] To renew with regard to any state or quality; to restore; to bring again together into a whole, as the parts of anything; to reestablish; as, to reintegrate a nation. Bacon.

reintegration.c: Reintegration Re*in`te*gra"tion (-gr?"sh?n), n. A renewing, or making whole again. See Redintegration.

reinter.c: Reinter Re`in*ter" (r?`?n*t?r"), v. t. To inter again.

reinterrogate.c: Reinterrogate Re`in*ter"ro*gate (-t?r"r?*g?t), v. t. To interrogate again; to question repeatedly. Cotgrave.

reinthronize.c: Reinthronize Re`in*thron"ize (-?z), v. t. To enthrone again. [Obs.]

reintroduce.c: Reintroduce Re*in`tro*duce" (r?*?n`tr?*d?s"), v. t. To introduce again. -- Re*in`tro*duc"tion (-d?k"sh?n), n.

reinvest.c: Reinvest Re`in*vest" (r?`?n*v?st"), v. t. To invest again or anew.

reinvestigate.c: Reinvestigate Re`in*ves"ti*gate (-v?s"t?*g?t), v. t. To investigate again. -- Re`in*ves`ti*ga"tion (-g?"sh?n), n.

reinvestment.c: Reinvestment Re`in*vest"ment (-v?st"ment), n. The act of investing anew; a second or repeated investment.

reinvigorate.c: Reinvigorate Re`in*vig"or*ate (-v?g"?r*?t), v. t. To invigorate anew.

reinvolve.c: Reinvolve Re`in*volve" (-v?lv"), v. t. To involve anew.

reis.c: Reis ‖Re`is (r?"?s or r?z), n. [Pg., pl. of real, an ancient Portuguese coin.] The word is used as a Portuguese designation of money of account, one hundred reis being about equal in value to eleven cents.
Reis Reis (rīs), n. [Ar. raïs head, chief, prince.] A common title in the East for a person in authority, especially the captain of a ship. [Written also rais and ras.]
Reis Effendi ‖Reis` Ef*fen"di (r?s`?f*f?n"d?). [See 2d Reis, and Effendi.] A title formerly given to one of the chief Turkish officers of state. He was chancellor of the empire, etc.

reissners.c: Reissner's membrane Reiss"ner's mem"brane (r?s"n?rz m?m"br?n). [Named from E. Reissner, A German anatomist.] (Anat.) The thin membrane which separates the canal of the cochlea from the vestibular scala in the internal ear.

reissuable.c: Reissuable Re*is"su*a*ble (r?*?sh"?*?*b'l), a. Capable of being reissued.

reissue.c: Reissue Re*is"sue (r?*?sh"?), v. t. & i. To issue a second time.
Reissue Re*is"sue, n. A second or repeated issue.

reit.c: Reit Reit (r?t), n. Sedge; seaweed. [Obs. or Prov. Eng.]

reiter.c: Reiter ‖Rei"ter (r?"t?r), n. [G., rider.] A German cavalry soldier of the fourteenth and fifteenth centuries.

reiterant.c: Reiterant Re*it"er*ant (r?-?t"?r-aint), a. [See Reiterate.] Reiterating. [R.] Mrs. Browning.

reiterate.c: Reiterate Re*it"er*ate (-āt), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Reiterated (-ā`tĕd); p. pr. & vb. n. Reiterating.] [Pref. re- + iterate: cf. F. réitérer, LL. reiterare to question again.] To repeat again and again; to say or do repeatedly; sometimes, to repeat.

reiteration.c: Reiteration Re*it`er*a"tion (-?"sh?n), n. [Cf. F. réitération.] The act of reiterating; that which is reiterated.

reiterative.c: Reiterative Re*it"er*a*tive (r?-?t"?r-?-t?v), n. 1. (Gram.) A word expressing repeated or reiterated action.

reject.c: Reject Re*ject" (r?-j?kt"), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Rejected; p. pr. & vb. n. Rejecting.] [L. rejectus, p. p. of reicere, rejicere; pref. re- re- + jacere to throw: cf. F. rejeter, formerly also spelt rejecter. See Jet a shooting forth.] 1. To cast from one; to throw away; to discard.

rejectable.c: Rejectable Re*ject"a*ble (-?-b'l), a. Capable of being, or that ought to be, rejected.

rejectamenta.c: Rejectamenta ‖Re*jec`ta*men"ta (r?-j?k`t?-m?n"ta), n. pl. [NL., fr. L. rejectare, v. intens. fr. rejicere. See Reject.] Things thrown out or away; especially, things excreted by a living organism. J. Fleming.

rejectaneous.c: Rejectaneous Re`jec*ta"ne*ous (r?`j?k-t?"n?-?s), a. [L. rejectaneus.] Not chosen or received; rejected. [Obs.] “Profane, rejectaneous, and reprobate people.” Barrow.

rejection.c: Rejection Re*jec"tion (r?-j?k"sh?n), n. [L. rejectio: cf. F. réjection.] Act of rejecting, or state of being rejected.

rejectitious.c: Rejectitious Re`jec*ti"tious (r?`j?k-t?sh"?s), a. Implying or requiring rejection; rejectable. Cudworth.

rejective.c: Rejective Re*ject"ive (r?-j?kt"?v), a. Rejecting, or tending to reject.

rejectment.c: Rejectment Re*ject"ment (-ment), n. Act of rejecting; matter rejected, or thrown away. Eaton.

rejoice.c: Rejoice Re*joice" (re*jois"), v. i. [imp. & p. p. Rejoiced (-joist"); p. pr. & vb. n. Rejoicing (-joi"s?ng).] [OE. rejoissen, OF. resjouir, resjoir, F. réjouir; pref. re- re- + OF. esjouir, esjoir, F. éjouir, to rejoice; pref. es- (L. ex-) + OF. jouir, joir, F. jouir, from L. gaudere to rejoice. See Joy.] To feel joy; to experience gladness in a high degree; to have pleasurable satisfaction; to be delighted. “O, rejoice beyond a common joy.” Shak.
Rejoice Re*joice", v. t. 1. To enjoy. [Obs.] Bp. Peacock.
Rejoice Re*joice", n. The act of rejoicing. Sir T. Browne.

rejoicingly.c: Rejoicingly Re*joi"cing*ly, adv. With joy or exultation.

rejoin.c: Rejoin Re*join" (r?-join"), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Rejoined (-joind"); p. pr. & vb. n. Rejoining.] [F. rejoindre; pref. re- re- + joindre to join. See Join, and cf. Rejoinder.] 1. To join again; to unite after separation.
Rejoin Re*join", v. i. 1. To answer to a reply.

rejoinder.c: Rejoinder Re*join"der (-d?r), n. [From F. rejoindre, inf., to join again. See Rejoin.] 1. An answer to a reply; or, in general, an answer or reply.
Rejoinder Re*join"der, v. i. To make a rejoinder. [Archaic]

rejoindure.c: Rejoindure Re*join"dure (-d?r), n. Act of joining again. [Obs.] “Beguiles our lips of all rejoindure” Shak.

rejoint.c: Rejoint Re*joint" (re-joint"), v. t. 1. To reunite the joints of; to joint anew. Barrow.

rejolt.c: Rejolt Re*jolt" (r?-j?lt"), n. A reacting jolt or shock; a rebound or recoil. [R.]
Rejolt Re*jolt", v. t. To jolt or shake again. Locke.

rejourn.c: Rejourn Re*journ" (r?-j?rn"), v. t. [Cf. F. réajourner. See Adjourn.] To adjourn; to put off. [Obs.] Shak.

rejudge.c: Rejudge Re*judge" (r?-j?j"), v. t. To judge again; to reexamine; to review; to call to a new trial and decision.

rejuvenate.c: Rejuvenate Re*ju"ve*nate (r?-j?"v?-n?t), v. t. [Pref. re- re- + L. juventis young, youthful.] To render young again.

rejuvenated.c: Rejuvenated Re*ju"ve*na`ted (?), p. a. from Rejuvenate. 1. Rendered young again; as, rejuvenated life.

rejuvenescence.c: Rejuvenescence Re*ju`ve*nes"cence (-n?s"sens), n. 1. A renewing of youth; the state of being or growing young again.

rejuvenescent.c: Rejuvenescent Re*ju`ve*nes"cent (-sent), a. Becoming, or causing to become, rejuvenated; rejuvenating.

rekindle.c: Rekindle Re*kin"dle (r?-k?n"d'l), v. t. & i. To kindle again.

rekne.c: Rekne Rek"ne (r?k"ne), v. t. To reckon. [Obs.] Chaucer.

relade.c: Relade Re*lade" (rē*lād"), v. t. To lade or load again.

relaid.c: Relaid Re*laid" (rē*lād"), imp. & p. p. of Relay.

relais.c: Relais ‖Re*lais" (rei*la"), n. [F. See Relay, n.] (Fort.) A narrow space between the foot of the rampart and the scarp of the ditch, serving to receive the earth that may crumble off or be washed down, and prevent its falling into the ditch. Wilhelm.

reland.c: Reland Re*land" (r?-l?nd"), v. t. To land again; to put on land, as that which had been shipped or embarked.
Reland Re*land", v. i. To go on shore after having embarked; to land again.

relapse.c: Relapse Re*lapse" (r?-l?ps"), v. i. [imp. & p. p. Relapsed (-l?pst"); p. pr. & vb. n. Relapsing.] [L. relapsus, p. p. of relabi to slip back, to relapse; pref. re- re- + labi to fall, slip, slide. See Lapse.] 1. To slip or slide back, in a literal sense; to turn back. [Obs.] Dryden.

Relapse Re*lapse", n. [For sense 2 cf. F. relaps. See Relapse, v.] 1. A sliding or falling back, especially into a former bad state, either of body or morals; backsliding; the state of having fallen back.

relapser.c: Relapser Re*laps"er (-l?ps"?r), n. One who relapses. Bp. Hall.

relapsing.c: Relapsing Re*laps"ing, a. Marked by a relapse; falling back; tending to return to a former worse state.

relate.c: Relate Re*late" (r?-l?t"), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Related; p. pr. & vb. n. Relating.] [F. relater to recount, LL. relatare, fr. L. relatus, used as p. p. of referre. See Elate, and cf. Refer.] 1. To bring back; to restore. [Obs.]
Relate Re*late", v. i. 1. To stand in some relation; to have bearing or concern; to pertain; to refer; -- with to.

related.c: Related Re*lat"ed (-l?t"?d), p. p. & a. 1. Allied by kindred; connected by blood or alliance, particularly by consanguinity; as, persons related in the first or second degree.

relatedness.c: Relatedness Re*lat"ed*ness, n. The state or condition of being related; relationship; affinity. [R.] Emerson.

relater.c: Relater Re*lat"er (-?r), n. One who relates or narrates.

relation.c: Relation Re*la"tion (r?-l?"sh?n), n. [F. relation, L. relatio. See Relate.] 1. The act of relating or telling; also, that which is related; recital; account; narration; narrative; as, the relation of historical events.

relational.c: Relational Re*la"tion*al (r?-l?"sh?n-al), a. 1. Having relation or kindred; related.

relationist.c: Relationist Re*la"tion*ist, n. A relative; a relation. [Obs.]

relationship.c: Relationship Re*la"tion*ship, n. The state of being related by kindred, affinity, or other alliance. Mason.

relative.c: Relative Rel"a*tive (r?l"?-t?v), a. [F. relatif, L. relativus. See Relate.] 1. Having relation or reference; referring; respecting; standing in connection; pertaining; as, arguments not relative to the subject.

Relative Rel"a*tive, n. One who, or that which, relates to, or is considered in its relation to, something else; a relative object or term; one of two object or term; one of two objects directly connected by any relation. Specifically: (a) A person connected by blood or affinity; strictly, one allied by blood; a relation; a kinsman or kinswoman. “Confining our care... to ourselves and relatives.” Bp. Fell. (b) (Gram.) A relative pronoun; a word which relates to, or represents, another word or phrase, called its antecedent; as, the relatives “who”, “which”, “that”.

relatively.c: Relatively Rel"a*tive*ly, adv. In a relative manner; in relation or respect to something else; not absolutely.

relativeness.c: Relativeness Rel"a*tive*ness, n. The state of being relative, or having relation; relativity.

relativity.c: relativity rel`a*tiv"i*ty (-t?v"?-t?), n. 1. The state of being relative; as, the relativity of a subject. Coleridge.

relator.c: Relator Re*lat"or (r?-l?t"?r), n. [ L.: cf. F. relateur. See Relate.] 1. One who relates; a relater. “The several relators of this history.” Fuller.

relax.c: Relax Re*lax" (r?-l?ks"), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Relaxed (-l?kst"); p. pr. & vb. n. Relaxing.] [L. relaxare; pref. re- re- + laxare to loose, to slacken, from laxus loose. See Lax, and cf. Relay, n., Release.] 1. To make lax or loose; to make less close, firm, rigid, tense, or the like; to slacken; to loosen; to open; as, to relax a rope or cord; to relax the muscles or sinews.
Relax Re*lax", v. i. 1. To become lax, weak, or loose; as, to let one's grasp relax.
Relax Re**lax", a. Relaxed; lax; hence, remiss; careless.

relaxable.c: Relaxable Re*lax"a*ble (-?-b'l), a. Capable of being relaxed.

relaxant.c: Relaxant Re*lax"ant (r?-l?ks"ant), n. [L. relaxans, p. pr. of relaxare.] (Med.) A medicine that relaxes; a laxative.

relaxation.c: Relaxation Re`lax*a"tion (r?`l?ks-?"sh?n;277), n. [L. relaxatio; cf. F. relaxation.] 1. The act or process of relaxing, or the state of being relaxed; as, relaxation of the muscles; relaxation of a law.

relaxative.c: Relaxative Re*lax"a*tive (r?-l?ks"?-t?v), a. Having the quality of relaxing; laxative. -- n. A relaxant. B. Jonson.

relay.c: Relay Re*lay" (r?-l?"), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Relaid (-l?d); p. pr. & vb. n. Relaying.] [Pref. re- + lay, v.] To lay again; to lay a second time; as, to relay a pavement.

Relay Re*lay" (r?-l?"), n. [F. relais (cf. OF. relais relaxation, discontinuance, It. rilascio release, relief, rilasso relay), fr. OF. relaissier to abandon, release, fr. L. relaxare. See Relax.] 1. A supply of anything arranged beforehand for affording relief from time to time, or at successive stages; provision for successive relief. Specifically: (a) A supply of horses placced at stations to be in readiness to relieve others, so that a trveler may proceed without delay. (b) A supply of hunting dogs or horses kept in readiness at certain places to relive the tired dogs or horses, and to continue the pursuit of the game if it comes that way. (c) A number of men who relieve others in carrying on some work.

Relay Re*lay", a. (Mach.) Relating to, or having the characteristics of, an auxiliary apparatus put into action by a feeble force but itself capable of exerting greater force, used to control a comparatively powerful machine or appliance.
Relay cylinder Relay cylinder. In a variable expansion central-valve engine, a small auxiliary engine for automatically adjusting the steam distribution to the load on the main engine.
Relay governor Relay governor. A speed regulator, as a water-wheel governor, embodying the relay principle.

relbun.c: Relbun Rel"bun (r?l"b?n), n. The roots of the Chilian plant Calceolaria arachnoidea, -- used for dyeing crimson.

releasable.c: Releasable Re*leas"a*ble (r?-l?s"?-b'l), a. That may be released.

release.c: Release Re*lease" (r?-l?s"), v. t. [Pref. re + lease to let.] To lease again; to grant a new lease of; to let back.

Release Re*lease" (r?-l?s"), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Released (r?*l?st"); p. pr. & vb. n. Releasing.] [OE. relessen, OF. relassier, to release, to let free. See Relay, n., Relax, and cf. Release to lease again.] 1. To let loose again; to set free from restraint, confinement, or servitude; to give liberty to, or to set at liberty; to let go.

Release Re*lease", n. 1. The act of letting loose or freeing, or the state of being let loose or freed; liberation or discharge from restraint of any kind, as from confinement or bondage. “Who boast'st release from hell.” Milton.

releasee.c: Releasee Re*leas`ee" (-?"), n. One to whom a release is given.

releasement.c: Releasement Re*lease"ment (r?-l?s"ment), n. The act of releasing, as from confinement or obligation. Milton.

releaser.c: Releaser Re*leas"er (-?r), n. One who releases, or sets free.

releasor.c: Releasor Re*leas"or (-?r), n. One by whom a release is given.

relegate.c: Relegate Rel"e*gate (r?l"?-g?t), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Relegated (-g?`t?d); p. pr. & vb. n. Relegating.] [L. relegatus, p. p. of relegare; pref. re- re- + legare to send with a commission or charge. See Legate.] To remove, usually to an inferior position; to consign; to transfer; specifically, to send into exile; to banish.

relegation.c: Relegation Rel`e*ga"tion (-g?"sh?n), n. [L. relegatio: cf. F. relégation.] The act of relegating, or the state of being relegated; removal; banishment; exile.

relent.c: Relent Re*lent" (r?-l?nt"), v. i. [imp. & p. p. Relented; p. pr. & vb. n. Relenting.] [F. ralentir, fr. L. pref. re- re- + ad to + lentus pliant, flexible, slow. See Lithe.] 1. To become less rigid or hard; to yield; to dissolve; to melt; to deliquesce. [Obs.]
Relent Re*lent", v. t. 1. To slacken; to abate. [Obs.]

relentless.c: Relentless Re*lent"less, a. Unmoved by appeals for sympathy or forgiveness; insensible to the distresses of others; destitute of tenderness; unrelenting; unyielding; unpitying; as, a prey to relentless despotism.

relentment.c: Relentment Re*lent"ment (-meint), n. The act or process of relenting; the state of having relented. Sir T. Browne.

relesse.c: Relesse Re*lesse" (r?-l?s"), v. t. To release. [Obs.] Chaucer.

relet.c: Re-let Re-let" (r?-l?t"), v. t. To let anew, as a house.

relevancy.c: Relevancy Relevance { Rel"e*vance (r?l"?*vans), Rel"e*van*cy (-van*s?), } n. 1. The quality or state of being relevant; pertinency; applicability.

relevant.c: Relevant Rel"e*vant (-vant), a. [F. relevant, p. pr. of relever to raise again, to relieve. See Relieve.] 1. Relieving; lending aid or support. [R.] Pownall.

relevantly.c: Relevantly Rel"e*vant*ly, adv. In a relevant manner.

relevation.c: Relevation Rel`e*va"tion (-v?"sh?n), n. [L. relevatio, fr. relevare. See Relieve.] A raising or lifting up. [Obs.]

reliability.c: Reliability Re*li`a*bil"i*ty (r?-l?`?-b?l"?-t?), n. The state or quality of being reliable; reliableness.

reliable.c: Reliable Re*li"a*ble (r?-l?"?-b'l), a. Suitable or fit to be relied on; worthy of dependance or reliance; trustworthy. “A reliable witness to the truth of the miracles.” A. Norton.

reliance.c: Reliance Re*li"ance (-ans), n. [From Rely.] 1. The act of relying, or the condition or quality of being reliant; dependence; confidence; trust; repose of mind upon what is deemed sufficient support or authority.

reliant.c: Reliant Re*li"ant (-ant), a. Having, or characterized by, reliance; confident; trusting.

relic.c: Relic Rel"ic (r?l"?k), n. [F. relique, from L. reliquiae, pl., akin to relinquere to leave behind. See Relinquish.] [Formerly written also relique.] 1. That which remains; that which is left after loss or decay; a remaining portion; a remnant. Chaucer. Wyclif.

relicly.c: Relicly Rel"ic*ly, adv. In the manner of relics. [Obs.]

relict.c: Relict Rel"ict (-?kt), n. [L. relicta, fr. of relictus, p. p. of relinquere to leave behind. See Relinquish.] A woman whose husband is dead; a widow.

relicted.c: Relicted Re*lict"ed (r?-l?kt"?d), a. [L. relictus, p. p.] (Law) Left uncovered, as land by recession of water. Bouvier.

reliction.c: Reliction Re*lic"tion (r?-l?k"sh?n), n. [L. relictio a leaving behind.] (Law) A leaving dry; a recession of the sea or other water, leaving dry land; land left uncovered by such recession. Burrill.

relief.c: Relief Re*lief" (r?-l?f"), n. [OE. relef, F. relief, properly, a lifting up, a standing out. See Relieve, and cf. Basrelief, Rilievi.] 1. The act of relieving, or the state of being relieved; the removal, or partial removal, of any evil, or of anything oppressive or burdensome, by which some ease is obtained; succor; alleviation; comfort; ease; redress.

reliefless.c: Reliefless Re*lief"less, a. Destitute of relief; also, remediless.

relier.c: Relier Re*li"er (r?-l?"?r), n. [From Rely.] One who relies.

relievable.c: Relievable Re*liev"a*ble (r?-l?v"?-b'l), a. Capable of being relieved; fitted to recieve relief. Sir M. Hale.

relieve.c: Relieve Re*lieve" (r?-l?v"), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Relieved (-l?vd"); p. pr. & vb. n. Relieving.] [OE. releven, F. relever to raise again, discharge, relieve, fr. L. relevare to lift up, raise, make light, relieve; pref. re- re- + levare to raise, fr. levis light. See Levity, and cf. Relevant, Relief.] 1. To lift up; to raise again, as one who has fallen; to cause to rise. [Obs.] Piers Plowman.

relievement.c: Relievement Re*lieve"ment (-ment), n. The act of relieving, or the state of being relieved; relief; release. [Archaic.]

reliever.c: Reliever Re*liev"er (-?r), n. One who, or that which, relieves.
