relieving.c: Relieving Re*liev"ing, a. Serving or tending to relieve.

relievo.c: Relievo Re*lie"vo (r?-l?"v?), n. [It. rilievo.] See Relief, n., 5.

relight.c: Relight Re*light" (r?-l?t"), v. t. To light or kindle anew.

religieux.c: Religieux Religieuse { ‖Re*li`gi`euse" (rei-l?`zh?`?z"), n. f. ‖Re*li`gi`eux" (rei-l?`zh?`?"), n. m. } [F.] A person bound by monastic vows; a nun; a monk.

religion.c: Religion Re*li"gion (re*lĭj"ŭn), n. [F., from L. religio; cf. religens pious, revering the gods, Gr. 'ale`gein to heed, have a care. Cf. Neglect.] 1. The outward act or form by which men indicate their recognition of the existence of a god or of gods having power over their destiny, to whom obedience, service, and honor are due; the feeling or expression of human love, fear, or awe of some superhuman and overruling power, whether by profession of belief, by observance of rites and ceremonies, or by the conduct of life; a system of faith and worship; a manifestation of piety; as, ethical religions; monotheistic religions; natural religion; revealed religion; the religion of the Jews; the religion of idol worshipers.

religionary.c: Religionary Re*li"gion*a*ry (r?-l?j"?n-?-r?), a. Relating to religion; pious; as, religionary professions. [Obs.]

religioner.c: Religioner Religionary { Re*li"gion*a*ry, Re*li"gion*er (-?r), } n. A religionist. [R.]

religionism.c: Religionism Re*li"gion*ism (-?z'm), n. 1. The practice of, or devotion to, religion.

religionist.c: Religionist Re*li"gion*ist, n. One earnestly devoted or attached to a religion; a religious zealot.

religionize.c: Religionize Re*li"gion*ize (-?z), v. t. To bring under the influence of religion. [R.] Mallock.

religiosity.c: Religiosity Re*lig`i*os"i*ty (-l?j`?-?s"?-t?), n. [L. religiositas: cf. F. religiosit?.] The quality of being religious; religious feeling or sentiment; religiousness. [R.] M. Arnold.

religious.c: Religious Re*li"gious (r?-l?j"?s), a. [OF. religius, religious, F. religieux, from L. religiosus. See Religion.] 1. Of or pertaining to religion; concerned with religion; teaching, or setting forth, religion; set apart to religion; as, a religious society; a religious sect; a religious place; religious subjects, books, teachers, houses, wars.
Religious Re*li"gious, n. A person bound by monastic vows, or sequestered from secular concern, and devoted to a life of piety and religion; a monk or friar; a nun. Addison.

religiously.c: Religiously Re*li"gious*ly, adv. In a religious manner. Drayton.

religiousness.c: Religiousness Re*li"gious*ness, n. The quality of being religious.

relinquent.c: Relinquent Re*lin"quent (r?-l?n"kwent), a. [L. relinquens, p. pr. of relinqquere. See Relinquish.] Relinquishing. [R.]

relinquish.c: Relinquish Re*lin"quish (-kw?sh), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Relinquished (-kw?sht); p. pr. & vb. n. Relinquishing.] [OF. relinquir, L. relinquere to leave behind; pref. re- re + linquere to leave. See Loan, and cf. Relic, Relict.]

relinquishment.c: Relinquishment Re*lin"quish*ment (-ment), n. The act of relinquishing.

reliquary.c: Reliquary Rel"i*qua*ry (r?l"?-kw?-r?), n.; pl. -ries (-rĭz). [LL. reliquiarium, reliquiare: cf. F. reliquaire. See Relic.] A depositary, often a small box or casket, in which relics are kept.

reliquian.c: Reliquian Re*liq"ui*an (re*lĭk"wĭ*ain), a. Of or pertaining to a relic or relics; of the nature of a relic. [R.]

reliquidate.c: Reliquidate Re*liq"ui*date (rē*lĭk"wĭ*dāt), v. t. To liquidate anew; to adjust a second time.

reliquidation.c: Reliquidation Re*liq`ui*da"tion (rē*lĭk`wĭ*dā"shŭn), n. A second or renewed liquidation; a renewed adjustment. A. Hamilton.

relish.c: Relish Rel"ish (rĕl"ĭsh), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Relished (rĕl"ĭsht); p. pr. & vb. n. Relishing.] [Of. relechier to lick or taste anew; pref. re- re- + lechier to lick, F. lécher. See Lecher, Lick.] 1. To taste or eat with pleasure; to like the flavor of; to partake of with gratification; hence, to enjoy; to be pleased with or gratified by; to experience pleasure from; as, to relish food.
Relish Rel"ish, v. i. To have a pleasing or appetizing taste; to give gratification; to have a flavor.
Relish Rel"ish, n. 1. A pleasing taste; flavor that gratifies the palate; hence, enjoyable quality; power of pleasing.
Relish Rel"ish, n. (Carp.) The projection or shoulder at the side of, or around, a tenon, on a tenoned piece. Knight.

relishable.c: Relishable Rel"ish*a*ble (-?-b'l), a. Capable of being relished; agreeable to the taste; gratifying.

relive.c: Relive Re*live" (rē*lĭv"), v. i. To live again; to revive.
Relive Re*live", v. t. To recall to life; to revive. [Obs.]

reload.c: Reload Re*load" (r?-l?d"), v. t. To load again, as a gun.

reloan.c: Reloan Re*loan" (r?-l?n"), n. A second lending of the same thing; a renewal of a loan.

relocate.c: Relocate Re*lo"cate (rē*lō"kāt), v. t. To locate again.

relodge.c: Relodge Re*lodge" (rē*lŏj"), v. t. To lodge again.

relove.c: Relove Re*love" (rē*lŭv"), v. t. To love in return. [Obs.] Boyle.

relucent.c: Relucent Re*lu"cent (r?-l?"sent), a. [L. relucens, p. pr. relucere. See Lucent.] Reflecting light; shining; glittering; glistening; bright; luminous; splendid.

reluct.c: Reluct Re*luct" (r?-l?kt"), v. i. [L. reluctari, p. p. reluctatus, to struggle; pref. re- re- + luctari to struggle, fr. lucia a wresting.] To strive or struggle against anything; to make resistance; to draw back; to feel or show repugnance or reluctance.

reluctancy.c: Reluctancy Reluctance { Re*luc"tance (r?-l?k"tans), Re*luc"tan*cy (-tan-s?), } n. [See Reluctant.] 1. The state or quality of being reluctant; repugnance; aversion of mind; unwillingness; -- often followed by an infinitive, or by to and a noun, formerly sometimes by against. “Tempering the severity of his looks with a reluctance to the action.” Dryden.

reluctant.c: Reluctant Re*luc"tant (-tant), a. [L. reluctans, -antis, p. pr. of reluctari. See Reluct.] 1. Striving against; opposed in desire; unwilling; disinclined; loth.

reluctantly.c: Reluctantly Re*luc"tant*ly, adv. In a reluctant manner.

reluctate.c: Reluctate Re*luc"tate (-t?t), v. i. [See Reluct.] To struggle against anything; to resist; to oppose. [Obs.] “To delude their reluctating consciences.” Dr. H. More.

reluctation.c: Reluctation Rel`uc*ta"tion (r?l`?k-t?"sh?n), n. Repugnance; resistance; reluctance. [Obs.] Bacon.

relume.c: Relume Re*lume" (r?-l?m"), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Relumed (-l?md"); p. pr. & vb. n. Reluming.] [OF. relumer (cf. F. rallumer), L. reluminare; pref. re- re- + luminare to light. Cf. Reillume.] To rekindle; to light again.

relumine.c: Relumine Re*lu"mine (r?-l?"m?n), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Relumined (-m?nd); p. pr. & vb. n. Relumining.] [See Relume.] 1. To light anew; to rekindle. Shak.

rely.c: Rely Re*ly" (r?-l?"), v. i. [imp. & p. p. Relied (-l?d"); p. pr. & vb. n. Relying.] [Pref. re- + lie to rest.] To rest with confidence, as when fully satisfied of the veracity, integrity, or ability of persons, or of the certainty of facts or of evidence; to have confidence; to trust; to depend; -- with on, formerly also with in.

remade.c: Remade Re*made" (r?-m?d"), imp. & p. p. of Remake.

remain.c: Remain Re*main" (r?-m?n"), v. i. [imp. & p. p. Remained (-m?nd"); p. pr. & vb. n. Remaining.] [OF. remaindre, remanoir, L. remanere; pref. re- re- + manere to stay, remain. See Mansion, and cf. Remainder, Remnant.]
Remain Re*main", v. t. To await; to be left to. [Archaic]
Remain Re*main" n. 1. State of remaining; stay. [Obs.]

remainder.c: Remainder Re*main"der (r?-m?n"d?r), n. [OF. remaindre, inf. See Remain.] 1. Anything that remains, or is left, after the separation and removal of a part; residue; remnant. “The last remainders of unhappy Troy.” Dryden.
Remainder Re*main"der, a. Remaining; left; left over; refuse.

remainderman.c: Remainder-man Re*main"der-man (- măn), n.; pl. Remainder-men (-mĕn). (Law) One who has an estate after a particular estate is determined. See Remainder, n., 3. Blackstone.

remake.c: Remake Re*make" (r?-m?k"), v. t. To make anew.

remand.c: Remand Re*mand" (r?-m?nd"), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Remanded; p. pr. & vb. n. Remanding.] [F. remander to send word again, L. remandare; pref. re- re- + mandare to commit, order, send word. See Mandate.] To recommit; to send back.
Remand Re*mand", n. The act of remanding; the order for recommitment.

remanency.c: Remanency Remanence { Rem"a*nence (r?m"?*nens), Rem"a*nen*cy (-nen*s?), } n. [Cf. OF. remanence, LL. remanentia, fr. L. remanens. See Remanent, a.] The state of being remanent; continuance; permanence. [R.] Jer. Taylor.

remanent.c: Remanent Rem"a*nent (-nent), n. [See Remanent, a.] That which remains; a remnant; a residue.
Remanent Rem"a*nent, a. [L. remanens, p. pr. of remanere. See Remain, and cf. Remnant.] Remaining; residual.

remanet.c: Remanet ‖Rem"a*net (-n?t), n. [L., it remains.] (Legal Practice) A case for trial which can not be tried during the term; a postponed case. [Eng.]

remark.c: Re-mark Re-mark" (r?-m?rk"), v. t. [Pref. re- + mark.] To mark again, or a second time; to mark anew.

Remark Re*mark" (r?-m?rk"), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Remarked (-m?rkt"); p. pr. & vb. n. Remarking.] [F. remarquer; pref. re- re- + marquer to mark, marque a mark, of German origin, akin to E. mark. See Mark, v. & n.] 1. To mark in a notable manner; to distinquish clearly; to make noticeable or conspicuous; to piont out. [Obs.]
Remark Re*mark" (r?-m?rk"), v. i. To make a remark or remarks; to comment.
Remark Re*mark", n. [Cf. F. remarque.] 1. Act of remarking or attentively noticing; notice or observation.

remarkable.c: Remarkable Re*mark"a*ble (-?-b'l), a. [F. remarquable.] Worthy of being remarked or noticed; noticeable; conspicuous; hence, uncommon; extraordinary.

remarque.c: Remarque proof Remark Remarque Re*marque" (?), n. Also Remark. (Engraving) (a) A small design etched on the margin of a plate and supposed to be removed after the earliest proofs have been taken; also, any feature distinguishing a particular stage of the plate. (b) A print or proof so distinguished; -- commonly called a Remarque proof.

remarriage.c: Remarriage Re*mar"riage (r?-m?r"r?j), n. A second or repeated marriage.

remarry.c: Remarry Re*mar"ry (r?-m?r"rr?), v. t. & i. To marry again.

remast.c: Remast Re*mast" (r?-m?st"), v. t. To furnish with a new mast or set of masts.

remasticate.c: Remasticate Re*mas"ti*cate (r?-m?s"t?-k?t), v. t. To chew or masticate again; to chew over and over, as the cud.

remastication.c: Remastication Re*mas`ti*ca"tion (-k?"sh?n), n. The act of masticating or chewing again or repeatedly.

remblai.c: Remblai ‖Rem`blai" (r?n`bl?"), n. [F., fr. remblayer to fill up an excavation, to embank.] (Fort. & Engin.) Earth or materials made into a bank after having been excavated.

remble.c: Remble Rem"ble (r?m"b'l), v. t. [Cf. OF. embler to steal, fr. L. involare to fly into or at, to carry off.] To remove. [Prov. Eng.] Grose. Tennyson.

remean.c: Remean Re*mean" (r?-m?n"), v. t. To give meaning to; to explain the meaning of; to interpret. [Obs.] Wyclif.

remeant.c: Remeant Re"me*ant (r?"m?*ant), a. [L. remeans, -antis, p. pr. of remeare to go or come back.] Coming back; returning. [R.] “Like the remeant sun.” C. Kingsley.

remeasure.c: Remeasure Re*meas"ure (r?-m?zh"?r; 135), v. t. To measure again; to retrace.

remediable.c: Remediable Re*me"di*a*ble (r?-m?"d?-?-b'l), a. [L. remediabilis: cf. F. remédiable.] Capable of being remedied or cured.

remedial.c: Remedial Re*me"di*al (-al), a. [L. remedialis.] Affording a remedy; intended for a remedy, or for the removal or abatement of an evil; as, remedial treatment.

remedially.c: Remedially Re*me"di*al*ly, adv. In a remedial manner.

remediless.c: Remediless Re*med"i*less (r?-m?d"?-l?s or r?m"?-d?-l?s; 277), a. 1. Not admitting of a remedy; incapable of being restored or corrected; incurable; irreparable; as, a remediless mistake or loss. “Chains remedilesse.” Spenser.

remedy.c: Remedy Rem"e*dy (r?m"?-d?), n.; pl. Remedies (-d?z). [L. remedium; pref. re- re- + mederi to heal, to cure: cf. F. remède remedy, remédier to remedy. See Medical.]

Remedy Rem"e*dy, v. t. [imp. & p. p. Remedied (-d?d); p. pr. & vb. n. Remedying.] [L. remediare, remediari: cf. F. remédier. See Remedy, n.] To apply a remedy to; to relieve; to cure; to heal; to repair; to redress; to correct; to counteract.

remelt.c: Remelt Re*melt" (r?-m?lt"), v. t. To melt again.

remember.c: Remember Re*mem"ber (r?-m?m"b?r), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Remembered (-b?rd); p. pr. & vb. n. Remembering.] [OF. remebrer, L. rememorari; pref. re- re- + memorare to bring to remembrance, from memor mindful. See Memory, and cf. Rememorate.] 1. To have (a notion or idea) come into the mind again, as previously perceived, known, or felt; to have a renewed apprehension of; to bring to mind again; to think of again; to recollect; as, I remember the fact; he remembers the events of his childhood; I cannot remember dates.
Remember Re*mem"ber (r?-m?m"b?r), v. i. To execise or have the power of memory; as, some remember better than others. Shak.

rememberable.c: Rememberable Re*mem"ber*a*ble (-?-b'l), a. Capable or worthy of being remembered. -- Re*mem"ber*a*bly, adv.

remembrancer.c: Remembrancer Re*mem"bran*cer (-bran-s?r), n. 1. One who, or that which, serves to bring to, or keep in, mind; a memento; a memorial; a reminder.

rememorate.c: Rememorate Re*mem"o*rate (-?-r?t), v. i. [L. rememoratus, p. p. of rememorari. See Remember.] To recall something by means of memory; to remember. [Obs.] Bryskett.

rememoration.c: Rememoration Re*mem`o*ra"tion (-r?"sh?n), n. [F. remémoration, or L. rememoratio.] A recalling by the faculty of memory; remembrance. [Obs. & R.] Bp. Montagu.

rememorative.c: Rememorative Re*mem"o*ra*tive (r?-mEm"?-r?-t?v), a. Tending or serving to remind. [R.]

remercy.c: Remercy Remercie { Re*mer"cie, Re*mer"cy } (re-mẽr"sy̆), v. t. [F. remercier; pref. re- re- + OF. mercier to thank, from OF. & F. merci. See Mercy.] To thank. [Obs.]

remerge.c: Remerge Re*merge" (r?-m?rj"), v. i. To merge again. “Remerging in the general Soul.” Tennyson.

remewe.c: Remewe Remeve { Re*meve" (r?-mEv"), Re*mewe" (r?-m?") }, v. t. & i. To remove. [Obs.] Chaucer.

remiform.c: Remiform Rem"i*form (r?m"?*f?rm), a. [L. remus oar + -form.] Shaped like an oar.

remiges.c: Remiges ‖Rem"i*ges (r?m"?*j?z), n. pl.; sing. Remex. (r?"m?ks). [L. remex, -igis, an oarsman.] (Zool.) The quill feathers of the wings of a bird.

remigrate.c: Remigrate Rem"i*grate (r?m"?-gr?t or r?-m?"gr?t; 277), v. i. [L. remigrare. See Re-, and Migrate.] To migrate again; to go back; to return. Boyle.

remigration.c: Remigration Rem`i*gra"tion (r?m`?-gr?"sh?n), n. Migration back to the place from which one came. Sir M. Hale.

remind.c: Remind Re*mind" (r?-m?nd"), v. t. To put (one) in mind of something; to bring to the remembrance of; to bring to the notice or consideration of (a person).

reminder.c: Reminder Re*mind"er (-?r), n. One who, or that which, reminds; that which serves to awaken remembrance.

remindful.c: Remindful Re**mind"ful (f?l), a. Tending or adapted to remind; careful to remind. Southey.

reminiscence.c: Reminiscence Rem`i*nis"cence (r?m`?-n?s"sens), n. [F. réminiscence, L. reminiscentia.] 1. The act or power of recalling past experience; the state of being reminiscent; remembrance; memory.

reminiscent.c: Reminiscent Rem`i*nis"cent (-sent), a. [L. reminiscens, -entis, p. pr. of reminisci to recall to mind, to recollect; pref. re- re + a word akin to mens mind, memini I remember. See Mind.] Recalling to mind, or capable of recalling to mind; having remembrance; reminding one of something.
Reminiscent Rem`i*nis"cent (r?m`?-n?s"sent), n. One who is addicted to indulging, narrating, or recording reminiscences.

reminiscential.c: Reminiscential Rem`i*nis*cen"tial (-n?s-s?n"shal), a. Of or pertaining to reminiscence, or remembrance. Sir T. Browne.

remiped.c: Remiped Rem"i*ped (r?m"?-p?d), a. [L. remus oar + pes, pedis, foot: cf. F. rémipède.] (Zool.) Having feet or legs that are used as oars; -- said of certain crustaceans and insects.
Remiped Rem"i*ped, n. (Zool.) (a) An animal having limbs like oars, especially one of certain crustaceans. (b) One of a group of aquatic beetles having tarsi adapted for swimming. See Water beetle.

remise.c: Remise Re*mise" (r?-m?z"), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Remised (-m?zd"); p. pr. & vb. n. Remising.] [F. remise delivery, surrender, fr. remettre to put back, deliver, L. remittere. See Remit.] To send, give, or grant back; to release a claim to; to resign or surrender by deed; to return. Blackstone.
Remise Re*mise", n. (Law) A giving or granting back; surrender; return; release, as of a claim.
Remise Re*mise" (?), n. 1. A house for covered carriages; a chaise house. Sterne.

remiss.c: Remiss Re*miss" (r?-m?s"), a. [L. remissus, p. p. of remittere to send back, relax. See Remit.] Not energetic or exact in duty or business; not careful or prompt in fulfilling engagements; negligent; careless; tardy; behindhand; lagging; slack; hence, lacking earnestness or activity; languid; slow.
Remiss Re*miss", n. The act of being remiss; inefficiency; failure. [Obs.] “Remisses of laws.” Puttenham.

remissful.c: Remissful Re*miss"ful (-f?l), a. Inclined to remit punishment; lenient; clement. Drayton.

remissibility.c: Remissibility Re*mis`si*bil"i*ty (r?-m?s`s?-b?l"?-t?), n. The state or quality of being remissible. Jer. Taylor.

remissible.c: Remissible Re*mis"si*ble (r?-m?s"s?-b'l), a. [L. remissibilis: cf. F. rémissible. See Remit.] Capable of being remitted or forgiven. Feltham.

remission.c: Remission Re*mis"sion (r?-m?sh"?n), n. [F. rémission, L. remissio. See Remit.] 1. The act of remitting, surrendering, resigning, or giving up.

remissive.c: Remissive Re*mis"sive (r?-m?s"s?v), a. [L. remissivus. See Remit.] Remitting; forgiving; abating. Bp. Hacket.

remissly.c: Remissly Re*miss"ly (r?-m?s"l?), adv. In a remiss or negligent manner; carelessly.

remissness.c: Remissness Re*miss"ness, n. Quality or state of being remiss.

remissory.c: Remissory Re*mis"so*ry (r?-m?s"s?-r?), a. Serving or tending to remit, or to secure remission; remissive. “A sacrifice expiatory or remissory.” Latimer.

remit.c: Remit Re*mit" (r?-m?t"), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Remitted; p. pr. & vb. n. Remitting.] [L. remittere, remissum, to send back, to slacken, relax; pref. re- re- + mittere to send. See Mission, and cf. Remise, Remiss.] 1. To send back; to give up; to surrender; to resign.
Remit Re*mit", v. i. 1. To abate in force or in violence; to grow less intense; to become moderated; to abate; to relax; as, a fever remits; the severity of the weather remits.

remitment.c: Remitment Re*mit"ment (-ment), n. The act of remitting, or the state of being remitted; remission.

remittal.c: Remittal Re*mit"tal (-tal), n. A remitting; a giving up; surrender; as, the remittal of the first fruits. Swift.

remittance.c: Remittance Re*mit"tance (r?-m?t"tans), n. 1. The act of transmitting money, bills, or the like, esp. to a distant place, as in satisfaction of a demand, or in discharge of an obligation.

remittee.c: Remittee Re*mit`tee" (r?-m?t`t?"), n. (Com.) One to whom a remittance is sent.

remittent.c: Remittent Re*mit"tent (r?-m?t"tent), a. [L. remittens, p. pr.: cf. F. rémittent.] Remitting; characterized by remission; having remissions.

remitter.c: Remitter Re*mit"ter (-t?r), n. 1. One who remits. Specifically: (a) One who pardons. (b) One who makes remittance.

remittitur.c: Remittitur ‖Re*mit"ti*tur (-t?-t?r), n. [L., (it) is remitted.] (Law) (a) A remission or surrender, -- remittitur damnut being a remission of excess of damages. (b) A sending back, as when a record is remitted by a superior to an inferior court. Wharton.

remittor.c: Remittor Re*mit"tor (-t?r), n. (Law) One who makes a remittance; a remitter.

remix.c: Remix Re*mix" (r?-m?ks"), v. t. To mix again or repeatedly.

remnant.c: Remnant Rem"nant (r?m"nant), a. [OF. remanant, p. pr. of remanoir, remaindre. See Remanent, Remain.] Remaining; yet left. [R.] “Because of the remnant dregs of his disease.” Fuller.
Remnant Rem"nant, n. [OF. remanant. See Remnant, a.]

remodel.c: Remodel Re*mod"el (r?-m?d"?l), v. t. To model or fashion anew; to change the form of.

remodification.c: Remodification Re*mod`i*fi*ca"tion (-?-f?-k?"sh?n), n. The act of remodifying; the state of being remodified.

remodify.c: Remodify Re*mod"i*fy (r?-m?d"?-f?), v. t. To modify again or anew; to reshape.

remoulad.c: Remoulad Remolade { ‖Ré`mo`lade" (r?`m?`l?d"), ‖Ré`mou`lad" (r?`m??`l?d"), } n. [F.] 1. A kind of piquant sauce or salad dressing resembling mayonnaise.

remould.c: Remould Remold { Re*mold", Re*mould" } (rē*mōld"), v. t. To mold or shape anew or again; to reshape.

remollient.c: Remollient Re*mol"lient (r?-m?l"yent or -l?-ent), a. [L. remolliens, p. pr. of remollire to mollify: cf. F. rémollient. See Mollient.] Mollifying; softening. [R.]

remonetization.c: Remonetization Re*mon`e*ti*za"tion (r?-m?n`?-t?-z?"sh?n or -m?n`-), n. The act of remonetizing.

remonetize.c: Remonetize Re*mon"e*tize (-t?z), v. t. To restore to use as money; as, to remonetize silver.

remonstrance.c: Remonstrance Re*mon"strance (-m?n"strans), n. [Cf. OF. remonstrance, F. remonstrance. See Remonstrate.] 1. The act of remonstrating; as: (a) A pointing out; manifestation; proof; demonstration. [Obs.]

remonstrant.c: Remonstrant Re*mon"strant (-strant), a. [LL. remonstranc, -antis, p. pr. of remonstrare: cf. OF. remonstrant, F. remontrant.] Inclined or tending to remonstrate; expostulatory; urging reasons in opposition to something.

Remonstrant Re*mon"strant, n. One who remonstrates; specifically (Eccl. Hist.), one of the Arminians who remonstrated against the attacks of the Calvinists in 1610, but were subsequently condemned by the decisions of the Synod of Dort in 1618. See Arminian.

remonstrantly.c: Remonstrantly Re*mon"strant*ly, adv. In a remonstrant manner.

remonstrate.c: Remonstrate Re*mon"strate (-str?t), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Remonstrated (-str?*t?d); p. pr. & vb. n. Remonstrating.] [LL. remonstratus, p. p. of remonstrare to remonstrate; L. pref. re- + monstrare to show. See Monster.] To point out; to show clearly; to make plain or manifest; hence, to prove; to demonstrate. [Obs.] Jer. Taylor.

Remonstrate Re*mon"strate, v. i. To present and urge reasons in opposition to an act, measure, or any course of proceedings; to expostulate; as, to remonstrate with a person regarding his habits; to remonstrate against proposed taxation.

remonstration.c: Remonstration Re`mon*stra"tion (r?`m?n*str?"sh?n), n. [Cf. OF. remonstration, LL. remonstratio.] The act of remonstrating; remonstrance. [R.] Todd.

remonstrative.c: Remonstrative Re*mon"stra*tive (r?*m?n"str?*t?v), a. Having the character of a remonstrance; expressing remonstrance.

remonstrator.c: Remonstrator Re*mon"stra*tor (r?*m?n"str?*t?r), n. One who remonstrates; a remonsrant. Bp. Burnet.

remontant.c: Remontant Re*mon"tant (-tant), a.[F.] (Hort.) Rising again; -- applied to a class of roses which bloom more than once in a season; the hybrid perpetual roses, of which the Jacqueminot is a well-known example.

remontoir.c: Remontoir ‖Re*mon`toir" (re-m?n"tw?r"; E. r?-m?n"tw?r), n. [F.] (Horology) See under Escapement.

remorate.c: Remorate Rem"o*rate (-r?t), v. t. [L. remoratus, p. p. of remorari; pref. re- re- + morari to delay.] To hinder; to delay. [Obs.] Johnson.

remord.c: Remord Re*mord" (r?-m?rd"), v. t. [L. remordere to bite again, to torment: cf. F. remordre. See Remorse.] To excite to remorse; to rebuke. [Obs.] Skelton.
Remord Re*mord", v. i. To feel remorse. [Obs.] Sir T. Elyot.

remordency.c: Remordency Re*mord"en*cy (-en*s?), n. Remorse; compunction; compassion. [Obs.] Killingbeck.

remorse.c: Remorse Re*morse" (r?*m?rs"), n. [OE. remors, OF. remors,F. remords, LL. remorsus, fr. L. remordere, remorsum, to bite again or back, to torment; pref. re- re- + mordere to bite. See Morsel.] 1. The anguish, like gnawing pain, excited by a sense of guilt; compunction of conscience for a crime committed, or for the sins of one's past life. “Nero will be tainted with remorse.” Shak.

remorseless.c: Remorseless Re*morse"less, a. Being without remorse; having no pity; hence, destitute of sensibility; cruel; insensible to distress; merciless. “Remorseless adversaries.” South. “With remorseless cruelty.” Milton.

remote.c: Remote Re*mote" (r?-m?t"), a. [Compar. Remoter (-?r); superl. Remotest.] [L. remotus, p. p. of removere to remove. See Remove.] 1. Removed to a distance; not near; far away; distant; -- said in respect to time or to place; as, remote ages; remote lands.

remotion.c: Remotion Re*mo"tion (r?-m?"sh?n), n. [L. remotio. See Remove.] 1. The act of removing; removal. [Obs.]

remount.c: Remount Re*mount" (r?-mount"), v. t. & i. To mount again.
Remount Re*mount", n. The opportunity of, or things necessary for, remounting; specifically, a fresh horse, with his equipments; as, to give one a remount.

removable.c: Removable Re*mov"a*ble (r?-m??v"?-b'l), a. Admitting of being removed. Ayliffe. -- Re*mov`a*bil"i*ty (-?-b?l"?-t?), n.

removal.c: Removal Re*mov"al (-al), n. The act of removing, or the state of being removed.

remove.c: Remove Re*move" (r?-m??v"), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Removed (-m??vd"); p. pr. & vb. n. Removing.] [OF. removoir, remouvoir, L. removere, remotum; pref. re- re- + movere to move. See Move.] 1. To move away from the position occupied; to cause to change place; to displace; as, to remove a building.
Remove Re*move" (r?-m??v"), v. i. To change place in any manner, or to make a change in place; to move or go from one residence, position, or place to another.
Remove Re*move", n. 1. The act of removing; a removal.

remover.c: Remover Re*mov"er (-?r), n. One who removes; as, a remover of landmarks. Bacon.

remuable.c: Remuable Re*mu"a*ble (r?-m?"?-b'l), a. [F.] That may be removed; removable. [Obs.] Gower.

remue.c: Remue Re*mue" (r?-m?"), v. t. [F. remuer. See Mew to molt.] To remove. [Obs.] Chaucer.

remugient.c: Remugient Re*mu"gi*ent (r?-m?"j?-ent), a. [L. remugiens, p. pr. of remugire. See Mugient.] Rebellowing. Dr. H. More.

remunerable.c: Remunerable Re**mu"ner*a*ble (r?-m?"n?r-?-b'l), a. [See Remunerate.] Admitting, or worthy, of remuneration. -- Re*mu`ner*a*bil"i*ty (r?-m?"n?r-?-b?l"i-t?), n.

remunerate.c: Remunerate Re*mu"ner*ate (-?t), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Remunerated (-?"t?d); p. pr. & vb. n. Remunerating.] [L. remuneratus, p. p. of remunerare, remunerari; pref. re- re- + munerare, munerari, to give, present, from munus, muneris, a gift, present. Cf. Munificent.] To pay an equivalent to for any service, loss, expense, or other sacrifice; to recompense; to requite; as, to remunerate men for labor.

remuneration.c: Remuneration Re*mu`ner*a"tion (-?"sh?n), n. [L. remuneratio: cf. F. rémunération.] 1. The act of remunerating.

remunerative.c: Remunerative Re*mu"ner*a*tive (r?-m?"n?r-?-t?v), a. [Cf.F. rémun?ratif.] Affording remuneration; as, a remunerative payment for services; a remunerative business. -Re*mu"ner*a*tive*ly, adv. -- Re*mu"ner*a*tive*ness, n.

remuneratory.c: Remuneratory Re*mu"ner*a*to*ry (-t?-r?), a. [Cf. F. rémun?ratoire.] Remunerative. Johnson.

remurmur.c: Remurmur Re*mur"mur (r?-m?r"m?r), v. t. & i. [Pref. re- + murmur: cf. F. remurmurare.] To murmur again; to utter back, or reply, in murmurs.

ren.c: Ren Ren (r?n), v. t. & i. See Renne. [Obs.] Chaucer.

renable.c: Renable Ren"a*ble (r?n"?-b'l), a. [OF. resnable.] Reasonable; also, loquacious. [Obs.] “Most renable of tongue.” Piers Plowman. -- Ren"a*bly, adv. [Obs.] Chaucer.

renaissance.c: Renaissance ‖Re*nais`sance" (F. rei-na`säNs"; E. re-nās"sains), n. [F., fr. renaître to be born again. Cf. Renascence.] A new birth, or revival. Specifically: (a) The transitional movement in Europe, marked by the revival of classical learning and art in Italy in the 15th century, and the similar revival following in other countries. (b) The style of art which prevailed at this epoch.

renaissant.c: Renaissant Re*nais"sant (r?-n?s"sant), a. Of or pertaining to the Renaissance.

renal.c: Renal Re"nal (rē"nail), a. [L. renalis, fr. renes the kidneys or reins: cf. F. rénal. See Reins.] (Anat.) Of or pertaining to the kidneys; in the region of the kidneys.

renalportal.c: Renal-portal Re"nal-por`tal (r?"nal-p?r"tal), a. (Anat.) Both renal and portal. See Portal.

rename.c: Rename Re*name" (r?*n?m"), v. t. To give a new name to.

renard.c: Renard Ren"ard (r?n"?rd), n. [F. renard the fox, the name of the fox in a celebrated epic poem, and of German origin, G. Reinhard, OHG. Reginhard, properly, strong in counsel; regin counsel (akin to Goth. ragin) + hart hard. See Hard.] A fox; -- so called in fables or familiar tales, and in poetry. [Written also reynard.]

renardine.c: Renardine Ren"ard*ine (-?n), a. Of or pertaining to Renard, the fox, or the tales in which Renard is mentioned.

renascence.c: Renascence Re*nas"cence (r?-n?s"sens), n. [See Renascent, and cf. Renaissance.] 1. The state of being renascent.

renascency.c: Renascency Re*nas"cen*cy (-sen-s?), n. State of being renascent.

renascent.c: Renascent Re*nas"cent (-sent), a. [L. renascens, p. pr. of renasci to be born again; pref. re- re- + nasci to be born. See Nascent.] 1. Springing or rising again into being; being born again, or reproduced.

renascible.c: Renascible Re*nas"ci*ble (-s?-b'l), a. [LL. renascibilis, from L. renasci to be born again.] Capable of being reproduced; ablle to spring again into being.

renate.c: Renate Re*nate" (r?-n?t"), a. [L. renatus, p. p. of renasci.] Born again; regenerate; renewed. [Obs.] Beau. & Fl.

renavigate.c: Renavigate Re*nav"i*gate (r?-n?v"?-g?t), v. t. To navigate again.

renay.c: Renay Re*nay" (r?-n?"), v. t. [OF. reneier, F. renier, F. renier; L. pref. re- re- + negare to deny. See Renegade.] To deny; to disown. [Obs.]

rencontre.c: Rencontre Ren*con"tre (r?n-k?n"t?r; F. r?N`k?n"tr'), n. [F.] Same as Rencounter, n.

rencounter.c: Rencounter Ren*coun"ter (r?n-koun"t?r), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Rencountered (-t?rd); p. pr. & vb/ n. Rencountering.] [F. rencontrer; pref. re- + OF. encontrer to encounter. See Encounter.] 1. To meet unexpectedly; to encounter.
Rencounter Ren*coun"ter, v. i. To meet unexpectedly; to encounter in a hostile manner; to come in collision; to skirmish.

Rencounter Ren*coun"ter, n. [F. rencontre, from renconter to meet.] 1. A meeting of two persons or bodies; a collision; especially, a meeting in opposition or contest; a combat, action, or engagement.

rend.c: Rend Rend (rĕnd), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Rent (rĕnt); p. pr. & vb. n. Rending.] [AS. rendan, hrendan; cf. OFries. renda, randa, Fries. renne to cut, rend, Icel. hrinda to push, thrust, AS. hrindan; or cf. Icel. ræna to rob, plunder, Ir. rannaim to divide, share, part, W. rhanu, Armor. ranna.] 1. To separate into parts with force or sudden violence; to tear asunder; to split; to burst; as, powder rends a rock in blasting; lightning rends an oak.
Rend Rend, v. i. To be rent or torn; to become parted; to separate; to split. Jer. Taylor.

render.c: Render Rend"er (-?r), n. [From Rend.] One who rends.

Render Ren"der (r?n"d?r), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Rendered (-d?rd);p. pr. & vb. n. Rendering.] [F. rendre, LL. rendre, fr. L. reddere; pref. red-, re-, re- + dare to give. See Datetime, and cf. Reddition, Rent.] 1. To return; to pay back; to restore.
Render Ren"der, v. i. 1. To give an account; to make explanation or confession. [Obs.]

renderable.c: Renderable Ren"der*a*ble (r?n"d?r-?-b'l), a. Capable of being rendered.

rendering.c: Rendering Ren"der*ing, n. The act of one who renders, or that which is rendered. Specifically: (a) A version; translation; as, the rendering of the Hebrew text. Lowth. (b) In art, the presentation, expression, or interpretation of an idea, theme, or part. (c) The act of laying the first coat of plaster on brickwork or stonework. (d) The coat of plaster thus laid on. Gwilt. (e) The process of trying out or extracting lard, tallow, etc., from animal fat.

rendezvous.c: Rendezvous Ren"dez*vous (r?n"d?*vōo or r?n"-; 277), n.; pl. Rendezvouses (r?n"d?-vōo`z?z). [F. rendez-vous, properly, render yourselves, repair to a place. See Render.] 1. A place appointed for a meeting, or at which persons customarily meet.
Rendezvous Ren"dez*vous (rĕn"dĕ*vōo or räN"-; 277), v. i. [imp. & p. p. Rendezvoused (-vōod); p. pr. & vb. n. Rendezvousing (-vōo*ĭng).] To assemble or meet at a particular place.
Rendezvous Ren"dez*vous, v. t. To bring together at a certain place; to cause to be assembled. Echard.

rendible.c: Rendible Rend"i*ble (r?nd"?-b'l), a. [From Rend.] Capable of being rent or torn.
Rendible Ren"di*ble (r?n"d?-b'l), a. [See Render.] Capable, or admitting, of being rendered.

rendition.c: Rendition Ren*di"tion (r?n-d?sh"?n), n. [LL. rendere to render: cf. L. redditio. See Render, and cf. Reddition.]

rendrock.c: Rendrock Rend"rock` (r?nd"r?k`), n. A kind of dynamite used in blasting. [U.S.]

renegade.c: Renegade Ren"e*gade (r?n"?-g?d), n. [Sp. renegado, LL. renegatus, fr. renegare to deny; L. pref. re- re- + negare to deny. See Negation, and cf. Runagate.] One faithless to principle or party. Specifically: (a) An apostate from Christianity or from any form of religious faith.

renegat.c: Renegat Ren"e*gat (r?n"?-g?t), n. [See Runegate.] A renegade. [Obs.] Chaucer.

renegation.c: Renegation Ren`e*ga"tion (r?n`?-ga"sh?n), n. A denial. [R.] “Absolute renegation of Christ.” Milman.

renege.c: Renege Re*nege" (r?-n?j" or r?-n?g"), v. t. [LL. renegare. See Renegade.] To deny; to disown. [Obs.] Shak.
Renege Re*nege", v. i. 1. To deny. [Obs.] Shak.

renerve.c: Renerve Re*nerve" (r?-n?rv"), v. t. To nerve again; to give new vigor to; to reinvigorate.

renew.c: Renew Re*new" (r?-n?"), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Reneved (-n?d"); p. pr. & vb. n. Renewing.] [Pref. re- + new. Cf. Renovate.] 1. To make new again; to restore to freshness, perfection, or vigor; to give new life to; to rejuvenate; to reëstablish; to recreate; to rebuild.
Renew Re*new", v. i. To become new, or as new; to grow or begin again.

renewability.c: Renewability Re*new`a*bil"i*ty (-?-b?l"?-t?), n. The quality or state of being renewable. [R.]

renewable.c: Renewable Re*new"a*ble (r?-n?"?-b'l), a. Capable of being renewed; as, a lease renewable at pleasure. Swift.

renewal.c: Renewal Re*new"al (-al), n. The act of renewing, or the state of being renewed; as, the renewal of a treaty.

renewedness.c: Renewedness Re*new"ed*ness, n. The state of being renewed.

renewer.c: Renewer Re*new"er (-?r), n. One who, or that which, renews.

reneye.c: Reneye Re*neye" (r?-n?"), v. t. [See Renay.] To deny; to reject; to renounce. [Obs.]

reng.c: Reng Reng (r?ng), n. [See Rank, n.] 1. A rank; a row. [Obs.] “In two renges fair.” Chaucer.

renidification.c: Renidification Re*nid`i*fi*ca"tion (r?-n?d`?-f?-k?"sh?n), n. (Zool.) The act of rebuilding a nest.

reniform.c: Reniform Ren"i*form (r?n"?-f?rm; 277), a. [L. renes kidneys + -form: cf. F. réniforme.] Having the form or shape of a kidney; as, a reniform mineral; a reniform leaf.

renitency.c: Renitency Renitence { Re*ni"tence (r?-n?"tens), Re*ni"ten*cy (-te-s?), } n. [Cf. F. rénitence.] The state or quality of being renitent; resistance; reluctance. Sterne.

renitent.c: Renitent Re*ni"tent (-tent), a. [L. renitens, -entis, p. pr. of renit to strive or struggle against, resist; pref. re- re- + niti to struggle or strive: cf. F. rénitent.] 1. Resisting pressure or the effect of it; acting against impulse by elastic force. “[Muscles] soft and yet renitent.” Ray.

renne.c: Renne Ren"ne (r?n"ne), v. t. To plunder; -- only in the phrase “to rape and renne.” See under Rap, v. t., to snatch. [Obs.] Chaucer.
Renne Ren"ne, v. i. To run. [Obs.] Chaucer.

rennet.c: Rennet Ren"net (r?n"n?t), n. [F. rainette, reinette, perhaps fr. raine a tree frog, L. rana, because it is spotted like this kind of frog. Cf. Ranunculus.] (Bot.) A name of many different kinds of apples. Cf. Reinette. Mortimer.
Rennet Ren"net, n. [AS. rinnan, rennan, to run, cf. gerinnan to curdle, coagulate. √11. See Run, v.] 1. The inner, or mucous, membrane of the fourth stomach of the calf, or other young ruminant.

renneted.c: Renneted Ren"net*ed, a. Provided or treated with rennet. [R.] “Pressed milk renneted.” Chapman.

rennin.c: Rennin Ren"nin (rĕn"nĭn), n. (Biochem.) A milk-clotting enzyme obtained from the true stomach (abomasum) of a suckling calf. Mol. wt. about 31,000. Also called chymosin, rennase, and abomasal enzyme. [Merck Man. 11]

renounce.c: Renounce Re*nounce" (re*nouns"), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Renounced (-nounst"); p. pr. & vb. n. Renouncing (-noun"s?ng).] [F. renoncer, L. renuntiare to bring back word, announce, revoke, retract, renounce; pref. re- re- + nuntiare to announce, fr. nuncius, a messenger. See Nuncio, and cf. Renunciation.] 1. To declare against; to reject or decline formally; to refuse to own or acknowledge as belonging to one; to disclaim; as, to renounce a title to land or to a throne.
Renounce Re*nounce", v. i. 1. To make renunciation. [Obs.]
Renounce Re*nounce", n. (Card Playing) Act of renouncing.

renouncement.c: Renouncement Re*nounce"ment (-ment), n. [Cf. F. renoncement.] The act of disclaiming or rejecting; renunciation. Shak.

renovate.c: Renovate Ren"o*vate (r?n"?-v?t), v. t. [L. renovatus, p. p. of renovare;pref. re- re- + novare to make new, fr. novus new. See New, and?? Renew.] To make over again; to restore to freshness or vigor; to renew.

renovation.c: Renovation Ren`o**va"tion (-v?"sh?n), n. [L. renovatio: cf. F. rénovation.] The act or process of renovating; the state of being renovated or renewed. Thomson.

renovator.c: Renovator Ren"o*va`tor (r?n"?-v?`t?r), n. [L.: cf. F. rénovateur.] One who, or that which, renovates. Foster.

renovel.c: Renovel Re*nov"el (r?-n?v"el), v. t. [F. renouveler to renew.] To renew; to renovate. [Obs.] Chaucer.

renown.c: Renown Re*nown" (r?-noun"), n. [F. renom. See Noun, and cf. Renown, v.] 1. The state of being much known and talked of; exalted reputation derived from the extensive praise of great achievements or accomplishments; fame; celebrity; -- always in a good sense.

Renown Re*nown" (r?-noun"), v. t. [F. renommer to name again, celebrate, make famous; pref. re- re- + nommer to name, L. nominare, fr. nomen a name. See Noun.] To make famous; to give renown to. [Obs.]

renowned.c: Renowned Re*nowned" (r?-nound"), a. Famous; celebrated for great achievements, for distinguished qualities, or for grandeur; eminent; as, a renowned king. “Some renowned metropolis with glistering spires.” Milton.

renowner.c: Renowner Re*nown"er (-?r), n. One who gives renown. [R.]

renownful.c: Renownful Re*nown"ful (-f?l), a. Having great renown; famous. “Renownful Scipio.” Marston.

rensselaerite.c: Rensselaerite Rens"se*laer*ite (r?ns"se-l?r-?t), n. (Min.) A soft, compact variety of talc,, being an altered pyroxene. It is often worked in a lathe into inkstands and other articles.

rent.c: Rent Rent (rĕnt), v. i. To rant. [R. & Obs.] Hudibras.
Rent Rent (rĕnt), imp. & p. p. of Rend.
Rent Rent (rĕnt), n. [From Rend.] 1. An opening made by rending; a break or breach made by force; a tear.
Rent Rent (rĕnt), v. t. To tear. See Rend. [Obs.] Chaucer.

Rent Rent (rĕnt), n. [F. rente, LL. renta, fr. L. reddita, fem. sing. or neut. pl. of redditus, p. p. of reddere to give back, pay. See Render.] 1. Income; revenue. See Catel. [Obs.] “Catel had they enough and rent.” Chaucer.

Rent Rent, v. t. [imp. & p. p. Rented; p. pr. & vb. n. Renting.] [F. renter. See Rent, n.] 1. To grant the possession and enjoyment of, for a rent; to lease; as, the owwner of an estate or house rents it.
Rent Rent, v. i. To be leased, or let for rent; as, an estate rents for five hundred dollars a year.

rentable.c: Rentable Rent"a*ble (-?-b'l), a. Capable of being rented, or suitable for renting.

rental.c: Rental Rent"al (-al), n. [LL. rentale, fr. renta. See Rent income.] 1. A schedule, account, or list of rents, with the names of the tenants, etc.; a rent roll.

rente.c: Rente ‖Rente (räNt), n. [F. See Rent income.] In France, interest payable by government on indebtedness; the bonds, shares, stocks, etc., which represent government indebtedness.

renter.c: Renter Rent"er (r?nt"?r), n. One who rents or leases an estate; -- usually said of a lessee or tenant.

Renter Ren"ter (r?n"t?r), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Rentered (-t?rd); p. pr. & vb. n. Rentering.] [F. rentraire; L. pref. re- re- + in into, in + trahere to draw.] 1. To sew together so that the seam is scarcely visible; to sew up with skill and nicety; to finedraw.

rentier.c: Rentier ‖Ren`tier" (r?N`ty?"), n. [F. See 5th Rent.] One who has a fixed income, as from lands, stocks, or the like.

renumerate.c: Renumerate Re*nu"mer*ate (r?-n?"m?r-?t), v. t. [L. renumeratus, p. p. of renumerare to count over, count up; pref. re- re- + numerare to count. See Numerate.] To recount.

renunciation.c: Renunciation Re*nun`ci*a"tion (r?-n?n`s?-?"sh?n or -sh?-?"sh?n; 277), n. [Cf. F. renonciation, L. renuntiatio ann announcement. See Renounce.] 1. The act of renouncing.

renunciatory.c: Renunciatory Re*nun"ci*a*to*ry (r?-n?n"sh?-?-t?-r?), a. [Cf. LL. renuntiatorius.] Pertaining to renunciation; containing or declaring a renunciation; as, renunciatory vows.

renverse.c: Renverse Ren*verse" (r?n-vErs"), v. t. [F. renverser; L. pref. re- re- + in in, into + versare, v. intens. fr. vertere to turn.] To reverse. [Obs.]
Renverse Renverse { Ren*verse" (r?n*v?rs"), or ‖Ren`ver`sé" (r?n`v?r`s?") }, a. [F. renversé, p. p. ] (Her.) Reversed; set with the head downward; turned contrary to the natural position.

renvoy.c: Renvoy Ren*voy" (-voi"), v. t. [F. renvoyer.] To send back. [Obs.] “Not dismissing or renvoying her.” Bacon.
Renvoy Ren*voy", n. [F. renvoi.] A sending back. [Obs.]

reobtain.c: Reobtain Re`ob*tain" (r?`?b-t?n"), v. t. To obtain again.

reobtainable.c: Reobtainable Re`ob*tain"a*ble (-?-b'l), a. That may be reobtained.

reoccupy.c: Reoccupy Re*oc"cu*py (r?-?k"k?-p?), v. t. To occupy again.

reopen.c: Reopen Re*o"pen (r?-?"p'n), v. t. & i. To open again.

reoppose.c: Reoppose Re`op*pose" (r?`?p-p?z"), v. t. To oppose again.

reordain.c: Reordain Re`or*dain" (r?`?r-d?n"), v. t. [Pref. re- re- + ordain: cf. F. réordonner.] To ordain again, as when the first ordination is considered defective. Bp. Burnet.

reorder.c: Reorder Re*or"der (r?-?r"d?r), v. t. To order a second time.

reorganization.c: Reorganization Re*or`gan*i*za"tion (-gan-?-z?"sh?n), n. The act of reorganizing; a reorganized existence; as, reorganization of the troops.

reorganize.c: reorganize re-organize Re*or"gan*ize, Re-or"gan*ize (re*ôr"gain*īz), v. t. & i. To organize again or anew; as, to reorganize a society or an army.

rep.c: Rep Rep (rĕp), n. [Prob. a corruption of rib: cf. F. reps.] A fabric made of silk or wool, or of silk and wool, and having a transversely corded or ribbed surface.
Rep Rep (rĕp), a. Formed with a surface closely corded, or ribbed transversely; -- applied to textile fabrics of silk or wool; as, rep silk.

repace.c: Repace Re*pace" (r?-p?s"), v. t. To pace again; to walk over again in a contrary direction.

repacify.c: Repacify Re*pac"i*fy (r?-p?s"?-f?), v. t. To pacify again.

repack.c: Repack Re*pack" (r?-p?k"), v. t. To pack a second time or anew; as, to repack beef; to repack a trunk.

repaganize.c: Repaganize Re*pa"gan*ize (r?-p?"gan-?z), v. t. To paganize anew; to bring back to paganism.

repaid.c: Repaid Re*paid" (r?-p?d"), imp. & p. p. of Repay.

repaint.c: Repaint Re*paint" (r?-p?nt"), v. t. To paint anew or again; as, to repaint a house; to repaint the ground of a picture.

repair.c: Repair Re*pair" (r?-p?r"), v. i. [OE. repairen, OF. repairier to return, fr. L. repatriare to return to one's contry, to go home again; pref. re- re- + patria native country, fr. pater father. See Father, and cf. Repatriate.] 1. To return. [Obs.]
Repair Re*pair", n. [OF. repaire retreat, asylum, abode. See Repair to go.] 1. The act of repairing or resorting to a place. [R.] Chaucer.

Repair Re*pair", v. t. [imp. & p. p. Repaired (-p?rd"); p. pr. & vb. n. Repairing.] [F. réparer, L. reparare; pref. re- re- + parare to prepare. See Pare, and cf. Reparation.] 1. To restore to a sound or good state after decay, injury, dilapidation, or partial destruction; to renew; to restore; to mend; as, to repair a house, a road, a shoe, or a ship; to repair a shattered fortune.

Repair Re*pair", n. 1. Restoration to a sound or good state after decay, waste, injury, or partial restruction; supply of loss; reparation; as, materials are collected for the repair of a church or of a city.

repairer.c: Repairer Re*pair"er (-?r), n. One who, or that which, repairs, restores, or makes amends.

repand.c: Repand Re*pand" (r?*p?nd), a. [L. repandus bent backward, turned up; pref. re- re- + pandus bent, crooked.] (Bot. & Zool.) Having a slightly undulating margin; -- said of leaves.

reparability.c: Reparability Rep`a*ra*bil"i*ty (r?p`?-r?-b?l"?-t?), n. The quality or state of being reparable.

reparable.c: Reparable Rep"a*ra*ble (r?p"?-r?-b'l), a. [L. reparabilis: cf. F. réparable.] Capable of being repaired, restored to a sound or good state, or made good; restorable; as, a reparable injury.

reparably.c: Reparably Rep"a*ra*bly, adv. In a reparable manner.

reparation.c: Reparation Rep`a*ra"tion (-r?"sh?n), n. [F. réparation, L. reparatio. See Repair to mend.] 1. The act of renewing, restoring, etc., or the state of being renewed or repaired; as, the reparation of a bridge or of a highway; -- in this sense, repair is oftener used. Arbuthnot.

reparative.c: Reparative Re*par"a*tive (r?-p?r"?-t?v), a. Repairing, or tending to repair. Jer. Taylor.
Reparative Re*par"a*tive, n. That which repairs. Sir H. Wotton.

reparel.c: Reparel Re*par"el (-?l), n. [Cf. Reapparel.] A change of apparel; a second or different suit. [Obs.] Beau. & Fl.

repartee.c: Repartee Rep`ar*tee" (r?p`3r-t?"), n. [F. repartie, fr. repartir to reply, depart again; pref. re- re- partir to part, depart. See Part.] A smart, ready, and witty reply.
Repartee Rep`ar*tee", v. i. [imp. & p. p. Reparteed (-t?d"); p. pr. & vb. n. Reparteeing.] To make smart and witty replies. [R.] Prior.

repartimiento.c: Repartimiento ‖Re`par*ti`mi*en"to (r?`p?r-t?`m?-?n"t?), n. [Sp., fr. repartir to divide.] A partition or distribution, especially of slaves; also, an assessment of taxes. W. Irving.

repartotion.c: Repartotion Re`par*to"tion (r?-p?r-t?sh"?n), n. Another, or an additional, separation into parts.

repass.c: Repass Re*pass" (r?-p?s"), v. t. [Pref. re- + pass: cf. F. repasser. Cf. Repace.] To pass again; to pass or travel over in the opposite direction; to pass a second time; as, to repass a bridge or a river; to repass the sea.
Repass Re*pass", v. i. To pass or go back; to move back; as, troops passing and repassing before our eyes.

repassage.c: Repassage Re*pas"sage (r?-p?s"s?j;48), n. The act of repassing; passage back. Hakluyt.

repassant.c: Repassant Re*pas"sant (r?-p?s"sant), a. [Cf. F. repassant, p. pr.] (Her.) Counterpassant.

repast.c: Repast Re*past" (r?-p?st"), n. [OF. repast, F. repas, LL. repastus, fr. L. repascere to feed again; pref. re- re- + pascere, pastum, to pasture, feed. See Pasture.] 1. The act of taking food.
Repast Re*past", v. t. & i. To supply food to; to feast; to take food. [Obs.] “Repast them with my blood.” Shak.

repaster.c: Repaster Re*past"er (-?r), n. One who takes a repast. [Obs.]

repatriate.c: Repatriate Re*pa"tri*ate (r?-p?"tr?-?t), v. t. [L. repatriare. See 1st Repair.] To restore to one's own country.

repatriation.c: Repatriation Re*pa`tri*a"tion (-?"sh?n), n. [Cf. LL. repatriatio return to one's country.] Restoration to one's country.

repay.c: Repay Re*pay" (r?-p?"), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Repaid (-p?d"); p. pr. & vb. n. Repaying.] [Pref. re- + pay: cf. F. repayer.] 1. To pay back; to refund; as, to repay money borrowed or advanced.

repayable.c: Repayable Re*pay"a*ble (-?-b'l), a. Capable of being, or proper to be, repaid; due; as, a loan repayable in ten days; services repayable in kind.

repayment.c: Repayment Re*pay"ment (-ment), n. 1. The act of repaying; reimbursement. Jer. Taylor.

repeal.c: Repeal Re*peal" (r?-p?l"), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Repealed (-p?ld"); p. pr. & vb. n. Repealing.] [OF. repeler to call back, F. rappeler; pref. re- re- + OF. apeler, F. appeler, to call, L. appellare. See Appeal, and. cf. Repel.] 1. To recall; to summon again, as persons. [Obs.]
Repeal Re*peal", n. 1. Recall, as from exile. [Obs.]

repealability.c: Repealability Re*peal`a*bil"i*ty (-?-b?l"?-t?), n. The quality or state of being repealable.

repealable.c: Repealable Re*peal"a*ble (r?-p?l"?-b'l), a. Capable of being repealed. -- Re*peal"a*ble*ness, n.

repealer.c: Repealer Re*peal"er (-?r), n. One who repeals; one who seeks a repeal; specifically, an advocate for the repeal of the Articles of Union between Great Britain and Ireland.

repealment.c: Repealment Re*peal"ment (-ment), n. Recall, as from banishment. [Obs.]

repeat.c: Repeat Re*peat" (-p?t"), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Repeated; p. pr. & vb. n. Repeating.] [F. répéter, L. repetere; pref. re- re- + petere to fall upon, attack. See Petition.]
Repeat Re*peat" (r?-p?t"), n. 1. The act of repeating; repetition.

repeatedly.c: Repeatedly Re*peat"ed*ly, adv. More than once; again and again; indefinitely.

repeater.c: Repeater Re*peat"er (-?r), n. One who, or that which, repeats. Specifically: (a) A watch with a striking apparatus which, upon pressure of a spring, will indicate the time, usually in hours and quarters. (b) A repeating firearm. (c) (Teleg.) An instrument for resending a telegraphic message automatically at an intermediate point. (d) A person who votes more than once at an election. [U.S.] (e) See Circulating decimal, under Decimal. (f) (Naut.) A pennant used to indicate that a certain flag in a hoist of signal is duplicated. Ham. Nav. Encyc.

repeating.c: Repeating Re*peat"ing, a. Doing the same thing over again; accomplishing a given result many times in succession; as, a repeating firearm; a repeating watch.

repedation.c: Repedation Rep"e*da"tion (r?p`?-da"sh?n), n. [L. repedare to step back; pref. re- re- + pes, pedis, foot.] A stepping or going back. [Obs.] Dr. H. More.

repel.c: Repel Re**pel" (r?-p?l"), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Repelled (-p?ld"); p. pr. & vb. n. Repelling.] [L. repellere, repulsum; pref. re- re- + pellere to drive. See Pulse a beating, and cf. Repulse, Repeal.] 1. To drive back; to force to return; to check the advance of; to repulse as, to repel an enemy or an assailant.
Repel Re*pel", v. i. To act with force in opposition to force impressed; to exercise repulsion.

repellency.c: Repellency Repellence { Re*pel"lence (-lens), Re*pel"len*cy (-len-s?), } n. The principle of repulsion; the quality or capacity of repelling; repulsion.

repellent.c: Repellent Re*pel"lent (-lent), a. [L. repellens, -entis, p. pr. ] Driving back; able or tending to repel.

repeller.c: Repeller Re*pel"ler (-l?r), n. One who, or that which, repels.

repent.c: Repent Re"pent (r?"p?nt), a. [L. repens, -entis, creeping, p. pr. of repere to creep.] 1. (Bot.) Prostrate and rooting; -- said of stems. Gray.

Repent Re*pent" (r?-p?nt"), v. i. [imp. & p. p. Repented; p. pr. & vb. n. Repenting.] [F. se repentir; L. pref. re- re- + poenitere to make repent, poenitet me it repents me, I repent. See Penitent.] 1. To feel pain, sorrow, or regret, for what one has done or omitted to do.
Repent Re*pent", v. t. 1. To feel pain on account of; to remember with sorrow.

repentance.c: Repentance Re*pent"ance (re*pĕnt"ains), n. [F. repentance.] The act of repenting, or the state of being penitent; sorrow for what one has done or omitted to do; especially, contrition for sin. Chaucer.

repentant.c: Repentant Re*pent"ant (-aint), a. [F. repentant.] 1. Penitent; sorry for sin. Chaucer.
Repentant Re*pent"ant, n. One who repents, especially one who repents of sin; a penitent.

repentantly.c: Repentantly Re*pent"ant*ly, adv. In a repentant manner.

repeople.c: Repeople Re*peo"ple (rē*pē"p'l), v. t. [Pref. re- + people: cf. F. repeupler.] To people anew.

reperception.c: Reperception Re`per*cep"tion (r?`p?r-s?p"sh?n), n. The act of perceiving again; a repeated perception of the same object.

repercuss.c: Repercuss Re`per*cuss" (-kŭs"), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Repercussed (-k?st");p. pr. & vb. n. Repercussing.] [L. repercusus, p. p. of repercutere to drive back; pref. re- re- + percutere. See Percussion.] To drive or beat back; hence, to reflect; to reverberate.

repercussion.c: Repercussion Re`per*cus"sion (-k?sh"?n), n. [L. repercussio: cf. F. répercussion.] 1. The act of driving back, or the state of being driven back; reflection; reverberation; as, the repercussion of sound.

repertitious.c: Repertitious Rep`er*ti"tious (r?p`?r-t?sh"?s), a. [L. reperticius. See Repertory.] Found; gained by finding. [Obs.]

repertoire.c: Repertoire ‖Ré`per`toire" (F. ra`pâr`twär"; E. rĕp"ẽr*twär), n. [F. See Repertory.] A list of dramas, operas, pieces, parts, etc., which a company or a person has rehearsed and is prepared to perform.

repertory.c: Repertory Rep"er*to*ry (r?p"?r-t?-r?), n. [L. repertorium, fr. reperire to find again; pref. re- re + parire, parere, to bring forth, procure: cf. F. répertoire. Cf. Parent.]

reperusal.c: Reperusal Re`pe*rus"al (r?`p?-r?z"al), n. A second or repeated perusal.

reperuse.c: Reperuse Re`pe*ruse" (-r?z"), v. t. To peruse again. Ld. Lytton.

repetend.c: Repetend Rep`e*tend (r?p`?-t?nd"), n. [L. repetendus to be repeated, fr. repetere to repeat.] (Math.) That part of a circulating decimal which recurs continually, ad infinitum: -- sometimes indicated by a dot over the first and last figures; thus, in the circulating decimal.728328328 + (otherwise.7repetend is 283.

repetition.c: Repetition Rep`e*ti"tion (rĕp`e-tĭsh"ŭn), n. [L. repetitio: cf. F. répétition. See Repeat.] 1. The act of repeating; a doing or saying again; iteration.

repetitionary.c: Repetitionary Repetitional { Rep`e*ti"tion*al (-al). Rep`e*ti"tion*a*ry (-?-r?) }, a. Of the nature of, or containing, repetition. [R.]

repetitious.c: Repetitious Rep`e*ti"tious (-t?sh"?s), a. Repeating; containing repetition. [U.S.] Dr. T. Dwight.

repetitor.c: Repetitor ‖Rep"e*ti`tor (r?p"?-t?`t?r), n. [Cf. L. repetitor a reclaimer.] (Ger.Univ.) A private instructor.

repine.c: Repine Re*pine" (r?-p?n"), v. i. [Pref. re- + pine to languish.]

repiningly.c: Repiningly Re*pin"ing*ly, adv. With repening or murmuring.

repkie.c: Repkie ‖Rep"kie (r?p"k?), n. [From the native name.] (Zool.) Any edible sea urchin. [Alaska]

replace.c: Replace Re*place" (r?-pl?s"), v. t. [Pref. re- + place: cf. F. replacer.] 1. To place again; to restore to a former place, position, condition, or the like.

replaceability.c: Replaceability Re*place`a*bil"i*ty (-?-b?l"?-t?), n. The quality, state, or degree of being replaceable.

replaceable.c: Replaceable Re*place"a*ble (r?-pl?s"?-b'l), a. 1. Capable or admitting of being put back into a place.

replacement.c: Replacement Re*place"ment (-ment), n. 1. The act of replacing.

replait.c: Replait Re*plait" (r?-pl?t"), v. t. To plait or fold again; to fold, as one part over another, again and again.

replant.c: Replant Re*plant" (rE-pl?nt"), v. t. To plant again.

replantable.c: Replantable Re*plant"a*ble (-?-b'l), a. That may be planted again.

replantation.c: Replantation Re`plan*ta"tion (r?`pl?n-t?"sh?n), n. The act of planting again; a replanting. [R.] Hallywell.

replead.c: Replead Re*plead" (r?-pl?d"), v. t. & i. To plead again.

repleader.c: Repleader Re*plead"er (-?r), n. (Law) A second pleading, or course of pleadings; also, the right of pleading again.

replenish.c: Replenish Re*plen"ish (r?-pl?n"?sh), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Replenished (-?sht); p. pr. & vb. n. Replenishing.] [OE. replenissen, OF. replenir; L. pref. re- re- + plenus full. See Full, -ish, and cf. Replete.] 1. To fill again after having been diminished or emptied; to stock anew; hence, to fill completely; to cause to abound.
Replenish Re*plen"ish, v. i. To recover former fullness. [Obs.]

replenishment.c: Replenishment Re*plen"ish*ment (-ment), n. 1. The act of replenishing, or the state of being replenished.

replete.c: Replete Re*plete" (r?-pl?t"), a. [L. repletus, p. p. of replere to fill again, fill up; pref. re- re- + plere to fill, akin to plenus full: cf. F. replet corpulent. See Plenty, Replenish.] Filled again; completely filled; full; charged; abounding. “His words replete with guile.” Milton.
Replete Re*plete", v. t. To fill completely, or to satiety. [R.]

repleteness.c: Repleteness Re*plete"ness, n. The state of being replete.

repletion.c: Repletion Re*ple"tion (r?-pl?"sh?n), n. [L. repletio a filling up: cf. F. réplétion. See Replete.] 1. The state of being replete; superabundant fullness.

repletive.c: Repletive Re*ple"tive (-t?v), a. [Cf. F. réplétif.] Tending to make replete; filling. -- Re*ple"tive*ly, adv.

repleviable.c: Repleviable Re*plev"i*a*ble (r?-pl?v"?-?-b'l), a. [See Replevy.] (Law) Capable of being replevied.

replevin.c: Replevin Re*plev"in (-?n), n. [LL. replevina. See Replevy, and cf. Plevin.] 1. (Law) A personal action which lies to recover possession of goods and chattle wrongfully taken or detained. Originally, it was a remedy peculiar to cases for wrongful distress, but it may generally now be brought in all cases of wrongful taking or detention. Bouvier.

replevisable.c: Replevisable Re*plev"i*sa*ble (-?-s?-b'l), a. [OF. replevisable.] Repleviable. Sir M. Hale.

replevy.c: Replevy Re*plev"y (-?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Replevied (-?d); p. pr. & vb. n. Replevying.] [OF. replevir, LL. replevire. See Pledge, Replevin.] 1. (Law) To take or get back, by a writ for that purpose (goods and chattels wrongfully taken or detained), upon giving security to try the right to them in a suit at law, and, if that should be determined against the plaintiff, to return the property replevied.

replicated.c: Replicated Replicate { Rep"li*cate (l?-k?t), Rep"li*ca`ted (-k?`t?d), } a. [L. replicatus, p. p. of replicare. See Reply.] Folded over or backward; folded back upon itself; as, a replicate leaf or petal; a replicate margin of a shell.

replication.c: Replication Rep`li*ca"tion (-k?"sh?n), n. [L. replicatio. See Reply.] 1. An answer; a reply. Shak.

replier.c: Replier Re*pli"er (r?-pl?"?r), n. One who replies. Bacon.

replum.c: Replum ‖Re"plum (r?"pl?m), n. [L., doorcase.] (Bot.) The framework of some pods, as the cress, which remains after the valves drop off. Gray.

reply.c: Reply Re*ply" (r?-pl?"), v. i. [imp. & p. p. Replied (-pl?d"); p. pr. & vb. n. Replying.] [OE. replien, OF. replier, F. répliquer, fr. L. replicare to fold back, make a reply; pref. re- re- + plicare to fold. See Ply, and cf. Replica.] 1. To make a return in words or writing; to respond; to answer.
Reply Re*ply", v. t. To return for an answer. Milton.
Reply Re*ply", n.; pl. Replies (-pl?z"). [See Reply, v. i., and cf. Replica.] That which is said, written, or done in answer to what is said, written, or done by another; an answer; a response.

repolish.c: Repolish Re*pol"ish (r?-p?l"?sh), v. t. To polish again.

repone.c: Repone Re*pone" (r?-p?n"), v. t. [L. reponere; pref. re- re- + ponere to place.] To replace. R. Baillie.

repopulation.c: Repopulation Re*pop`u*la"tion (r?*p?p`?*l?"sh?n), n. The act of repeopling; act of furnishing with a population anew.

report.c: Report Re*port" (r?-p?rt"), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Reported; p. pr. & vb. n. Reporting.] [F. reporter to carry back, carry (cf. rapporter; see Rapport), L. reportare to bear or bring back; pref. re- re- + portare to bear or bring. See Port bearing, demeanor.] 1. To refer. [Obs.]
Report Re*port" (r?-p?rt"), v. i. 1. To make a report, or response, in respect of a matter inquired of, a duty enjoined, or information expected; as, the committee will report at twelve o'clock.

Report Re*port" (re*pōrt"), n. [Cf. F. rapport. See Report.v. t.] 1. That which is reported. Specifically: (a) An account or statement of the results of examination or inquiry made by request or direction; relation. “From Thetis sent as spies to make report.” Waller. (b) A story or statement circulating by common talk; a rumor; hence, fame; repute; reputation.

reportable.c: Reportable Re*port"a*ble (-ȧ*b'l), a. Capable or admitting of being reported.

reporter.c: Reporter Re*port"er (-ẽr), n. One who reports. Specifically: (a) An officer or person who makes authorized statements of law proceedings and decisions, or of legislative debates. (b) One who reports speeches, the proceedings of public meetings, news, etc., for the newspapers.

reportingly.c: Reportingly Re*port"ing*ly, adv. By report or common fame.

reportorial.c: Reportorial Re`por*to"ri*al (rē`por*tō"rĭ*ail), a. Of or pertaining to a reporter or reporters; as, the reportorial staff of a newspaper.

reposal.c: Reposal Re*pos"al (re*pōz"ail), n. [From Repose.] 1. The act or state of reposing; as, the reposal of a trust. Shak.

repose.c: Repose Re*pose" (re*pōz"), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Reposed (-p?zd"); p. pr. & vb. n. Reposing.] [F. reposer; L. pref. re- re- + pausare to pause. See Pause, Pose, v.] 1. To cause to stop or to rest after motion; hence, to deposit; to lay down; to lodge; to reposit. [Obs.]
Repose Re*pose", v. i. 1. To lie at rest; to rest.
Repose Re*pose", n. [F. repos. See Repose, v.] 1. A lying at rest; sleep; rest; quiet.

reposed.c: Reposed Re*posed" (re*pōzd"), a. Composed; calm; tranquil; at rest. Bacon. -- Re*pos"ed*ly (re*pōz"ĕd*ly̆), adv. -- Re*pos"ed*ness, n.

reposeful.c: Reposeful Re*pose"ful (re*pōz"fụl), a. Full of repose; quiet.

reposit.c: Reposit Re*pos"it (re*pŏz"ĭt), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Reposited; p. pr. & vb. n. Repositing.] [L. repositus, p. p. of reponere to put back; pref. re- re- + ponere to put. See Position.] To cause to rest or stay; to lay away; to lodge, as for safety or preservation; to place; to store.

reposition.c: Reposition Re`po*si"tion (re`po*zĭsh"ŭn), n. [L. repositio.] The act of repositing; a laying up.

repositor.c: Repositor Re*pos"i*tor (re*pŏz"ĭ*tẽr), n. (Surg.) An instrument employed for replacing a displaced organ or part.

repository.c: Repository Re*pos"i*to*ry (re*pŏz"ĭ*to*ry̆), n. [L. repositorium, repostorium: cf. OF. repositoire.] A place where things are or may be reposited, or laid up, for safety or preservation; a depository. Locke.

repossess.c: Repossess Re`pos*sess" (re`pŏz*zĕs" or re`pŏs*sĕs"), v. t. 1. To possess again; as, to repossess the land. Pope.

repossession.c: Repossession Re`pos*ses"sion (r?`p?z-z?sh"?n or -p?s s?sh"?n), n. The act or the state of possessing again.

repour.c: Repour Re*pour" (r?-p?r"), v. t. To pour again.

repoussage.c: Repoussage ‖Re*pous`sage" (?), n. [F. See Repoussé.] (Art) Art or process of hammering out or pressing thin metal from the reverse side: (1) in producing repoussé work; (2) in leveling up any part of an etched plate that has been worked so as to cause a depression.

repousse.c: Repousse ‖Re*pous`sé" (re -p??`s?"), a. [F., p. p. of repousser to thrust back; pref re- + pousser to push. See Push.] (a) Formed in relief, as a pattern on metal. (b) Ornamented with patterns in relief made by pressing or hammering on the reverse side; -- said of thin metal, or of a vessel made of thin metal. -- n. Repoussé work.

reprehend.c: Reprehend Rep`re*hend" (r?p`r?-h?nd"), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Reprehended; p. pr. & vb. n. Reprehending.] [L. reprehendere, reprehensum, to hold back, seize, check, blame; pref. re- re- + prehendere to lay hold of. See Prehensile, and cf. Reprisal. ] To reprove or reprimand with a view of restraining, checking, or preventing; to make charge of fault against; to disapprove of; to chide; to blame; to censure. Chaucer.

reprehensible.c: Reprehensible Rep`re*hen"si*ble (-h?n"s?-b'l), a. [L. reprehensibilis: cf. F. répréhensible.] Worthy of reprehension; culpable; censurable; blamable. -- Rep`re*hen"si*ble*ness, n. -- Rep`re*hen"si*bly, adv.

reprehension.c: Reprehension Rep`re*hen"sion (-sh?n), n. [L. reprehensio: cf. F. répréhension.] Reproof; censure; blame; disapproval.

reprehensive.c: Reprehensive Rep`re*hen"sive (-h?n"s?v), a. [Cf. F. répréhensif.] Containing reprehension; conveying reproof. South.

reprehensory.c: Reprehensory Rep`re*hen"so*ry (-s?-r?), a. Containing reproof; reprehensive; as, reprehensory complaint. Johnson.

represent.c: Re-present Re`-pre*sent" (r?`pr?-z?nt"), v. t. To present again; as, to re-present the points of an argument.

Represent Rep`re*sent" (r?p`r?-z?nt"), v. t. [F. représenter, L. repraesentare, repraesentatum; pref. re- re- + preesentare to place before, present. See Present, v. t.] 1. To present again or anew; to present by means of something standing in the place of; to exhibit the counterpart or image of; to typify.

representable.c: Representable Rep`re*sent"a*ble (-?-b'l), a. Capable of being represented.

representant.c: Representant Rep`re*sent"ant (-ant), a. [Cf. F. repr?sentant.] Appearing or acting for another; representing.
Representant Rep`re*sent"ant, n. [F. representant.] A representative. [Obs.] Sir H. Wotton.

representation.c: Representation Rep`re*sen*ta"tion (-z?n-t?"sh?n), n. [F. repr?sentation, L. representatio.] 1. The act of representing, in any sense of the verb.

Re-presentation Re-pres`en*ta"tion (r?-prez`?n-t?"sh?n), n. [See Re-present.] The act of re-presenting, or the state of being presented again; a new presentation; as, re-presentation of facts previously stated.

representative.c: Representative Rep`re*sent"a*tive (-z?nt`?-t?v), a. [Cf. F. repr?sentatif.] 1. Fitted to represent; exhibiting a similitude.

representatively.c: Representatively Rep`re*sent"a*tive*ly, adv. In a representative manner; vicariously.

representativeness.c: Representativeness Rep`re*sent"a*tive*ness, n. The quality or state of being representative.

representer.c: Representer Rep`re*sent"er (-?r), n. 1. One who shows, exhibits, or describes. Sir T. Browne.

repress.c: Repress Re*press" (r?-pr?s"), v. t. [Pref. re- + press.] To press again.

Repress Re*press" (r?-pr?s"), v. t. [Pref. re- + press: cf. L. reprimere, repressum. Cf. Reprimand.] 1. To press back or down effectually; to crush down or out; to quell; to subdue; to supress; as, to repress sedition or rebellion; to repress the first risings of discontent.
Repress Re*press", n. The act of repressing. [Obs.]

represser.c: Represser Re*press"er (-?r), n. One who, or that which, represses.

repressible.c: Repressible Re*press"i*ble (-?-b'l), a. Capable of being repressed.

repressive.c: Repressive Re*press"ive (r?-pr?s"?v), a. [Cf. F. répressif. LL. repressivus.] Having power, or tending, to repress; as, repressive acts or measures. -- Re*press"ive*ly, adv.

repreve.c: Repreve Re*preve" (r?-pr?v"), v. t. [See Reprieve, v. t.] To reprove. [Obs.] “Repreve him of his vice.” Chaucer.

reprieve.c: Reprieve Re*prieve (r?-pr?v"), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Reprieved (-pr?vd"); p. pr. & vb. n. Reprieving.] [OE. repreven to reject, disallow, OF. reprover to blame, reproach, condemn (pres. il reprueve), F. réprouver to disapprove, fr. L. reprobare to reject, condemn; pref. re- re- + probare to try, prove. See Prove, and cf. Reprove, Reprobate.]
Reprieve Re*prieve" (r?-pr?v"), n. 1. A temporary suspension of the execution of a sentence, especially of a sentence of death.

reprimand.c: Reprimand Rep"ri*mand (r?p"r?-m?nd), n. [F. réprimande, fr. L. reprimendus, reprimenda, that is to be checked or suppressed, fr. reprimere to check, repress; pref. re- re + premere to press. See Press, and cf. Repress.] Severe or formal reproof; reprehension, private or public.

Reprimand Rep"ri*mand, v. t. [imp. & p. p. Reprimanded; p. pr. & vb. n. Reprimanding.] [Cf. F. réprimander. See Reprimand, n.] 1. To reprove severely; to reprehend; to chide for a fault; to consure formally.

reprimer.c: Reprimer Re*prim"er (r?-pr?m"?r), n. (Firearms) A machine or implement for applying fresh primers to spent cartridge shells, so that the shells be used again.

reprint.c: Reprint Re*print" (r?-pr?nt"), v. t. 1. To print again; to print a second or a new edition of.
Reprint Re"print` (r?"pr?nt`), n. A second or a new impression or edition of any printed work; specifically, the publication in one country of a work previously published in another.

reprisal.c: Reprisal Re*pris"al (r?-priz"al), n. [F. repr?saille, It. ripresaglia, rappresaglia, LL. reprensaliae, fr. L. reprehendere, reprehensum. See Reprehend, Reprise.] 1. The act of taking from an enemy by way of reteliation or indemnity.

reprise.c: Reprise Re*prise" (r?-pr?z"), n. [F. reprise, fr. reprendre, repris, to take back, L. reprehendere. See Reprehend.]
Reprise Re*prise", v. t. [Written also reprize.] 1. To take again; to retake. [Obs.] Spenser.

repristinate.c: Repristinate Re*pris"tin*ate (r?-pr?s"t?n-?t), v. t. [Pref. re- + pristine.] To restore to an original state. [R.] Shedd.

repristination.c: Repristination Re*pris`ti*na"tion (-t?-n?"sh?n), n. Restoration to an original state; renewal of purity. [R.] R. Browning.

reprive.c: Reprive Re*prive" (r?-pr?v"), v. t. [Pref. re- + L. privare to deprive.] To take back or away. [Obs.] Spenser.
Reprive Re*prive", v. t. To reprieve. [Obs.] Howell.

reprize.c: Reprize Re*prize" (-pr?z"), v. t. See Reprise. [Obs.] Spenser.

reprizes.c: Reprizes Re*priz"es (-pr?z"?z), n. pl. (Law) See Reprise, n., 2.

reproach.c: Reproach Re*proach" (r?-pr?ch"), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Reproached (-pr?cht"); p. pr. & vb. n. Reproaching.] [F. reprocher, OF. reprochier, (assumed) LL. reproriare; L. pref. re- again, against, back + prope near; hence, originally, to bring near to, throw in one's teeth. Cf. Approach.] 1. To come back to, or come home to, as a matter of blame; to bring shame or disgrace upon; to disgrace. [Obs.]
Reproach Re*proach", n. [F. reproche. See Reproach, v.]

reproachful.c: Reproachful Re*proach"ful (-f?l), a. 1. Expressing or containing reproach; upbraiding; opprobrious; abusive.

reprobate.c: Reprobate Rep"ro*bate (-b?t), a. [L. reprobatus, p. p. of reprobare to disapprove, condemn. See Reprieve, Reprove.]
Reprobate Rep"ro*bate, n. One morally abandoned and lost.

Reprobate Rep"ro*bate (-b?t), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Reprobated (-b?`t?d); p. pr. & vb. n. Reprobating.] 1. To disapprove with detestation or marks of extreme dislike; to condemn as unworthy; to disallow; to reject.

reprobateness.c: Reprobateness Rep"ro*bate*ness, n. The state of being reprobate.

reprobation.c: Reprobation Rep`ro*ba"tion (-b?`sh?n), n. [F. réprobation, or L. reprobatio.] 1. The act of reprobating; the state of being reprobated; strong disapproval or censure.

reprobationer.c: Reprobationer Rep`ro*ba"tion*er (-?r), n. (Theol.) One who believes in reprobation. See Reprobation, 2. South.

reprobative.c: Reprobative Rep"ro*ba*tive (-b?-t?v), a. Of or pertaining to reprobation; expressing reprobation.

reproduce.c: Reproduce Re`pro*duce" (r?`pr?-d?s"), v. t. To produce again. Especially: (a) To bring forward again; as, to reproduce a witness; to reproduce charges; to reproduce a play. (b) To cause to exist again.

reproducer.c: Reproducer Re`pro*du"cer (-d?"s?r), n. 1. One who, or that which, reproduces. Burke.

reproduction.c: Reproduction Re`pro*duc"tion (-d?k"sh?n), n. [Cf. F. reproduction.] 1. The act or process of reproducing; the state of being reproduced; specifically (Biol.), the process by which plants and animals give rise to offspring.

reproductive.c: Reproductive Re`pro*duc"tive (-t?v), a. [Cf. F. reproductif.] Tending, or pertaining, to reproduction; employed in reproduction. Lyell.

reproof.c: Reproof Re*proof" (r?-pr??f"), n. [OE. reproef. See Proof, Reprove.] 1. Refutation; confutation; contradiction. [Obs.]

reprovable.c: Reprovable Re*prov"a*ble (r?-pr??v"?-b'l), a. [Cf. F. réprouvable.] Worthy of reproof or censure. Jer. Taylor.

reprove.c: Reprove Re*prove" (r?-pr??v"), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Reproved (-pr??vd"); p. pr. & vb. n. Reproving.] [F. réprouver, OF. reprover, fr. L. reprobare. See Reprieve, Reprobate, and cf. Reproof.] 1. To convince. [Obs.]

reprover.c: Reprover Re*prov"er (r?-pr??v"?r), n. One who, or that which, reproves.

reprovingly.c: Reprovingly Re*prov"ing*ly, adv. In a reproving manner.

reprune.c: Reprune Re*prune" (rē*prün"), v. t. To prune again or anew.

repsilver.c: Rep-silver Rep"-sil`ver (r?p"s?l`v?r), n. [See Reap.] Money anciently paid by servile tenants to their lord, in lieu of the customary service of reaping his corn or grain.

reptant.c: Reptant Rep"tant (r?p"tant), a. [L. reptans, -antis, p. pr. of reptare, v. intens. from repere to creep. See Reptile.]

reptantia.c: Reptantia ‖Rep*tan"ti*a (r?p-t?n"sh?-?), n. pl. [NL.] (Zool.) A division of gastropods; the Pectinibranchiata.

reptation.c: Reptation Rep*ta"tion (r?p-t?"sh?n), n. [L. reptatio, from reptare: cf. F. reptation.] (Zool.) The act of creeping.

reptile.c: Reptile Rep"tile (r?p"t?l;277), a. [F. reptile, L. reptilis, fr. repere, reptum, to creep; cf. Lith. reploti; perh. akin to L. serpere. Cf. Serpent.] 1. Creeping; moving on the belly, or by means of small and short legs.
Reptile Rep"tile, n. 1. (Zool.) An animal that crawls, or moves on its belly, as snakes,, or by means of small, short legs, as lizards, and the like.

reptilia.c: Reptilia ‖Rep*til"i*a (r?p-t?l"?-?), n. pl. [NL.] (Zool.) A class of air-breathing oviparous vertebrates, usually covered with scales or bony plates. The heart generally has two auricles and one ventricle. The development of the young is the same as that of birds.

reptilian.c: Reptilian Rep*til"i*an (-an), a. Belonging to the reptiles.
Reptilian Rep*til"i*an, n. (Zool.) One of the Reptilia; a reptile.

republic.c: Republic Re*pub"lic (r?-p?b"l?k), n. [F. république, L. respublica commonwealth; res a thing, an affair + publicus, publica, public. See Real, a., and Public.]

republican.c: Republican Re*pub"lic*an (-l?-kan), a. [F. républicain.] 1. Of or pertaining to a republic.
Republican Re*pub"lic*an (r?-p?b"l?-kan), n. 1. One who favors or prefers a republican form of government.

republicanism.c: Republicanism Re*pub"lic*an*ism (-?z'm), n. [Cf. F. républicanisme.] 1. A republican form or system of government; the principles or theory of republican government.

republicanize.c: Republicanize Re*pub"lic*an*ize (-?z), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Republicanized (-?zd); p. pr. & vb. n. Republicanizing (-?`z?ng).] [Cf. F. républicaniser.] To change, as a state, into a republic; to republican principles; as, France was republicanized; to republicanize the rising generation. D. Ramsay.

republicate.c: Republicate Re*pub"li*cate (r?*p?b"l?*k?t), v. t. [Cf. LL. republicare.] To make public again; to republish. [Obs.]

republication.c: Republication Re*pub`li*ca"tion (r?-p?b`l?-k?"sh?n), n. A second publication, or a new publication of something before published, as of a former will, of a volume already published, or the like; specifically, the publication in one country of a work first issued in another; a reprint.

republish.c: Republish Re*pub"lish (r?-p?b"l?sh), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Republished (-l?sht); p. pr. & vb. n. Republishing.] To publish anew; specifically, to publish in one country (a work first published in another); also, to revive (a will) by re?xecution or codicil.

repudiable.c: repudiable re*pu"di*a*ble (re*pū"dĭ*ȧ*b'l), a. [See repudiate.] Admitting of repudiation; fit or proper to be put away.

repudiate.c: Repudiate Re*pu"di*ate (re*pū"dĭ*āt), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Repudiated (-?`t?d); p. pr. & vb. n. Repudiating.] [L. repudiatus, p. p. of repudiare to repudiate, reject, fr. repudium separation, divorce; pref. re- re- + pudere to be ashamed.]

repudiation.c: Repudiation Re*pu`di*a"tion (re*pū`dĭ*ā"shŭn), n. [Cf.F. répudiation, L. repudiatio.] The act of repudiating, or the state of being repuddiated; as, the repudiation of a doctrine, a wife, a debt, etc.
Repudiation Re*pu`di*a"tion, n. One who favors repudiation, especially of a public debt.

repudiator.c: Repudiator Re*pu"di*a`tor (r?-p?"d?-?`t?r), n. [L., a rejecter, contemner.] One who repudiates.

repugn.c: Repugn Re*pugn" (r?-p?n"), v. t. [F. répugner, L. repugnare, repugnatum; pref. re- + pugnare to fight. See Pugnacious.] To fight against; to oppose; to resist. [R.]

repugnable.c: Repugnable Re*pug"na*ble (r?-p?g"n?-b'l), a. Capable of being repugned or resisted. [R.] Sir T. North.

repugnancy.c: Repugnancy Repugnance { Re*pug"nance (-nans), Re*pug"nan*cy (-nan-s?), } n. [F. répugnance, L. repugnantia.] The state or condition of being repugnant; opposition; contrariety; especially, a strong instinctive antagonism; aversion; reluctance; unwillingness, as of mind, passions, principles, qualities, and the like.

repugnant.c: Repugnant Re*pug"nant (-nant), a. [F. répugnant, or L. repugnans, -antis, p. pr. of repugnare. See Repugn.] Disposed to fight against; hostile; at war with; being at variance; contrary; inconsistent; refractory; disobedient; also, distasteful in a high degree; offensive; -- usually followed by to, rarely and less properly by with; as, all rudeness was repugnant to her nature.

repugnantly.c: Repugnantly Re*pug"nant*ly, adv. In a repugnant manner.

repugnate.c: Repugnate Re*pug"nate (-n?t), v. t. [From L. repugnare. See Repugn.] To oppose; to fight against. [Obs.]

repullulate.c: Repullulate Re*pul"lu*late (r?-p?l"l?-l?t), v. i. [L. repullulare, repullulatum. See Pullulate.] To bud again.

repullulation.c: Repullulation Re*pul`lu*la"tion (r?-p?l`l?-l?"sh?n), n. The act of budding again; the state of having budded again.

repulse.c: Repulse Re*pulse" (r?-p?ls"), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Repulsed (-p?lst"); p. pr. & vb. n. Repulsing.] [L. repulsus, p. p. of repellere. See Repel.] 1. To repel; to beat or drive back; as, to repulse an assault; to repulse the enemy.
Repulse Re*pulse", n. [L. repulsa, fr. repellere, repulsum.]

repulseless.c: Repulseless Re*pulse"less, a. Not capable of being repulsed.

repulser.c: Repulser Re*puls"er (-?r), n. One who repulses, or drives back.

repulsion.c: Repulsion Re*pul"sion (r?-p?l"sh?n), n. [L. repulsio: cf. F. répulsion.] 1. The act of repulsing or repelling, or the state of being repulsed or repelled.

repulsive.c: Repulsive Re*pul"sive (-s?v), a. [Cf. F. répulsif.] 1. Serving, or able, to repulse; repellent; as, a repulsive force.

repulsory.c: Repulsory Re*pul"so*ry (-s?-r?), a. [L. repulsorius.] Repulsive; driving back.

repurchase.c: Repurchase Re*pur"chase (r?*p?r"ch?s; 48), v. t. To buy back or again; to regain by purchase. Sir M. Hale.
Repurchase Re*pur"chase, n. The act of repurchasing.

repurify.c: Repurify Re*pu"ri*fy (r?-p?"r?-f?), v. t. To purify again.

reputable.c: Reputable Rep"u*ta*ble (r?p"?-t?-b'l), a. [From Repute.] Having, or worthy of, good repute; held in esteem; honorable; praiseworthy; as, a reputable man or character; reputable conduct.

reputation.c: Reputation Rep`u*ta"tion (-t?"sh?n), n. [F. réputation, L. reputatio a reckoning, consideration. See Repute, v. t.]

repute.c: Repute Re*pute" (r?-p?t"), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Reputed; p. pr. & vb. n. Reputing.] [F. réputer, L. reputare to count over, think over; pref. re- re- + putare to count, think. See Putative.] To hold in thought; to account; to estimate; to hold; to think; to reckon.
Repute Re*pute", n. 1. Character reputed or attributed; reputation, whether good or bad; established opinion; public estimate.

reputedly.c: Reputedly Re*put"ed*ly (r?-p?t"?d-l?), adv. In common opinion or estimation; by repute.

reputeless.c: Reputeless Re*pute"less, a. Not having good repute; disreputable; disgraceful; inglorius. [R.] Shak.

request.c: Request Re*quest" (re*kwĕst"), n. [OE. requeste, OF. requeste, F. requête, LL. requesta, for requisita, fr. L. requirere, requisitum, to seek again, ask for. See Require, and cf.
