Quest.] 1. The act of asking for anything desired; expression of desire or demand; solicitation; prayer; petition; entreaty.

Request Re*quest" (r?-kw?st"), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Requested; p. pr. & vb. n. Requesting.] [Cf. OF. requester, F. requêter.] 1. To ask for (something); to express desire ffor; to solicit; as, to request his presence, or a favor.

requester.c: Requester Re*quest"er (-?r), n. One who requests; a petitioner.

requicken.c: Requicken Re*quick"en (r?-kw?k"'n), v. t. To quicken anew; to reanimate; to give new life to. Shak.

requiem.c: Requiem Re"qui*em (r?"kw?-?m;277), n. [Acc. of L. requies rest, the first words of the Mass being “Requiem aeternam dona eis, Domine,” give eternal rest to them, O lord; pref. re- re + quies quiet. See Quiet, n., and cf. Requin.] 1. (R.C.Ch.) A mass said or sung for the repose of a departed soul.

requietory.c: Requietory Re*qui"e*to*ry (r?-kw?"?-t?-r?), n. [L. requietorium, fr. requiescere, requietum, to rest. See Re-, and Quiesce.] A sepulcher. [Obs.] Weever.

requin.c: Requin Re"quin (r?"kw?n), n. [F., fr. reqiem a Mass sung for the dead. See Requiem.] (Zool.) The man-eater, or white shark (Carcharodon carcharias); -- so called on account of its causing requiems to be sung.

requirable.c: Requirable Re*quir"a*ble (r?-kw?r"?-b'l), a. Capable of being required; proper to be required. Sir M. Hale.

require.c: Require Re*quire" (r?-kw?r"), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Required (-kw?rd"); p. pr. & vb. n. Requiring.] [OE. requeren, requiren, OF. requerre, F. requ?rir; L. pref. re- re- + quaerere to ask; cf. L. requirere. See Query, and cf. Request, Requisite.] 1. To demand; to insist upon having; to claim as by right and authority; to exact; as, to require the surrender of property.

requirement.c: Requirement Re*quire"ment (-ment), n. 1. The act of requiring; demand; requisition.

requisite.c: Requisite Req"ui*site (r?k"w?-z?t), n. That which is required, or is necessary; something indispensable.

Requisite Req"ui*site, a. [L. requisitus, p. p. requirere; pref. re- re- + quaerere to ask. See Require.] Required by the nature of things, or by circumstances; so needful that it can not be dispensed with; necessary; indispensable.

requisition.c: Requisition Req`ui*si"tion (r?k`w?-z?sh"?n), n.[Cf. F. réquisition, L. requisitio a searching.] 1. The act of requiring, as of right; a demand or application made as by authority. Specifically: (a) (International Law) A formal demand made by one state or government upon another for the surrender or extradition of a fugitive from justice. Kent. (b) (Law) A notarial demand of a debt. Wharton. (c) (Mil.) A demand by the invader upon the people of an invaded country for supplies, as of provision, forage, transportation, etc. Farrow. (d) A formal application by one officer to another for things needed in the public service; as, a requisition for clothing, troops, or money.
Requisition Req`ui*si"tion, v. t. 1. To make a reqisition on or for; as, to requisition a district for forage; to requisition troops.

requisitionist.c: Requisitionist Req`ui*si"tion*ist, n. One who makes or signs a requisition.

requisitive.c: Requisitive Re*quis"i*tive (r?-kw?z"?-t?v), a. Expressing or implying demand. [R.] Harris.
Requisitive Re*quis"i*tive, n. One who, or that which, makes requisition; a requisitionist. [R.]

requisitor.c: Requisitor Re*quis"i*tor (-t?r), n. One who makes reqisition; esp., one authorized by a requisition to investigate facts.

requisitory.c: Requisitory Re*quis"i*to*ry (-t?-r?), a. Sought for; demanded. [R.] Summary on Du Bartas (1621).

requitable.c: Requitable Re*quit"a*ble (-kw?t"?-b'l), a. That may be requited.

requital.c: Requital Re*quit"al (-al), n. [From Requite.] The act of requiting; also, that which requites; return, good or bad, for anything done; in a good sense, compensation; recompense; as, the requital of services; in a bad sense, retaliation, or punishment; as, the requital of evil deeds.

requite.c: Requite Re"quite" (r?-kw?t"), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Requited; p. pr. & vb. n. Requiting.] [Pref. re- + quit.] To repay; in a good sense, to recompense; to return (an equivalent) in good; to reward; in a bad sense, to retaliate; to return (evil) for evil; to punish.

rerebrace.c: Rerebrace Rere"brace` (r?r"br?s"), n. [F. arri?re-bras.] (Anc. Armor) Armor for the upper part of the arm. Fairholt.

reredemain.c: Reredemain Rere`de*main" (-d?-m?n"), n. [F. arri?re back + de of + main hand.] A backward stroke. [Obs.]

reredos.c: Reredos Rere"dos (r?r"d?s), n. [From rear + F. dos back, L. dorsum. Cf. Dorsal.] (Arch.) (a) A screen or partition wall behind an altar. (b) The back of a fireplace. (c) The open hearth, upon which fires were lighted, immediately under the louver, in the center of ancient halls. [Also spelt reredosse.] Fairholt.

rerefief.c: Rerefief Rere"fief` (r?r"f?f`), n. [F. arrière-fief. See Rear hinder, and Fief.] (Scots Law) A fief held of a superior feudatory; a fief held by an under tenant. Blackstone.

rereign.c: Rereign Re*reign" (r?-r?n"), v. i. To reign again.

rereiterate.c: Re-reiterate Re`-re*it"er*ate (r?`r?-?t"?r-?t), v. t. To reiterate many times. [R.] “My re-reiterated wish.” Tennyson.

reresolve.c: Re-resolve Re`-re*solve" (r?`r?-z?lv"), v. t. & i. To resolve again.

rereward.c: Rereward Rere"ward` (r?r"w?rd`), n. [See Rearward.] The rear guard of an army. [Obs.]

res.c: Res ‖Res (r?z), n.; pl. Res. [L.] A thing; the particular thing; a matter; a point.

resail.c: Resail Re*sail" (r?-s?l"), v. t. & i. To sail again; also, to sail back, as to a former port.

resale.c: Resale Re*sale" (r?-s?l" or r?"s?l), n. A sale at second hand, or at retail; also, a second sale. Bacon.

resalute.c: Resalute Re`sa*lute" (r?`s?-l?t"), v. t. To salute again.

resaw.c: Resaw Re*saw" (r?-s?"), v. t. To saw again; specifically, to saw a balk, or a timber, which has already been squared, into dimension lumber, as joists, boards, etc.

rescat.c: Rescat Res"cat (r?s"k?t), v. t. [Sp. rescattar.] To ransom; to release; to rescue. [Obs.] Howell.

rescind.c: Rescind Re*scind" (r?-s?nd"), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Rescinded; p. pr. & vb. n. Rescinding.] [L. rescindere, rescissum; pref re- re- + scindere to cut, split: cf. F. rescinder. See Shism.] 1. To cut off; to abrogate; to annul.

rescindable.c: Rescindable Re*scind"a*ble (-?-b'l), a. Capable of being rescinded.

rescindment.c: Rescindment Re*scind"ment (-ment), n. The act of rescinding; rescission.

rescission.c: Rescission Re*scis"sion (r?-s?zh"?n), n. [L. rescissio: cf. F. rescission. See Rescind.] The act of rescinding, abrogating, annulling, or vacating; as, the rescission of a law, decree, or judgment.

rescissory.c: Rescissory Re*scis"so*ry (r?-s?z"?-r? or r?-s?s"-), a. [L. rescissorius: cf. F. rescisoire.] Tending to rescind; rescinding.

rescous.c: Rescous Res"cous (r?s"k?s), n. [OE., fr. OF. rescousse, fr. rescourre, p. p. rescous, to rescue. See Rescue.] 1. Rescue; deliverance. [Obs.] Chaucer.

rescowe.c: Rescowe Res"cowe (r?s"kou), v. t. To rescue. [Obs.] Chaucer.

rescribe.c: Rescribe Re*scribe" (r?-skr?b"), v. t. [L. rescribere; pref. re- re- + scribere to write. See Scribe.] 1. To write back; to write in reply. Ayliffe.

rescript.c: Rescript Re"script (r?"skr?pt), n. [L. rescriptum: cf. F. rescrit, formerly also spelt rescript. See Rescribe,v. t.]

rescription.c: Rescription Re*scrip"tion (r?-skr?p"sh?n), n. [L. rescriptio: cf. F. rescription. See Rescribe.] A writing back; the answering of a letter. Loveday.

rescriptive.c: Rescriptive Re*scrip"tive (-t?v), a. Pertaining to, or answering the purpose of, a rescript; hence, deciding; settling; determining.

rescuable.c: Rescuable Res"cu*a*ble (r?s"k?-?-b'l), a. That may be rescued.

rescue.c: Rescue Res"cue (rĕs"ku), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Rescued (-k?d);p. pr. & vb. n. Rescuing.] [OE. rescopuen, OF. rescourre, rescurre, rescorre; L. pref. re- re- + excutere to shake or drive out; ex out + quatere to shake. See Qtash to crush, Rercussion.] To free or deliver from any confinement, violence, danger, or evil; to liberate from actual restraint; to remove or withdraw from a state of exposure to evil; as, to rescue a prisoner from the enemy; to rescue seamen from destruction.
Rescue Res"cue (rĕs"ku), n. [From Rescue, v.; cf. Rescous.]

rescueless.c: Rescueless Res"cue*less, a. Without rescue or release.

rescussee.c: Rescussee Res`cus*see" (r?s`k?s-s?"), n. (O.Eng. Law) The party in whose favor a rescue is made. Crabb.

rescussor.c: Rescussor Res*cus"sor (r?s-k?s"s?r), n. [LL.] (O.Eng.Law) One who makes an unlawful rescue; a rescuer. Burril.

rese.c: Rese Rese (rēz), v. i. To shake; to quake; to tremble. [Obs.] “It made all the gates for to rese.” Chaucer.

research.c: Re-search Re-search" (r?-s?rch"), v. t. [Pref. re- + search.] To search again; to examine anew.

Research Re*search" (r?-s?rch"), n. [Pref. re- + search: cf OF. recerche, F. recherche.] 1. Diligent inquiry or examination in seeking facts or principles; laborious or continued search after truth; as, researches of human wisdom; to research a topic in the library; medical research.
research re*search", v. t. [Pref. re- + search: cf. OF. recerchier, F. rechercher.] To search or examine with continued care; to seek diligently.

researcher.c: Researcher Re*search"er (-ẽr), n. One who conducts research. In the field of scientific research, also called an investigator or scientist.

researchful.c: Researchful Re*search"ful (-f?l), a. Making researches; inquisitive. [R.] Coleridge.

reseat.c: Reseat Re*seat" (r?-s?t"), v. t. 1. To seat or set again, as on a chair, throne, etc. Dryden.

reseau.c: Reseau ‖Ré`seau" (rā`zō"), n. [F.] A network; specif.: (a) (Astron.) A system of lines forming small squares of standard size, which is photographed, by a separate exposure, on the same plate with star images to facilitate measurements, detect changes of the film, etc. (b) In lace, a ground or foundation of regular meshes, like network.

resect.c: Resect Re*sect" (r?-s?kt"), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Resected;p. pr. & vb. n. Resecting.] [L. resectus, p. p. of resecare to cut off; pref. re- re- + secare to cut.] To cut or pare off; to remove by cutting.

resection.c: Resection Re*sec"tion (r?-s?k"sh?n), n. [L. resectio: cf. F. résection.] 1. The act of cutting or paring off. Cotgrave.

reseda.c: Reseda Re*se"da (r?-s?"d?), n. [L., a kind of plant.] 1. (Bot.) A genus of plants, the type of which is mignonette.

reseek.c: Reseek Re*seek" (r?-s?k"), v. t. To seek again. J. Barlow.

reseize.c: Reseize Re*seize" (r?-s?z"), v. t. [Pref. re- + seize: cf. F. ressaisir.] 1. To seize again, or a second time.

reseizer.c: Reseizer Re*seiz"er (-s?z"?r), n. 1. One who seizes again.

reseizure.c: Reseizure Re*sei"zure (r?-s?"zh?r; 135), n. A second seizure; the act of seizing again. Bacon.

resell.c: Resell Re*sell" (r?-s?l"), v. t. To sell again; to sell what has been bought or sold; to retail.

resemblable.c: Resemblable Re*sem"bla*ble (r?-z?m"bl?-b'l), a. [See Resemble.] Admitting of being compared; like. [Obs.] Gower.

resemblance.c: Resemblance Re*sem"blance (-blans), n. [Cf. F. ressemblance. See Resemble.] 1. The quality or state of resembling; likeness; similitude; similarity.

resemblant.c: Resemblant Re*sem"blant (-blant), a. [F., a. and p. pr. fr. ressembler to resemble. See Resemble.] Having or exhibiting resemblance; resembling. [R.] Gower.

resemble.c: Resemble Re*sem"ble (r?-z?m"b'l), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Resembled (-b'ld); p. pr. & vb. n. Resembling (-bl?ng).] [F. ressembler; pref. re- re- + sembler to seem, resemble, fr. L. similare, simulare, to imitate, fr. similis like, similar. See Similar.] 1. To be like or similar to; to bear the similitude of, either in appearance or qualities; as, these brothers resemble each other.

resemblingly.c: Resemblingly Re*sem"bling*ly (-bl?ng-l?), adv. So as to resemble; with resemblance or likeness.

reseminate.c: Reseminate Re*sem"i*nate (-s?m"?-n?t), v. t. [L. pref. re- again + seminatus, p. p. of seminare to sow.] To produce again by means of seed. [Obs.] Sir. T. Browne.

resend.c: Resend Re*send" (r?-s?nd"), v. t. 1. To send again; as, to resend a message.

resent.c: Resent Re*sent" (r?-z?nt"), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Resented; p. pr. & vb. n. Resenting.] [F. ressentir; L. pref. re- re- + sentire to feel. See Sense.] 1. To be sensible of; to feel; as: (a) In a good sense, to take well; to receive with satisfaction. [Obs.]
Resent Re*sent", v. i. 1. To feel resentment. Swift.

resenter.c: Resenter Re*sent"er (-?r), n. One who resents. Sir H. Wotton.

resentful.c: Resentful Re*sent"ful (-f?l), a. Inclined to resent; easily provoked to anger; irritable. -- Re*sent"ful*ly, adv.

resentingly.c: Resentingly Re*sent"ing*ly, adv. 1. With deep sense or strong perception. [Obs.] Dr. H. More.

resentment.c: Resentment Re*sent"ment (-ment), n. [F. ressentiment.] 1. The act of resenting.

reserate.c: Reserate Res"er*ate (r?s"?r-?t), v. t. [L. reseratus, p. p. of reserare to unlock.] To unlock; to open. [Obs.] Boyle.

reservation.c: Reservation Res`er*va"tion (r?z`?r-v?"sh?n), n. [Cf. F. réservation, LL. reservatio. See Reserve.] 1. The act of reserving, or keeping back; concealment, or withholding from disclosure; reserve. A. Smith.

reservative.c: Reservative Re*serv"a*tive (r?-z?rv"?-t?v), a. Tending to reserve or keep; keeping; reserving.

reservatory.c: Reservatory Re*serv"a*to*ry (-t?-r?), n. [LL. reservatorium,fr. L. resservare. See Reserve, v. t., and cf. Reservior.] A place in which things are reserved or kept. Woodward.

reserve.c: Reserve Re*serve" (r?-z?rv"), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Reserved. (z?rvd");p. pr. & vb. n. Reserving.] [F. réserver, L. reservare, reservatum; pref. re- re- + servare to keep. See Serve.] 1. To keep back; to retain; not to deliver, make over, or disclose. “I have reserved to myself nothing.” Shak.
Reserve Re*serve", n. [F. réserve.] 1. The act of reserving, or keeping back; reservation.

Reserve city Reserve city. (Banking) In the national banking system of the United States, any of certain cities in which the national banks are required (U. S. Rev. Stat. sec. 5191) to keep a larger reserve (25 per cent) than the minimum (15 per cent) required of all other banks. The banks in certain of the reserve cities (specifically called central reserve cities) are required to keep their reserve on hand in cash; banks in other reserve cities may keep half of their reserve as deposits in these banks (U. S. Rev. Stat. sec. 5195).

reserved.c: Reserved Re*served" (-z?rvd"), a. 1. Kept for future or special use, or for an exigency; as, reserved troops; a reserved seat in a theater.

reservee.c: Reservee Res`er*vee" (rĕz`ẽr*vē"), n. One to, or for, whom anything is reserved; -- contrasted with reservor.

reservist.c: Reservist Re*serv"ist, n. A member of a reserve force of soldiers or militia. [Eng.]

reservoir.c: Reservoir Res"er*voir` (rĕz"ẽr*vwôr`; 277), n. [F. réservoir, fr. LL. reservatorium. See Reservatory.] 1. A place where anything is kept in store; especially, a place where water is collected and kept for use when wanted, as to supply a fountain, a canal, or a city by means of aqueducts, or to drive a mill wheel, or the like.

reservor.c: Reservor Re*serv"or (r?-z?rv"?r or r?z`?r-v?r), n. One who reserves; a reserver.

reset.c: Reset re-set re-set", Re*set" (r?-s?t"), v. t. 1. To set again; as, to reset type; to reset copy; to reset a diamond.
Reset Re"set (r?"s?t), n. 1. The act of resetting.
Reset Re*set" (r?-s?t"), n. [OF. recete, recepte, a receiving. Cf. Receipt.] (Scots Law) The receiving of stolen goods, or harboring an outlaw. Jamieson.
Reset Re*set", v. t. (Scots Law) To harbor or secrete; to hide, as stolen goods or a criminal.

resetter.c: Resetter Re*set"ter (-t?r), n. (Scots Law) One who receives or conceals, as stolen goods or criminal.
Resetter Re*set"ter (r?-S?t"t?r), n. One who resets, or sets again.

resettle.c: Resettle Re*set"tle (r?-s?t"t'l), v. t. To settle again. Swift.
Resettle Re*set"tle, v. i. To settle again, or a second time.

resettlement.c: Resettlement Re*set"tle*ment (-ment), n. Act of settling again, or state of being settled again; as, the resettlement of lees.

reshape.c: Reshape Re*shape" (r?-sh?p"), v. t. To shape again.

reship.c: Reship Re*ship" (r?-sh?p"), v. t. To ship again; to put on board of a vessel a second time; to send on a second voyage; as, to reship bonded merchandise.
Reship Re*ship", v. i. To engage one's self again for service on board of a vessel after having been discharged.

reshipment.c: Reshipment Re*ship"ment (-ment), n. The act of reshipping; also, that which is reshipped.

resiance.c: Resiance Res`i*ance (r?z"?-ans), n. [LL. reseantia,?? OF. reseance.] Residence; abode. [Obs.] Bacon.

resiant.c: Resiant Res"i*ant (-ant), a. [OF. reseant, resseant, L. residens. See Resident.] Resident; present in a place. [Obs.]
Resiant Res"i*ant, n. A resident. [Obs.] Sir T. More.

reside.c: Reside Re*side" (r?-z?d"), v. i. [imp. & p. p. Resided; p. pr. & vb. n. Residing.] [F. résider, L. residere; pref. re- re- + sedere to sit. See Sit. ] 1. To dwell permanently or for a considerable time; to have a settled abode for a time; to abide continuosly; to have one's domicile of home; to remain for a long time.

residence.c: Residence Res"i*dence (r?z"?-dens), n. [F. résidence. See Resident.] 1. The act or fact of residing, abiding, or dwelling in a place for some continuance of time; as, the residence of an American in France or Italy for a year.

residencia.c: Residencia ‖Re`si*den"cia (?), n. [Sp.] In Spanish countries, a court or trial held, sometimes as long as six months, by a newly elected official, as the governor of a province, to examine into the conduct of a predecessor.

resident.c: Resident Res"i*dent (-dent), a. [F. résident, L. residens, -entis, p. pr. of residere. See Reside.] 1. Dwelling, or having an abode, in a place for a continued length of time; residing on one's own estate; -- opposed to nonresident; as, resident in the city or in the country.
Resident Res"i*dent, n. 1. One who resides or dwells in a place for some time.

residenter.c: Residenter Res"i*dent*er (-$r), n. A resident. [Obs. or Colloq.]

residential.c: Residential Res`i*den""tial (-d?n"shal), a. 1. Of or pertaining to a residence or residents; as, residential trade; a residential part of town.

residentiary.c: Residentiary Res`i*den"tia*ry (-d?n"sh?-r?; 277), a. [LL. residentiaris.] Having residence; as, a canon residentary; a residentiary guardian. Dr. H. More.
Residentiary Res`i*den"tia*ry, n. 1. One who is resident.

residentiaryship.c: Residentiaryship Res`i*den"tia*ry*ship, n. The office or condition of a residentiary.

residentship.c: Residentship Res"i*dent*ship (r?z"?-dent-sh?p), n. The office or condition of a resident.

resider.c: Resider Re*sid"er (r?-z?d"?r), n. One who resides in a place.

residual.c: Residual Re*sid"u*al (r?-z?d"?-al), a. [See Residue.] Pertaining to a residue; remaining after a part is taken.

Residual Re*sid"u*al, n. (Math.) (a) The difference of the results obtained by observation, and by computation from a formula. (b) The difference between the mean of several observations and any one of them.

residuary.c: Residuary Re*sid"u*a*ry (-?-r?), a. [See Residue.] Consisting of residue; as, residuary matter; pertaining to the residue, or part remaining; as, the residuary advantage of an estate. Ayliffe.

residue.c: Residue Res"i*due (r?z"?-d?), n. [F. résidu, L. residuum, fr. residuus that is left behind, remaining, fr. residere to remain behind. See Reside, and cf. Residuum.] 1. That which remains after a part is taken, separated, removed, or designated; remnant; remainder.

residuous.c: Residuous Re*sid"u*ous (r?-z?d"?-?s), a. [L. residuus.] Remaining; residual. Landor.

residuum.c: Residuum Re*sid"u*um (-?m), n. [L. See Residue.] That which is left after any process of separation or purification; that which remains after certain specified deductions are made; residue.

resiege.c: Resiege Re*siege" (r?-s?j"), v. t. [Pref. re- + siege a seat.] To seat again; to reinstate. [Obs.] Spenser.

resign.c: Re-sign Re-sign" (r?-s?n"), v. t. [Pref. re- + sign.] To affix one's signature to, a second time; to sign again.

Resign Re*sign" (r?-z?n"), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Resigned (-z?nd"); p. pr. & vb. n. Resigning.] [F. résigner, L. resignare to unseal, annul, assign, resign; pref. re- re- + signare to seal, stamp. See Sign, and cf. Resignation.]

resignation.c: Resignation Res`ig*na"tion (rĕz`ĭg*nā"shŭn), n. [F. résignation. See Resign.] 1. The act of resigning or giving up, as a claim, possession, office, or the like; surrender; as, the resignation of a crown or commission.

resigned.c: Resigned Re*signed" (re*zīnd"), a. Submissive; yielding; not disposed to resist or murmur.

resignee.c: Resignee Res`ign*ee" (rĕz`ĭ*nē"), n. One to whom anything is resigned, or in whose favor a resignation is made.

resignment.c: Resignment Re*sign"ment (re*zīn"meint), n. The act of resigning.

resile.c: resile re*sile" (re*zīl"), v. i. [imp. & p. p. resiled (-zīld"); p. pr. & vb. n. resiling.] [L. resilire to leap or spring back; pref. re- re- + salire to leap, spring. See Salient.] To start back; to recoil; to recede from a purpose. J. Ellis.

resiliency.c: resiliency resilience { re*sil"i*ence (re*zĭl"ĭ*eins), re*sil"i*en*cy (re*zĭl"ĭ*ein*sy̆), } n. 1. The act of springing back, rebounding, or resiling; as, the resilience of a ball or of sound.

resilient.c: Resilient Re*sil"i*ent (-ent), a. [L. resiliens, p. pr.] Leaping back; rebounding; recoiling.

resin.c: Resin Res"in (rĕz"ĭn), n. [F. résine, L. resina; cf. Gr. "rhti`nh Cf. Rosin.] Any one of a class of yellowish brown solid inflammable substances, of vegetable origin, which are nonconductors of electricity, have a vitreous fracture, and are soluble in ether, alcohol, and essential oils, but not in water; specif., pine resin (see Rosin).

resinaceous.c: Resinaceous Res`in*a"ceous (rĕz`ĭn*ā"shŭs), a. Having the quality of resin; resinous.

resinate.c: Resinate Res"in*ate (rĕz"ĭn*at), n. (Chem.) Any one of the salts the resinic acids.

resinic.c: Resinic Re*sin"ic (re*zĭn"ĭk), a. (Chem.) Pertaining to, or obtained from, resin; as, the resinic acids.

resiniferous.c: Resiniferous Res`in*if"er*ous (r?z`?n-?f"?r-?s), a. [Resin + -ferous: cf. F. résinifère.] Yielding resin; as, a resiniferous tree or vessel.

resiniform.c: Resiniform Res"in*i*form (r?z"?n-?-f?rm), a. [Resin + -form: cf. F. résiniforme.] Having the form of resin.

resinoelectric.c: Resino-electric Res`in*o-e*lec"tric (-?-?-l?k"tr?k), a. (Elec.) Containing or exhibiting resinous electricity.

resinous.c: Resinous Res"in*ous (-?s), a. [L. resinous: cf. F. résineux. See Resin.] Of or pertaining to resin; of the nature of resin; resembling or obtained from resin.

resinously.c: Resinously Res"in*ous*ly, adv. By means, or in the manner, of resin.

resinousness.c: Resinousness Res"in*ous*ness, n. The quality of being resinous.

resipiscence.c: Resipiscence Res`i*pis"cence (r?s`?-p?s"sens), n. [L. resipiscentia, from resipiscere to recover one's senses: cf. F. résipiscence.] Wisdom derived from severe experience; hence, repentance. [R.] Bp. Montagu.

resist.c: Resist Re*sist" (r?-z?st"), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Resisted; p. pr. & vb. n. Resisting.] [F. résister, L. resistere, pref. re- re- + sistere to stand, cause to stand, v. causative of stare to stand. See Stand.] 1. To stand against; to withstand; to obstruct.
Resist Re*sist", v. i. To make opposition. Shak.

Resist Re*sist", n. 1. (Calico Printing) A substance used to prevent a color or mordant from fixing on those parts to which it has been applied, either by acting machanically in preventing the color, etc., from reaching the cloth, or chemically in changing the color so as to render it incapable of fixing itself in the fibers; -- also called reserve. The pastes prepared for this purpose are called resist pastes. F. C. Calvert.

resistance.c: Resistance Re*sist"ance (-ans), n. [F. résistance, LL. resistentia, fr. resistens, -entis, p. pr. See Resist.] 1. The act of resisting; opposition, passive or active.
Resistance frame Re*sist"ance frame`. (Elec.) A rheostat consisting of an open frame on which are stretched spirals of wire. Being freely exposed to the air, they radiate heat rapidly.

resistant.c: Resistant Re*sist"ant (-ant), a. [F. résistant: cf. L. resistens. See Resist.] Making resistance; resisting. -- n. One who, or that which, resists. Bp. Pearson.

resistibility.c: Resistibility Re*sist`i*bil"i*ty (-?-b?l"?-t?), n.. 1. The quality of being resistible; resistibleness.

resistible.c: Resistible Re*sist"i*ble (r?-z?st"?-b'l), a. [Cf. F. résistible.] Capable of being resisted; as, a resistible force. Sir M. Hale. -- Re*sist"i*ble*ness, n. -- Re*sist"i*bly, adv.

resisting.c: Resisting Re*sist"ing, a. Making resistance; opposing; as, a resisting medium. -- Re*sist"ing ly, adv.

resistive.c: Resistive Re*sist"ive (-?v), a. Serving to resist. B. Jonsosn.

resistless.c: Resistless Re*sist"less, a. 1. Having no power to resist; making no opposition. [Obs. or R.] Spenser.

resoluble.c: Resoluble Res"o*lu*ble (r?z"?-l?-b'l), a.[L. resolubolis: cf. F. résoluble. See Resolve, and cf. Resolvable.] Admitting of being resolved; resolvable; as, bodies resoluble by fire. Boyle. -- Res"o*lu*ble*ness, n.

resolute.c: Resolute Res"o*lute (r?z"?-l?t), a. [Cf. F. résolu. The L. resolutus (p. p. of resolvere) means, relaxed, enervated, effeminate. See Resolve, v. t. & i.] 1. Having a decided purpose; determined; resolved; fixed in a determination; hence, bold; firm; steady.
Resolute Res"o*lute (r?z"?-l?t), n. 1. One who is resolute; hence, a desperado. [Obs.] Shak.

resolutely.c: Resolutely Res"o*lute*ly, adv. In a resolute manner; with fixed purpose; boldly; firmly; steadily; with perseverance.

resoluteness.c: Resoluteness Res"o*lute*ness, n. The quality of being resolute.

resolution.c: Resolution Res`o*lu"tion (-l?"sh?n), n. [F. résolution. L. resolutio a loosening, solution. See Resolve.] 1. The act, operation, or process of resolving. Specifically: (a) The act of separating a compound into its elements or component parts. (b) The act of analyzing a complex notion, or solving a vexed question or difficult problem.

resolutioner.c: Resolutioner Res`o*lu"tion*er (-?r), n. One who makes a resolution; one who joins with others in a declaration or resolution; specifically, one of a party in the Scottish Church in the 17th century.

resolutionist.c: Resolutionist Res`o*lu"tion*ist, n. One who makes a resolution.

resolutive.c: Resolutive Res"o*lu`tive (r?z"?-lu`t?v), a. [Cf.F. résolutif.] Serving to dissolve or relax. [R.] Johnson.

resolvability.c: Resolvability Re*solv`a*bil"i*ty (r?-z?lv`?-b?l"?-t?), n. The quality or condition of being resolvable; resolvableness.

resolvable.c: Resolvable Re*solv"a*ble (r?-z?lv"?-b'l), a. [See Resolve, and cf. Resoluble.] Admitting of being resolved; admitting separation into constituent parts, or reduction to first principles; admitting solution or explanation; as, resolvable compounds; resolvable ideas or difficulties.

resolvableness.c: Resolvableness Re*solv"a*ble*ness, n. The quality of being resolvable; resolvability.

resolve.c: Resolve Re*solve" (r?*z?lv"), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Resolved (-z?lvd"); p. pr. & vb. n. Resolving.] [L. resolvere, resolutum, to untie, loosen, relax, enfeeble; pref. re- re- + solvere to loosen, dissolve: cf. F. résoudare to resolve. See Solve, and cf. Resolve, v. i., Resolute, Resolution.] 1. To separate the component parts of; to reduce to the constituent elements; -- said of compound substances; hence, sometimes, to melt, or dissolve.
Resolve Re*solve" (r?-z?lv"), v. i. [The sense “to be convinced, to determine” comes from the idea of loosening, breaking up into parts, analyzing, hence, determining.]
Resolve Re*solve", n. 1. The act of resolving or making clear; resolution; solution. “To give a full resolve of that which is so much controverted.” Milton.

resolved.c: Resolved Re*solved" (r?-z?lvd"), p. p. & a. Having a fixed purpose; determined; resolute; -- usually placed after its noun; as, a man resolved to be rich.

resolvedly.c: Resolvedly Re*solv"ed*ly (r?z?lv"?d-l?), adv. 1. So as to resolve or clear up difficulties; clearly. [Obs.]

resolvedness.c: Resolvedness Re*solv"ed*ness, n. Fixedness of purpose; firmness; resolution. Dr. H. More.

resolvent.c: Resolvent Re*solv"ent (-ent), a. Having power to resolve; causing solution; solvent.
Resolvent Re*solv"ent, n. [L. resolvens, p. pr. of resolvere: cf. F. résolvant. See Resolve.] 1. That which has the power of resolving, or causing solution; a solvent.

resolver.c: Resolver Re*solv"er (r?-z?lv"?r), n. 1. That which decomposes, or dissolves. Boyle.

resonance.c: Resonance Res"o*nance (r?z"?-nans), n. [Cf. F. résonance, L. resonantia an echo.] 1. The act of resounding; the quality or state of being resonant.

resonant.c: Resonant Res"o*nant (-nant), a. [L. resonans, p. pr. of resonare to resound: cf. F. résonnant. See Resound.] 1. Returning, or capable of returning, sound; fitted to resound; resounding; echoing back.

resonantly.c: Resonantly Res"o*nant*ly, adv. In a resonant manner.

resonator.c: Resonator Res"o*na`tor (-n?`t?r), n. [NL. & G.] 1. (Acoustics) Anything which resounds; specifically, a vessel in the form of a cylinder open at one end, or a hollow ball of brass with two apertures, so contrived as to greatly intensify a musical tone by its resonance. It is used for the study and analysis of complex sounds.

resorb.c: Resorb Re*sorb" (r?-s?rb"), v. t. [L. reorbere; pref. re- re- + sorbere to suck or drink in.] 1. To swallow up.

resorbent.c: Resorbent Re*sorb"ent (-ent), a. [L. resorbens, p. pr. of resorbere.] Swallowing up. Wodhull.

resorcin.c: Resorcin Res*or"cin (r?z-?r"s?n), n. [Resin + orcin. So called because in its higher homologue it resembles orcin.] (Chem.) A colorless crystalline substance of the phenol series, obtained by melting certain resins, as galbanum, asafetida, etc., with caustic potash. It is also produced artificially and used in making certain dyestuffs, as phthalein, fluorescein, and eosin.

resorcylic.c: Resorcylic Res`or*cyl"ic (r?z`?r-s?l"?k), a. (Chem.) Of, or pertaining to, or producing, resorcin; as, resorcylic acid.

resorption.c: Resorption Re*sorp"tion (r?*s?rp"sh?n), n. 1. The act of resorbing; also, the act of absorbing again; reabsorption.

resort.c: Resort Re*sort" (r?*z?rt"), n. [F. ressort.] Active power or movement; spring. [A Gallicism] [Obs.]

Resort Re*sort", v. i. [imp. & p. p. Resorted; p. pr. & vb. n. Resorting.] [OF. resortir to withdraw, take refuge, F. ressortir to be in the jurisdiction, LL. resortire; pref. re- re- + L. sortiri to draw lots, obtain by lot, from sors lot. See Sort. The meaning is first to reobtain (by lot), then to gain by appeal to a higher court (as a law term), to appeal, go for protection or refuge.] 1. To go; to repair; to betake one's self.

Resort Re*sort" (r?*z?rt"), n. [Cf. F. ressort jurisdiction. See Resort, v.] 1. The act of going to, or making application; a betaking one's self; the act of visiting or seeking; recourse; as, a place of popular resort; -- often figuratively; as, to have resort to force.

resorter.c: Resorter Re*sort"er (-?r), n. One who resorts; a frequenter.

resoun.c: Resoun Re*soun", v. i. & t. To resound. [Obs.] Chaucer.

resound.c: Re-sound Re-sound" (r?*sound"), v. t. & i. [Pref. re- + sound.] To sound again or anew.

Resound Re*sound" (r?*zound"), v. i. [imp. & p. p. Resounded; p. pr. & vb. n. Resounding.] [OE. resounen, OF. resoner, F. résonner, from L. resonare; pref. re- re- + sonare to sound, sonus sound. See Sound to make a noise.] 1. To sound loudly; as, his voice resounded far.
Resound Re*sound", v. t. 1. To throw back, or return, the sound of; to echo; to reverberate.
Resound Re*sound", n. Return of sound; echo. Beaumont.

resource.c: Resource Re*source" (r?*s?rs"), n. [F. ressource, fr. OF. ressourdre, resourdre, to spring forth or up again; pref. re- re- + sourdre to spring forth. See Source.] 1. That to which one resorts orr on which one depends for supply or support; means of overcoming a difficulty; resort; expedient.

resourceless.c: Resourceless Re*source"less, a. Destitute of resources. Burke.

resow.c: Resow Re*sow" (r?*s?"), v. t. To sow again. Bacon.

respeak.c: Respeak Re*speak" (rē*spēk"), v. t. 1. To speak or utter again.

respect.c: Respect Re*spect" (r?*sp?kt"), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Respected; p. pr. & vb. n. Respecting.] [L. respectare, v. intens. from respicere, respectum, to look back, respect; pref. re- re- + specere, spicere, to look, to view: cf. F. respecter. See Spy, and cf. Respite.] 1. To take notice of; to regard with special attention; to regard as worthy of special consideration; hence, to care for; to heed.
Respect Re*spect", n. [L. respectus: cf. F. respect. See Respect, v., and cf. Respite.] 1. The act of noticing with attention; the giving particular consideration to; hence, care; caution.

respectability.c: Respectability Re*spect`a*bil"i*ty (r?*sp?kt`?*b?l"?*t?), n. The state or quality of being respectable; the state or quality which deserves or commands respect.

respectable.c: Respectable Re*spect"a*ble (-?-b'l), a. [F. respectable, LL. respectabilis.] 1. Worthy of respect; fitted to awaken esteem; deserving regard; hence, of good repute; not mean; as, a respectable citizen. “The respectable quarter of Sicca.” J. H. Newman.

respectant.c: Respectant Re*spect"ant (-ant), a. [F., p. pr. of respecter. See Respect.] (Her.) Placed so as to face one another; -- said of animals.

respectful.c: Respectful Re*spect"ful (-f?l), a. Marked or characterized by respect; as, respectful deportment.

respecting.c: Respecting Re*spect"ing, prep. With regard or relation to; regarding; concerning; as, respecting his conduct there is but one opinion.

respection.c: Respection Re*spec"tion (re*spĕk"shŭn), n. [Cf.LL. respectio.] The act of respecting; respect; regard. [Obs.]

respective.c: Respective Re*spec"tive (re*spĕk"tĭv), a. [Cf. F. respectif, LL. respectivus. See Respect.] 1. Noticing with attention; hence, careful; wary; considerate. [Obs.]

respectively.c: Respectively Re*spec"tive*ly, adv. 1. As relating to each; particularly; as each belongs to each; as each refers to each in order; as, let each man respectively perform his duty.

respectless.c: Respectless Re*spect"less (re*spĕk"lĕs), a. Having no respect; without regard; regardless.

respectuous.c: Respectuous Re*spec"tu*ous (r?*sp?k"t?*?s;135), a. 1. Respectful; as, a respectuous silence. [Obs.] Boyle.

respell.c: Respell Re*spell" (r?*sp?l"), v. t. To spell again.

resperse.c: Resperse Re*sperse" (r?*sp?rs"), v. t. [L. respersus, p. p. of respergere; pref. re- re- + spargere to srew, sprinkle.] To sprinkle; to scatter. [Obs.] Jer. Taylor.

respersion.c: Respersion Re*sper"sion (r?*sp?r"sh?n), n. [L. respersio.] The act of sprinkling or scattering. [Obs.]

respirability.c: Respirability Re*spir`a*bil"i*ty (r?*sp?r`?*b?l"?*t? or r?s`p?*r?-), n. [Cf. F. respirabilit?.] The quality or state of being respirable; respirableness.

respirable.c: Respirable Re*spir"a*ble (r?*sp?r"?*b'l or r?s"p?*r?*b'l), a. [Cf. F. respirable.] Suitable for being breathed; adapted for respiration. -- Re*spir"a*ble*ness, n.

respiration.c: Respiration Res`pi*ra"tion (r?s`p?*r?"sh?n), n. [L. respiratio: cf. F. respiration. See Respire.] 1. The act of respiring or breathing again, or catching one's breath.

respirational.c: Respirational Res`pi*ra"tion*al (r?s`p?*r?"sh?n-al), a. Of or pertaining to respiration; as, respirational difficulties.

respirative.c: Respirative Re*spir"a*tive (r?*sp?*r?*t?v), a. Of or pertaining to respiration; as, respirative organs.

respirator.c: Respirator Res"pi*ra`tor (r?s"p?*r?`t?r), n. [Cf. F. respirateur.] A divice of gauze or wire, covering the mouth or nose, to prevent the inhalation of noxious substances, as dust or smoke. Being warmed by the breath, it tempers cold air passing through it, and may also be used for the inhalation of medicated vapors.

respiratory.c: Respiratory Re*spir"a*to*ry (r?*sp?r"?*t?*r? or r?s"p?*r?-), a. (Physiol.) Of or pertaining to respiration; serving for respiration; as, the respiratory organs; respiratory nerves; the respiratory function; respiratory changes.

respire.c: Respire Re*spire" (r?*sp?r), v. i. [imp. & p. p. Respired (-sp?rd"); p. pr. & vb. n. Respiring.] [L. respirare, respiratum; pref. re- re- + spirare to breathe: cf. F. respirer. See Spirit.] 1. To take breath again; hence, to take rest or refreshment. Spenser.
Respire Re*spire", v. t. 1. To breathe in and out; to inspire and expire,, as air; to breathe.

respite.c: Respite Res"pite (r?s"p?t), n. [OF. respit, F. répit, from L. respectus respect, regard, delay, in LL., the deferring of a day. See Respect.] 1. A putting off of that which was appointed; a postponement or delay.

Respite Res"pite, v. t. [imp. & p. p. Respited; p. pr. & vb. n. Respiting.] [OF. respiter, LL. respectare. See Respite, n.] To give or grant a respite to. Specifically: (a) To delay or postpone; to put off. (b) To keep back from execution; to reprieve.

resplendency.c: Resplendency Resplendence { Re*splen"dence (r?*spl?n"dens), Re*splen"den*cy (-den*s?), } n. [L. resplendentia.] The quality or state of being resplendent; brilliant luster; vivid brightness; splendor.

resplendent.c: Resplendent Re*splen"dent (-dent), a. [L. resplendens, -entis, p. pr. of resplendere to shine brightly; pref. re- re- + splendere to shine. See Splendid.] Shining with brilliant luster; very bright. -- Re*splen"dent*ly, adv.

resplendishant.c: Resplendishant Re*splen"dish*ant (-d?sh*ant), a. Resplendent; brilliant. [R. & Obs.] Fabyan.

resplit.c: Resplit Re*split" (re*splĭt"), v. t. & i. To split again.

respond.c: Respond Re*spond" (re*spŏnd"), v. i. [imp. & p. p. Responded; p. pr. & vb. n. Responding.] [OF. respondre, F. répondre, fr. L. respondere, responsum; pref. re- re- + spondere to promise. See Sponsor.] 1. To say something in return; to answer; to reply; as, to respond to a question or an argument.
Respond Re*spond", v. t. 1. To answer; to reply.
Respond Re*spond", n. 1. An answer; a response. [R.]

respondency.c: Respondency Respondence { Re*spond"ence (-?ns), Re*spond"en*cy (-en*s?), } n. The act of responding; the state of being respondent; an answering. A. Chalmers.

respondent.c: Respondent Re*spond"ent (-ent), a. [L. respondens, p. pr. of respondere.] Disposed or expected to respond; answering; according; corresponding.

Respondent Re*spond"ent, n. [Cf. F. répondant.] One who responds. It corresponds in general to defendant. Specifically: (a) (Law) One who answers in certain suits or proceedings, generally those which are not according to the course of the common law, as in equity and admiralty causes, in petitions for partition, and the like; -- distinquished from appellant. (b) One who maintains a thesis in reply, and whose province it is to refute objections, or overthrow arguments; -- distinguished from opponent. I. Watts.

respondentia.c: Respondentia ‖Re`spon*den"ti*a (r?`sp?n*d?n"sh?*?), n. [NL. See Respondence.] (Commercial Law) A loan upon goods laden on board a ship. It differs from bottomry, which is a loan on the ship itself. Bouvier.

responsal.c: Responsal Re*spon"sal, n. [Cf.LL. resposalis.] 1. One who is answerable or responsible. [Obs.] Barrow.

response.c: Response Re*sponse" (r?*sp?ns"), n. [OF. response, respons, F. réponse, from L. responsum, from respondere. See Respond.] 1. The act of responding.

responsibility.c: Responsibility Re*spon`si*bil"i*ty (r?*sp?n`s?*b?l"?*t?), n.; pl. -ties (-t?z). [Cf. F. responsabilité.] 1. The state of being responsible, accountable, or answerable, as for a trust, debt, or obligation.

responsible.c: Responsible Re*spon"si*ble (r?*sp?n"s?*b'l), a. [Cf. F. responsable. See Respond.] 1. Liable to respond; likely to be called upon to answer; accountable; answerable; amenable; as, a guardian is responsible to the court for his conduct in the office.

responsion.c: Responsion Re*spon"sion (-sh?n), n. [L. responsio. See Respond.] 1. The act of answering. [Obs.]

responsive.c: Responsive Re*spon"sive (-s?v), a. [Cf. F. resposif.] 1. That responds; ready or inclined to respond.

responsorial.c: Responsorial Re`spon*so"ri*al (r?`sp?n*s?"r?-al), a. Responsory; antiphonal. J. H. Newman.

responsory.c: Responsory Re*spon"so*ry (r?*sp?n"s?*r?), a. Containing or making answer; answering. Johnson.

Responsory Re*spon"so*ry, n.; pl. -ries (-r?z). [LL. responsorium.] 1. (Eccl.) (a) The answer of the people to the priest in alternate speaking, in church service. (b) A versicle sung in answer to the priest, or as a refrain.

ressaldar.c: Ressaldar ‖Res"sal*dar (?), n. [Hind. risāldār, fr. risāltātroop of horse + Per. dār holding.] (Mil.) In the Anglo-Indian army, a native commander of a ressala.

rest.c: Rest Rest (rĕst), v. t. [For arrest.] To arrest. [Obs.]

Rest Rest, n. [AS. rest, ræst, rest; akin to D. rust, G. rast. OHG. rasta, Dan. & Sw. rast rest, repose, Icel. röst the distance between two resting places, a mole, Goth. rasta a mile, also to Goth. razn house, Icel. rann, and perhaps to G. ruhe rest, repose, AS. rōw, Gr. 'erwh`. Cf. Ransack.] 1. A state of quiet or repose; a cessation from motion or labor; tranquillity; as, rest from mental exertion; rest of body or mind. Chaucer.

Rest Rest (rĕst), v. i. [imp. & p. p. Rested; p. pr. & vb. n. Resting.] [AS. restan. See Rest, n.] 1. To cease from action or motion, especially from action which has caused weariness; to desist from labor or exertion.
Rest Rest, v. t. 1. To lay or place at rest; to quiet.

Rest Rest, n. [F. reste, fr. rester to remain, L. restare to stay back, remain; pref. re- re- + stare to stand, stay. See Stand, and cf. Arrest, Restive.] (With the definite article.) 1. That which is left, or which remains after the separation of a part, either in fact or in contemplation; remainder; residue.
Rest Rest, v. i. [F. rester. See Rest remainder.] To be left; to remain; to continue to be.
Rest cure Rest cure. (Med.) Treatment of severe nervous disorder, as neurasthenia, by rest and isolation with systematic feeding and the use of massage and electricity.

restagnant.c: Restagnant Re*stag"nant (re*stăg"naint), a. [L. restagnans, p. pr. ] Stagnant; motionless. [Obs.] Boyle.

restagnate.c: Restagnate Re*stag"nate (re*stăg"nāt), v. i. [L. restagnare to overflow.] To stagnate; to cease to flow. [Obs.] Wiseman.

restagnation.c: Restagnation Re`stag*na"tion (re`stăg*nā"shŭn), n. [L. restagnatio an inundation.] Stagnation. [Obs.]

restant.c: Restant Res"tant (rĕs"taint), a. [L. restans, p. pr. of restare: cf. F. restant. See Rest remainder.] (Bot.) Persistent.

restate.c: Restate Re*state" (rē*stāt"), v. t. To state anew. Palfrey.

restaurant.c: Restaurant Res"tau*rant (rĕs"to*rȧnt; 277), n. [F., fr. restaurer. See Restore.] An eating house.

restaurate.c: Restaurate Res"tau*rate (r?s"t?*r?t), v. t. [L. restauratus, p. p. of restaurare. See Restore.] To restore. [Obs.]

restaurateur.c: Restaurateur ‖Re`stau`ra`teur" (ra`stō`rȧ`tẽr"), n. [F.] The keeper of an eating house or a restaurant.

restauration.c: Restauration Res`tau*ra"tion (r?s`t?*r?"sh?n), n. [LL. restauratio: cf. F. restauration.] Restoration. [Obs.] Cower.

restem.c: Restem Re*stem" (re*stĕm"), v. t. 1. To force back against the current; as, to restem their backward course. Shak.

restful.c: Restful Rest"ful (r?st"f?l), a. 1. Being at rest; quiet. Shak.

restharrow.c: Rest-harrow Rest"-har`row (-h?r`r?), n. (Bot.) A European leguminous plant (Ononis arvensis) with long, tough roots.

restiff.c: Restiff Rest"iff, n. A restive or stubborn horse. [Obs.]

restiform.c: Restiform Res"ti*form (rĕs"tĭ*fôrm), a.[L. restis rope + -form.] (Anat.) Formed like a rope; -- applied especially to several ropelike bundles or masses of fibers on the dorsal side of the medulla oblongata.

restily.c: Restily Rest"i*ly (rĕst"ĭ*ly̆), adv. In a resty manner. [Obs.]

restinction.c: Restinction Re*stinc"tion (r?*st?nk"sh?n), n.[L. restinctio. See Restinguish.] Act of quenching or extingishing. [Obs.]

restiness.c: Restiness Rest"i*ness (r?st`ĭ*n?s), n. The quality or state of being resty; sluggishness. [Obs.]

resting.c: Resting Rest"ing, a. & n. from Rest, v. t. & i.

restinguish.c: Restinguish Re*stin"guish (r?*st?n"gw?sh), v. t. [L. restinquere, restinctum; pref. re- re- + stinquere to quench.] To quench or extinguish. [Obs.] R. Field.

restitute.c: Restitute Res"ti*tute (r?s"t?*t?t), v. t. [L. restitutus, p. p. of restituere; pref. re- re- + statuere to put, place. See Statute.] To restore to a former state. [R.] Dyer.
Restitute Res"ti*tute, n. That which is restored or offered in place of something; a substitute. [R.]

restitution.c: Restitution Res`ti*tu"tion (r?s`t?*t?"sh?n), n. [F. restitution, L. restitutio. See Restitute, v.] 1. The act of restoring anything to its rightful owner, or of making good, or of giving an equivalent for any loss, damage, or injury; indemnification.

restitutor.c: Restitutor Res"ti*tu`tor (r?s"t?*t?`t?r), n. [L.: cf. F. restituteur.] One who makes restitution. [R].

restive.c: Restive Rest"ive (r?st"?v), a. [OF. restif, F. rétif, fr. L. restare to stay back, withstand, resist. See Rest remainder, and cf. Restiff.]. Unwilling to go on; obstinate in refusing to move forward; stubborn; drawing back.

restless.c: Restless Rest"less, a. [AS. restleás.] 1. Never resting; unquiet; uneasy; continually moving; as, a restless child. Chaucer. “Restless revolution day by day.” Milton.

restorable.c: Restorable Re*stor"a*ble (r?*st?r"?*b'l), a. Admitting of being restored; capable of being reclaimed; as, restorable land. Swift. -- Re*stor"a*ble*ness, n.

restoration.c: Restoration Res`to*ra"tion (r?s`t?*r?"sh?n), n. [OE. restauracion, F. restauration, fr. L. restauratio. See Restore.] 1. The act of restoring or bringing back to a former place, station, or condition; the fact of being restored; renewal; reestablishment; as, the restoration of friendship between enemies; the restoration of peace after war.

restorationism.c: Restorationism Res`to*ra"tion*ism (-?z'm), n. The belief or doctrines of the Restorationists.

restorationist.c: Restorationist Res`to*ra"tion*ist, n. One who believes in a temporary future punishment and a final restoration of all to the favor and presence of God; a Universalist.

restorative.c: Restorative Re*stor"a*tive (r?*st?r"?*t?v), a. [Cf. F. restoratif.] Of or pertaining to restoration; having power to restore.
Restorative Re*stor"a*tive, n. Something which serves to restore; especially, a restorative medicine. Arbuthnot.

restoratively.c: Restoratively Re*stor"a*tive*ly, adv. In a restorative manner.

restore.c: Re-store Re-store" (rē*stōr"), v. t. [Pref. re- + store.] To store again; as, the goods taken out were re-stored.

Restore Re*store" (re*stōr"), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Restored (re*stōrd"); p. pr. & vb. n. Restoring.] [OE. restoren, OF. restorer, F. restaurer, fr. L. restaurare; pref. re- re- + an unused word; cf. Gr. stayro`s an upright pale or stake, Skr. sthāvara fixed, firm. Cf. Restaurant, Store.] To bring back to its former state; to bring back from a state of ruin, decay, disease, or the like; to repair; to renew; to recover. “To restore and to build Jerusalem.” Dan. ix. 25.

restorer.c: Restorer Re*stor"er (?), n. One who, or that which, restores.

restrain.c: Restrain Re*strain" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Restrained (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Restraining.] [OE. restreinen, F. restreindre, fr. L. restringere, restrictum; pref. re- re- + stringere to draw, bind, or press together. See Strain, v. t., and cf. Restrict.] 1. To draw back again; to hold back from acting, proceeding, or advancing, either by physical or moral force, or by any interposing obstacle; to repress or suppress; to keep down; to curb.

restrainable.c: Restrainable Re*strain"a*ble (?), a. Capable of being restrained; controllable. Sir T. Browne.

restrainer.c: Restrainer Re*strain"er (?), n. One who, or that which, restrains.

restrainment.c: Restrainment Re*strain"ment (?), n. The act of restraining.

restraint.c: Restraint Re*straint" (?), n. [OF. restraincte, fr. restrainct, F. restreint, p. p. of restraindre, restrendre. See Restrain.] 1. The act or process of restraining, or of holding back or hindering from motion or action, in any manner; hindrance of the will, or of any action, physical or mental.

restrengthen.c: Restrengthen Re*strength"en (?), v. t. To strengthen again; to fortify anew.

restrict.c: Restrict Re*strict" (?), a. [L. restrictus, p. p. of restringere. See Restrain.] Restricted. [Obs.]

Restrict Re*strict", v. t. [imp. & p. p. Restricted; p. pr. & vb. n. Restricting.] To restrain within bounds; to limit; to confine; as, to restrict worlds to a particular meaning; to restrict a patient to a certain diet.

restriction.c: Restriction Re*stric"tion (?), n. [F. restriction, L. restrictio.] 1. The act of restricting, or state of being restricted; confinement within limits or bounds.

restringe.c: Restringe Re*stringe" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Restringed (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Restringing (?).] [L. restringere. See Restrain.] To confine; to contract; to stringe. [Obs.]

restringency.c: Restringency Re*strin"gen*cy (?), n. Quality or state of being restringent; astringency. [Obs.] Sir W. Petty.

restringent.c: Restringent Re*strin"gent (?), a. [L. restringens, p. pr.: cf. F. restringent.] Restringing; astringent; styptic. [Obs.] -- n. A restringent medicine. [Obs.] Harvey.

restrive.c: Restrive Re*strive" (?), v. i. To strive anew.

resty.c: Resty Rest"y (?), a. Disposed to rest; indisposed toexercton; sluggish; also, restive. [Obs.] Burton.

resublime.c: Resublime Re`sub*lime" (?), v. t. To sublime again. Newton. -- Re*sub`li*ma"tion (#), n.

resudation.c: Resudation Re`su*da"tion (?), n. [L. resudare to sweat again. See Sudation.] Act of sweating again.

result.c: Result Re*sult" (?), v. i. [imp. & p. p. Resulted; p. pr. & vb. n. Resulting.] [F. résulter, fr. L. resultare, resultarum, to spring or leap back, v. intens. fr. resilire. See Resile.] 1. To leap back; to rebound. [Obs.]
Result Re*sult" (?), n. 1. A flying back; resilience. [Obs.]

resultance.c: Resultance Re*sult"ance (?), n. The act of resulting; that which results; a result. Donne.

resultant.c: Resultant Re*sult"ant (?), a. [L. resultans, p. pr.: cf. F. résultant.] Resulting or issuing from a combination; existing or following as a result or consequence.
Resultant Re*sult"ant, n. That which results. Specifically: (a) (Mech.) A reultant force or motion. (b) (Math.) An eliminant.

resultate.c: Resultate Re*sult"ate (?), n. [L. resultatus, p. p. ] A result. [Obs.] “The resultate of their counsil.” BAcon.

resultful.c: Resultful Re*sult"ful (?), a. HAving results or effects.

resultless.c: Resultless Re*sult"less, a. Being without result; as, resultless investigations.

resumable.c: Resumable Re*sum"a*ble (?), a. Capable of, or admitting of, being resumed. Sir M. Hale.

resume.c: Resume ‖Ré`su"mé" (?), n. [F. See Resume.] A summing up; a condensed statement; an abridgment or brief recapitulation.
Resume Re*sume" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Resumed (?);p. pr. & vb. n. Resuming.] [L. resumere, resumptum; pref. re- re- + sumere to take: cf. F. résumer. See Assume, Redeem.] 1. To take back.

resummon.c: Resummon Re*sum"mon (?), v. t. To summon again.

resumption.c: Resumption Re*sump"tion (?), n. [cf. F. résumption, L. resumptio restoration, recovery, fr. resumere. See Resume.] 1. The act of resuming; as, the resumption of a grant, of delegated powers, of an argument, of specie payments, etc.

resumptive.c: Resumptive Re*sump"tive (?), a. [cf. L. resumptivus restorative.] Taking back; resuming, or tending toward resumption; as, resumptive measures.

resupinate.c: Resupinate Re*su"pi*nate (?), a. [L. resupinatus, p. p. of resupinare to bend back. See Resupine.] Inverted in position; appearing to be upside down or reversed, as the flowers of the orchis and the leaves of some plants.

resupination.c: Resupination Re*su`pi*na"tion (?), n. The state of luing on the back; the state of being resupinate, or reversed.

resupine.c: Resupine Re`su*pine" (?), a. [L. resupinus; pref. re- re- + supinus bent backward, supine.] Lying on the back; supine; hence, careless. Sir K. Digby.

resupply.c: Resupply Re`sup*ply" (?), v. t. To supply again.

resurgence.c: Resurgence Re*sur"gence (?), n. The act of rising again; resurrection.

resurgent.c: Resurgent Re*sur"gent (?), a. [L. resurgens, -entis, p. pr. of resurgere. See Resurrection.] Rising again, as from the dead. Coleridge.
Resurgent Re*sur"gent, n. One who rises again, as from the dead. [R.] Sydney Smith.

resurrect.c: Resurrect Res`ur*rect" (?), v. t. [See Resurrection.] 1. To take from the grave; to disinter. [Slang]

resurrection.c: Resurrection Res`ur*rec"tion (?), n. [F. résurrection, L. resurrectio, fr. resurgere, resurrectum, to rise again; pref. re- re- + surgere to rise. See Source.] 1. A rising again; the resumption of vigor.

resurrectionist.c: Resurrectionist Res`ur*rec"tion*ist (?), n. One who steals bodies from the grave, as for dissection. [Slang]

resurrectionize.c: Resurrectionize Res`ur*rec"tion*ize (?), v. t. To raise from the dead. [R.] Southey.

resurvey.c: Resurvey Re`sur*vey" (?), v. t. To survey again or anew; to review. Shak.
Resurvey Re*sur"vey (?), n. A second or new survey.

resuscitable.c: Resuscitable Re*sus"ci*ta*ble (?), a. Capable of resuscitation; as, resuscitable plants. Boyle.

resuscitant.c: Resuscitant Re*sus"ci*tant (?), n. One who, or that which resuscitates. Also used adjectively.

resuscitate.c: Resuscitate Re*sus"ci*tate (?), a. [L. resuscitatus, p. p. of resuscitare; pref. re- re- + suscitare to raise, rouse. See Suscitate.] Restored to life. [R.] Bp. Gardiner.

Resuscitate Re*sus"ci*tate (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Resuscitated (?);p. pr. & vb. n. Resuscitating.] To revivify; to revive; especially, to recover or restore from apparent death; as, to resuscitate a drowned person; to resuscitate withered plants.
Resuscitate Re*sus"ci*tate, v. i. To come to life again; to revive.

resuscitation.c: Resuscitation Re*sus`ci*ta"tion (?), n. [L. resuscitatio.] The act of resuscitating, or state of being resuscitated.

resuscitative.c: Resuscitative Re*sus"ci*ta*tive (?), a. Tending to resuscitate; reviving; revivifying.

resuscitator.c: Resuscitator Re*sus"ci*ta`tor (?), n. [L.] 1. One who, or that which, resuscitates.

ret.c: Ret Ret (rĕt), v. t. See Aret. [Obs.] Chaucer.
Ret Ret, v. t. [Akin to rot.] To prepare for use, as flax, by separating the fibers from the woody part by process of soaking, macerating, and other treatment. Ure.

retable.c: Retable Re*ta"ble (re*tā"b'l), n. (Eccl.) A shelf behind the altar, for display of lights, vases of flowers, etc.

retail.c: Retail Re"tail (rē"tāl), n. [F. retaille piece cut off, shred, paring, or OF. retail, from retailler. See Retail, v.] The sale of commodities in small quantities or parcels; -- opposed to wholesale; sometimes, the sale of commodities at second hand.
Retail Re"tail, a. Done at retail; engaged in retailing commodities; as a retail trade; a retail grocer.

Retail Re*tail" (re*tāl"), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Retailed (?);p. pr. & vb. n. Retailing.] [Cf. F. retailler to cut again; pref. re- re + tailler to cut. See Retail, n., Tailor, and cf. Detail.] 1. To sell in small quantities, as by the single yard, pound, gallon, etc.; to sell directly to the consumer; as, to retail cloth or groceries.

retailer.c: Retailer Re*tail"er (?), n. One who retails anything; as, a retailer of merchandise; a retailer of gossip; -- used also of businesses, including large corporations; as, Sears, Roebuck is one the the country's largest retailers.

retailment.c: Retailment Re*tail"ment (?), n. The act of retailing.

retain.c: Retain Re*tain" (re*tān"), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Retained (re*tānd"); p. pr. & vb. n. Retaining.] [F. retainir, L. retinere; pref. re- re- + tenere to hold, keep. See Tenable, and cf. Rein of a bridle, Retention, Retinue.] 1. To continue to hold; to keep in possession; not to lose, part with, or dismiss; to restrain from departure, escape, or the like. “Thy shape invisible retain.” Shak.
Retain Re*tain", v. i. 1. To belong; to pertain. [Obs.]

retainable.c: Retainable Re*tain"a*ble (?), a. Capable of being retained.

retainal.c: Retainal Re*tain"al (?), n. The act of retaining; retention.

retainer.c: Retainer Re*tain"er (?), n. 1. One who, or that which, retains.

retainment.c: Retainment Re*tain"ment (?), n. The act of retaining; retention. Dr. H. More.

retake.c: Retake Re*take" (?), v. t. 1. To take or receive again.

retaker.c: Retaker Re*tak"er (?), n. One who takes again what has been taken; a recaptor. Kent.

retaliate.c: Retaliate Re*tal"i*ate (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Retaliated (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Retaliating.] [L. retaliatus, p. p. of retaliare to retaliate; pref. re- re- + a word akin to talio talion, retaliation. Cf. Talion.] To return the like for; to repay or requite by an act of the same kind; to return evil for (evil). [Now seldom used except in a bad sense.]
Retaliate Re*tal"i*ate, v. i. To return like for like; specifically, to return evil for evil; as, to retaliate upon an enemy.

retaliation.c: Retaliation Re*tal`i*a"tion (?), n. The act of retaliating, or of returning like for like; retribution; now, specifically, the return of evil for evil; e.g., an eye for an eye, a tooth for a tooth.

retaliatory.c: Retaliatory Re*tal"i*a*to*ry (?), a. Tending to, or involving, retaliation; retaliative; as retaliatory measures.

retard.c: Retard Re*tard" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Retarded; p. pr. & vb. n. Retarding.] [L. retardare, retardatum; pref. re- re- + tardare to make slow, to delay, fr. tardus slow: cf. F. retarder. See Tardy.] 1. To keep delaying; to continue to hinder; to prevent from progress; to render more slow in progress; to impede; to hinder; as, to retard the march of an army; to retard the motion of a ship; -- opposed to accelerate.
Retard Re*tard", v. i. To stay back. [Obs.] Sir. T. Browne.

retardation.c: Retardation Re`tar*da"tion (?), n. [L. retardatio: cf. F. retardation.] 1. The act of retarding; hindrance; the act of delaying; as, the retardation of the motion of a ship; -- opposed to acceleration.

retardative.c: Retardative Re*tard"a*tive (?), a. [Cf. F. retardatif.] Tending, or serving, to retard.

retarder.c: Retarder Re*tard"er (?), n. 1. One who, or that which, retards.

retardment.c: Retardment Re*tard"ment (?), n. [Cf. F. retardement.] The act of retarding; retardation. Cowley.

retch.c: Retch Retch (rĕch or rēch; 277), v. i. [imp. & p. p. Retched (rĕcht); p. pr. & vb. n. Retching.] [AS. hræcan to clear the throat, hawk, fr. hraca throat; akin to G. rachen, and perhaps to E. rack neck.] To make an effort to vomit; to strain, as in vomiting. [Written also reach.]
Retch Retch, v. t. & i. [See Reck.] To care for; to heed; to reck. [Obs.] Chaucer.

rete.c: Rete ‖Re"te (?), n. [L., a net.] (Anat.) A net or network; a plexus; particularly, a network of blood vessels or nerves, or a part resembling a network.

retecious.c: Retecious Re*te"cious (?), a. [L. rete a net.] Resembling network; retiform.

retection.c: Retection Re*tec"tion (?), n. [L. retegere, retectum, to uncover; pref. re- + tegere to cover.] Act of disclosing or uncovering something concealed. [Obs.] Boyle.

retell.c: Retell Re*tell (?), v. t. To tell again.

retene.c: Retene Ret"ene (?), n. [Gr.??? pine resin.] (Chem.) A white crystalline hydrocarbon, polymeric with benzene. It is extracted from pine tar, and is also found in certain fossil resins.

retent.c: Retent Re*tent" (?), n. [L. retentum, fr. retentus, p. p. See Retain.] That which is retained. Hickok.

retention.c: Retention Re*ten"tion (?), n. [L. retentio: cf. F. rétention. See Retain.] 1. The act of retaining, or the state of being ratined.

retentive.c: Retentive Re*ten"tive (?), a. [Cf. F. rétentif.] Having power to retain; as, a retentive memory.
Retentive Re*ten"tive, n. That which retains or confines; a restraint. [R.] Bp. Hall.

retentively.c: Retentively Re*ten"tive*ly, adv. In a retentive manner.

retentiveness.c: Retentiveness Re*ten"tive*ness, n. The quality of being retentive.

retentivity.c: Retentivity Re`ten*tiv"i*ty (?), n. The power of retaining; retentive force; as, the retentivity of a magnet.

retentor.c: Retentor ‖Re*ten"tor (?), n. [L., a retainer.] (Zool.) A muscle which serves to retain an organ or part in place, esp. when retracted. See Illust. of Phylactolemata.

retepore.c: Retepore Re`te*pore (?), n. [L. rete a net + porus pore.] (Zool.) Any one of several species of bryozoans of the genus Retepora. They form delicate calcareous corals, usually composed of thin fenestrated fronds.

retex.c: Retex Re*tex" (?), v. t. [L. retexere, lit., to unweave; pref. re- re + texere to weave. ] To annual, as orders. [Obs.] Bp. Hacket.

retexture.c: Retexture Re*tex"ture (?), n. The act of weaving or forming again. Carlyle.

rethor.c: Rethor Reth"or (?), n. [Cf. F. rhéteur. See Rhetor.] A rhetorician; a careful writer. [Obs.]

retiarius.c: Retiarius ‖Re`ti*a"ri*us (?), n. [L., fr. rete a net.] (Rom.Antiq.) A gladiator armed with a net for entangling his adversary and a trident for despatching him.

retiary.c: Retiary Re"ti*a*ry (?), n. [See Retiarius.] 1. (Zool.) Any spider which spins webs to catch its prey.

reticence.c: Reticence Ret"i*cence (?), n. [L. reticentia: cf. F. réticence.] 1. The quality or state of being reticent, or keeping silence; the state of holding one's tonque; refraining to speak of that which is suggested; uncommunicativeness.

reticent.c: Reticent Ret"i*cent (?), a. [L. reticens, p. pr. of reticere to keep silence; re- + tacere to be silent. See Tacit.] Inclined to keep silent; reserved; uncommunicative.

reticle.c: Reticle Ret"i*cle (?), n. [See Reticule.] 1. A small net.

reticular.c: Reticular Re*tic"u*lar (?), a. [Cf. F. réticulaire. See Reticule.] 1. Having the form of a net, or of network; formed with interstices; retiform; as, reticular cartilage; a reticular leaf.

reticularia.c: Reticularia ‖Re*tic`u*la"ri*a (?), n. pl. [NL. See Reticular.] (Zool.) An extensive division of rhizopods in which the pseudopodia are more or less slender and coalesce at certain points, forming irregular meshes. It includes the shelled Foraminifera, together with some groups which lack a true shell.

reticularian.c: Reticularian Re*tic`u*la"ri*an (?), n. (Zool.). One of the Reticularia.

reticularly.c: Reticularly Re*tic"u*lar*ly, adv. In a reticular manner.

reticulated.c: Reticulated Reticulate { Re*tic"u*late (?), Re*tic"u*la`ted (?) }, a. [L. reticulatus. See Reticule.] 1. Resembling network; having the form or appearance of a net; netted; as, a reticulated structure.

reticulation.c: Reticulation Re*tic`u*la"tion (?), n. The quality or state of being reticulated, or netlike; that which is reticulated; network; an organization resembling a net.

reticule.c: Reticule Ret"i*cule (?), n.. [F. réticule, L. reticulum, dim. of rete a net. Cf.Retina, Reticle.] 1. A little bag, originally of network; a woman's workbag, or a little bag to be carried in the hand. De Quincey.

reticulose.c: Reticulose Re*tic"u*lose` (?), a. Forming a network; characterized by a reticulated sructure.

reticulum.c: Reticulum ‖Re*tic"u*lum (?), n.;pl. Reticula (#). [L. dim. of rete a net.] (Anat.) (a) The second stomach of ruminants, in which folds of the mucous membrane form hexagonal cells; -- also called the honeycomb stomach. (b) The neuroglia.

retiform.c: Retiform Ret"i*form (?), a. [L. rete a net + -form. cf. F. rétiforme.] Composed of crossing lines and interstices; reticular; netlike; as, the retiform coat of the eye.

retina.c: Retina Ret"i*na (?), n. [NL., from L. rete a net. Cf. Reticule.] (Anat.) The delicate membrane by which the back part of the globe of the eye is lined, and in which the fibers of the optic nerve terminate. See Eye.

retinaculum.c: Retinaculum ‖Ret`i*nac"u*lum (?), n.; pl. Retinacula (#). [L., a holdfast, a band. See Retain.] 1. (Anat.) (a) A connecting band; a fraenum; as, the retinacula of the ileocaecal and ileocolic valves. (b) One of the annular ligaments which hold the tendons close to the bones at the larger joints, as at the wrist and ankle.

retinal.c: Retinal Ret"i*nal (?), a. (Anat.) Of or pertaining to the retina.

retinalite.c: Retinalite Re*tin"a*lite (?), n. [Gr.???? resin + -lite.] (Min.) A translucent variety of serpentine, of a honey yellow or greenish yellow color, having a waxy resinlike luster.

retinasphaltum.c: Retinasphaltum Retinasphalt { Ret`in*as"phalt (?), ‖Ret`in*as*phal"tum (?), } n. [Gr.???? resin +????? asphalt.] (Min.) Retinite.

retinerved.c: Retinerved Ret"i*nerved` (?), a. [L. rete a net + E. nerve.] (Bot.) Having reticulated veins.

retineum.c: Retineum ‖Ret`i*ne"um (?), n.; pl. Retinea (#). [NL. See Retina.] (Zool.) That part of the eye of an invertebrate which corresponds in function with the retina of a vertebrate.

retinic.c: Retinic Re*tin"ic (?), a. [Gr.???? resin.] (Min. Chem.) Of or pertaining to resin; derived from resin; specifically, designating an acid found in certain fossil resins and hydrocarbons.

retinite.c: Retinite Ret"i*nite (?), n. [Gr.??? resin: cf. F. rétinite.] (Min.) An inflammable mineral resin, usually of a yellowish brown color, found in roundish masses, sometimes with coal.

retinitis.c: Retinitis Ret`i*ni"tis (?), n. [NL., fr. NL. & E. retina + -tis.] (Med.) Inflammation of the retina.

retinoid.c: Retinoid Ret"i*noid (?), a. [Gr.??? resin + -oid.] Resinlike, or resinform; resembling a resin without being such.

retinol.c: Retinol Ret"i*nol (?), n. [Gr.??? resin + L. oleum oil.] 1. (Chem.) A hydrocarbon oil C32H16, obtained by the distillation of resin, -- used as a solvent, as an antiseptic, and in printer's ink.

retinophora.c: Retinophora ‖Ret`i*noph"o*ra (?), n.; pl. Retiniphorae (#). [NL., fr. NL. & E. retina + Gr. fe`rein to bear.] (Zool.) One of group of two to four united cells which occupy the axial part of the ocelli, or ommatidia, of the eyes of invertebrates, and contain the terminal nerve fibrillae. See Illust. under Ommatidium.

retinophoral.c: Retinophoral Ret`i*noph"o*ral (?), a. (Zool.) Of or pertaining to retinophorae.

retinoscopy.c: Retinoscopy Ret`i*nos"co*py (?), n. [Retina + -scopy.] (Physiol.) The study of the retina of the eye by means of the ophthalmoscope.

retinue.c: Retinue Ret"i*nue (?), n. [OE. retinue, OF. retinue, fr. retenir to retain, engage, hire. See Retain.] The body of retainers who follow a prince or other distinguished person; a train of attendants; a suite.

retinula.c: Retinula ‖Re*tin"u*la (?), n.; pl. Retinulae (#). [NL., dim. of NL. & E. retina.] (Zool.) One of the group of pigmented cells which surround the retinophorae of invertebrates. See Illust. under Ommatidium.

retinulate.c: Retinulate Re*tin"u*late (?), a. (Zool.) Having, or characterized by, retinul?.

retiped.c: Retiped Ret`i*ped (?), n. [L. rete a net + pes, pedis, a foot: cf. F. rétinopède.] (Zool.) A bird having small polygonal scales covering the tarsi.

retiracy.c: Retiracy Re*tir"a*cy (?), n. Retirement; -- mostly used in a jocose or burlesque way. [U.S.] Bartlett.

retirade.c: Retirade Ret`i*rade" (?), n. [F.; cf. Sp. retirada retreat. See Retire.] (Fort.) A kind of retrenchment, as in the body of a bastion, which may be disputed inch by inch after the defenses are dismantled. It usually consists of two faces which make a reentering angle.

retire.c: Retire Re*tire" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Retired (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Retiring.] [F. retirer; pref. re- re- + tirer to draw. See Tirade.] 1. To withdraw; to take away; -- sometimes used reflexively.

Retire Re*tire" (?), v. i. 1. To go back or return; to draw back or away; to keep aloof; to withdraw or retreat, as from observation; to go into privacy; as, to retire to his home; to retire from the world, or from notice.
Retire Re*tire", n. 1. The act of retiring, or the state of being retired; also, a place to which one retires. [Obs.]

retired.c: Retired Re*tired" (?), a. 1. Private; secluded; quiet; as, a retired life; a person of retired habits.

retirement.c: Retirement Re*tire"ment (?), n. [Cf. F. retirement.] 1. The act of retiring, or the state of being retired; withdrawal; seclusion; as, the retirement of an officer.

retiring.c: Retiring Re*tir"ing, a. 1. Reserved; shy; not forward or obtrusive; as, retiring modesty; retiring manners.

retistene.c: Retistene Ret"i*stene (?), n. (Chem.) A white crystalline hydrocarbon produced indirectly from retene.

retitelae.c: Retitelae ‖Ret`i*te"lae (?), n. pl. [NL., fr. rete a net + tela a web.] (Zool.) A group of spiders which spin irregular webs; -- called also Retitelariae.

retold.c: Retold Re*told" (?), imp. & p. p. of Retell.

retort.c: Retort Re*tort" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Retorted; p. pr. & vb. n. Retorting.] [L. retortus, p. p. of retorquere; pref. re- re- + torquere to turn twist. See Torsion, and cf. Retort, n., 2.] 1. To bend or curve back; as, a retorted line.
Retort Re*tort", v. i. To return an argument or a charge; to make a severe reply. Pope.
Retort Re*tort", n. [See Retort, v. t.] 1. The return of, or reply to, an argument, charge, censure, incivility, taunt, or witticism; a quick and witty or severe response.

retortion.c: Retortion Re*tor"tion (?), n. [Cf. F. rétorsion. See Retort, v. t.] 1. Act of retorting or throwing back; reflection or turning back. [Written also retorsion.]

retoss.c: Retoss Re*toss" (?), v. t. To toss back or again.

retouch.c: Retouch Re*touch" (?), v. t. [Pref. re- + touch: cf. F. retoucher.] 1. To touch again, or rework, in order to improve; to revise; as, to retouch a picture or an essay.
Retouch Re*touch", n. (Fine Arts) A partial reworking,as of a painting, a sculptor's clay model, or the like.

retrace.c: Retrace Re*trace" (?), v. t. [Pref. re- + trace: cf. F. retracer. Cf. Retract.] 1. To trace back, as a line.

retract.c: Retract Re*tract" (re*trākt"), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Retracted; p. pr. & vb. n. Retracting.] [F. rétracter, L. retractare, retractatum, to handle again, reconsider, retract, fr. retrahere, retractum, to draw back. See Retreat.] 1. To draw back; to draw up or shorten; as, the cat can retract its claws; to retract a muscle.
Retract Re*tract", v. i. 1. To draw back; to draw up; as, muscles retract after amputation.
Retract Re*tract", n. (Far.) The pricking of a horse's foot in nailing on a shoe.

retractable.c: Retractable Re*tract"a*ble (re*trākt"ȧ*b'l), a. [Cf. F. rétractable.] Capable of being retracted; retractile.

retractate.c: Retractate Re*tract"ate (re*trākt"āt), v. t. [L. retractatus, p. p. of retractare. See Retract.] To retract; to recant. [Obs.]

retractation.c: Retractation Re`trac*ta"tion (?), n. [Cf. F. rétractation, L. retractatio a revision, reconsideration. ] The act of retracting what has been said; recantation.

retractile.c: Retractile Re*tract"ile (re*trākt"ĭl), a. [Cf. F. -rétractile.] (Physiol.) Capable of retraction; capable of being drawn back or up; as, the claws of a cat are retractile.

retraction.c: Retraction Re*trac"tion (re*trāk"shŭn), n. [Cf. F. rétraction, L. retractio a drawing back, hesitation.] 1. The act of retracting, or drawing back; the state of being retracted; as, the retraction of a cat's claws.

retractive.c: Retractive Re*tract"ive (re*trākt"ĭv), a. Serving to retract; of the nature of a retraction. -- Re*tract"ive*ly, adv.
Retractive Re*tract"ive, n. That which retracts, or withdraws.

retractor.c: Retractor Re*tract"or (re*trākt"ẽr), n. One who, or that which, retracts. Specifically: (a) In breech-loading firearms, a device for withdrawing a cartridge shell from the barrel. (b) (Surg.) An instrument for holding apart the edges of a wound during amputation. (c) (Surg.) A bandage to protect the soft parts from injury by the saw during amputation. (d) (Anat. & Zool.) A muscle serving to draw in any organ or part. See Illust. under Phylactolaemata.

retrait.c: Retrait Re*trait" (re*trāt"), n. [It. ritratto, fr. ritrarre to draw back, draw, fr. L. retrahere. See Retract.] A portrait; a likeness. [Obs.]

retransform.c: Retransform Re`trans*form" (?), v. t. To transform anew or back. -- Re`trans*for*ma"tion (#), n.

retranslate.c: Retranslate Re`trans*late" (?), v. t. To translate anew; especially, to translate back into the original language.

retraxit.c: Retraxit ‖Re*trax"it (?), n. [L., (he) has withdrawn. See Retract.] (O. Eng. Law) The withdrawing, or open renunciation, of a suit in court by the plaintiff, by which he forever lost his right of action. Blackstone.

retread.c: Retread Re*tread" (?), v. t. & i. To tread again.

retreat.c: Retreat Re*treat" (?), n. [F. retraite, fr. retraire to withdraw, L. retrahere; pref. re- re- + trahere to draw. See Trace, and cf. Retract, Retrace.] 1. The act of retiring or withdrawing one's self, especially from what is dangerous or disagreeable.

Retreat Re*treat" (?), v. i. [imp. & p. p. Retreated; p. pr. & vb. n. Retreating.] To make a retreat; to retire from any position or place; to withdraw; as, the defeated army retreated from the field.

retreatful.c: Retreatful Re*treat"ful (?), a. Furnishing or serving as a retreat. [R.] “Our retreatful flood.” Chapman.

retreatment.c: Retreatment Re*treat"ment (?), n. The act of retreating; specifically, the Hegira. [R.] D'Urfey.

retrench.c: Retrench Re*trench" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Retrenched (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Retrenching.] [OF. retrenchier, F. retrancher; pref. re- re- + OF. trenchier, F. trancher, to cut. See Trench.] 1. To cut off; to pare away.
Retrench Re*trench", v. i. To cause or suffer retrenchment; specifically, to cut down living expenses; as, it is more reputable to retrench than to live embarrassed.

retrenchment.c: Retrenchment Re*trench"ment (?), n. [Cf. F. retrenchment.] 1. The act or process of retrenching; as, the retrenchment of words in a writing.

retrial.c: Retrial Re*tri"al (?), n. A secdond trial, experiment, or test; a second judicial trial, as of an accused person.

retribute.c: Retribute Re*trib"ute (?), v. t. [L. retributus, p. p. ofretribuere to retribute; pref re- + tribuere to bestow, assign, pay. See Tribute.] To pay back; to give in return, as payment, reward, or punishment; to requite; as, to retribute one for his kindness; to retribute just punishment to a criminal. [Obs. or R.] Locke.

retributer.c: Retributer Re*trib"u*ter (?), n. One who makes retribution.

retribution.c: Retribution Ret`ri*bu"tion (?), n. [L. retributio: cf. F. rétribution.] 1. The act of retributing; repayment.

retributory.c: Retributory Retributive { Re*trib"u*tive (?), Re*trib"u*to*ry }, a. [Cf. LL. retributorius worthy of retribution.] Of or pertaining to retribution; of the nature of retribution; involving retribution or repayment; as, retributive justice; retributory comforts.

retrievable.c: Retrievable Re*triev"a*ble (?), a. [From Retrieve.] That may be retrieved or recovered; admitting of retrieval. -- Re*triev"a*ble*ness, n. -- Re*triev"a*bly, adv.

retrieve.c: Retrieve Re*trieve" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Retrieved (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Retrieving.] [OE. retreven, OF. retrover to find again, recover (il retroevee finds again), F. retrouver; pref. re- re- + OF. trover to find, F. trouver. See Trover.] 1. To find again; to recover; to regain; to restore from loss or injury; as, to retrieve one's character; to retrieve independence.
Retrieve Re*trieve" (?), v. i. (Sport.) To discover and bring in game that has been killed or wounded; as, a dog naturally inclined to retrieve. Walsh.
Retrieve Re*trieve", n. 1. A seeking again; a discovery. [Obs.] B. Jonson.

retrim.c: Retrim Re*trim" (?), v. t. To trim again.

retro.c: Retro- Retro-. [L. retro, adv., backward, back. Cf. Re-.] A prefix or combining form signifying backward, back; as, retroact, to act backward; retrospect, a looking back.

retroact.c: Retroact Re`tro*act" (?), v. i. [Pref. retro- + act.] To act backward, or in return; to act in opposition; to be retrospective.

retroaction.c: Retroaction Re`tro*ac"tion (?), n. [Cf. F. rétroaction.] 1. Action returned, or action backward.

retroactive.c: Retroactive Re`tro*act"ive (?), a. [Cf. F. rétroactif.] Fitted or designed to retroact; operating by returned action; affecting what is past; retrospective. Beddoes.

retroactively.c: Retroactively Re`tro*act"ive*ly, adv. In a retroactive manner.

retrocede.c: Retrocede Re"tro*cede (?), v. t. [Pref. retro- + cede: cf. F. rétrocéder.] To cede or grant back; as, to retrocede a territory to a former proprietor.
Retrocede Re"tro*cede, v. i. [L. retrocedere; retro backward, back + cedere to go. See Cede.] To go back.

retrocedent.c: Retrocedent Re`tro*ced"ent (?), a. [L. retrocedens, p. pr.] Disposed or likely to retrocede; -- said of diseases which go from one part of the body to another, as the gout.

retrocession.c: Retrocession Re`tro*ces"sion (?), n. [Cf. F. rétrocession. See Retrocede.] 1. The act of retroceding.

retrochoir.c: Retrochoir Re"tro*choir (?), n. [Pref. retro- + choir.] (Eccl. Arch.) Any extension of a church behind the high altar, as a chapel; also, in an apsidal church, all the space beyond the line of the back or eastern face of the altar.

retrocopulant.c: Retrocopulant Re`tro*cop"u*lant (?), a. [See Retrocopulation.] Copulating backward, or from behind.

retrocopulation.c: Retrocopulation Re`tro*cop`u*la"tion (?), n. [Pref. retro- + copulation.] Copulation from behind. Sir T. Browne.

retroduction.c: Retroduction Re`tro*duc"tion (?), n. [L. retroducere, retroductum, to lead or bring back; retro backward + ducere to lead.] A leading or bringing back.

retroflexed.c: Retroflexed Retroflex { Re"tro*flex (?), Re"tro*flexed (?), } a. [Pref. retro- + L. flectere, flexum, to bend, to turn.] Reflexed; bent or turned abruptly backward.

retroflexion.c: Retroflexion Re`tro*flex"ion (?), n. The act of reflexing; the state of being retroflexed. Cf. Retroversion.

retrofracted.c: Retrofracted Retrofract { Re"tro*fract (?), Re"tro*fract`ed, } a. [Pref. retro- + L. fractus, p. p. of frangere to break.] (Bot.) Refracted; as, a retrofract stem.

retrogenerative.c: Retrogenerative Re`tro*gen"er*a*tive (?), a. [Pref. retro- + generative.] Begetting young by retrocopulation.

retrogradation.c: Retrogradation Re`tro*gra*da"tion (?), n. [F. rétrogradation or L. retrogradatio. See Retrograde.] 1. The act of retrograding, or moving backward.

retrograde.c: Retrograde Re"tro*grade (?), a. [L. retrogradus, from retrogradi, retrogressus, to retrograde; retro back + gradi to step: cf. F. rétrograde. See Grade.] 1. (Astron.) Apparently moving backward, and contrary to the succession of the signs, that is, from east to west, as a planet. Hutton.

Retrograde Re"tro*grade, v. i. [imp. & p. p. Retrograded (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Retrograding.] [L. retrogradare, retrogradi: cf. F. rétrograder.] 1. To go in a retrograde direction; to move, or appear to move, backward, as a planet.

retrogradingly.c: Retrogradingly Re"tro*gra`ding*ly (?), adv. By retrograding; so as to retrograde.

retrogress.c: Retrogress Re"tro*gress (?), n. [Cf. L. retrogressus.] Retrogression. [R.] H. Spenser.

retrogression.c: Retrogression Re`tro*gres"sion (?), n. [Cf. F. rétrogression. See Retrograde, and cf. Digression.] 1. The act of retrograding, or going backward; retrogradation.

retrogressive.c: Retrogressive Re`tro*gres"sive, a. [Cf. F. rétrogressif.] 1. Tending to retrograde; going or moving backward; declining from a better to a worse state.

retrogressively.c: Retrogressively Re`tro*gres"sive*ly, adv. In a retrogressive manner.

retromingency.c: Retromingency Re`tro*min"gen*cy (?), n. The quality or state of being retromingent. Sir T. Browne.
